text: “Send me back then this one word of sympathy, only sympathy, I swear to you; and oh! do not be angry with the audacity of despair, with the drowning man who has dared to make this last effort to save himself from perishing beneath the waters.

title: The Idiot
text: “This man assures me,” said Aglaya, scornfully, when the prince had finished reading the letter, “that the words ‘break off everything’ do not commit me to anything whatever; and himself gives me a written guarantee to that effect, in this letter. Observe how ingenuously he underlines certain words, and how crudely he glosses over his hidden thoughts. He must know that if he ‘broke off everything,’ first, by himself, and without telling me a word about it or having the slightest hope on my account, that in that case I should perhaps be able to change my opinion of him, and even accept his—friendship. He must know that, but his soul is such a wretched thing. He knows it and cannot make up his mind; he knows it and yet asks for guarantees. He cannot bring himself to trust, he wants me to give him hopes of myself before he lets go of his hundred thousand roubles. As to the ‘former word’ which he declares ‘lighted up the night of his life,’ he is simply an impudent liar; I merely pitied him once. But he is audacious and shameless. He immediately began to hope, at that very moment. I saw it. He has tried to catch me ever since; he is still fishing for me. Well, enough of this. Take the letter and give it back to him, as soon as you have left our house; not before, of course.”

title: The Idiot
text: “And what shall I tell him by way of answer?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Nothing—of course! That’s the best answer. Is it the case that you are going to live in his house?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, your father kindly recommended me to him.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Then look out for him, I warn you! He won’t forgive you easily, for taking back the letter.”

title: The Idiot
text: Aglaya pressed the prince’s hand and left the room.

title: The Idiot
text: Her face was serious and frowning; she did not even smile as she nodded good-bye to him at the door.

title: The Idiot
text: “I’ll just get my parcel and we’ll go,” said the prince to Gania, as he re-entered the drawing-room.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania stamped his foot with impatience.

title: The Idiot
text: His face looked dark and gloomy with rage.

title: The Idiot
text: At last they left the house behind them, the prince carrying his bundle.

title: The Idiot
text: “The answer—quick—the answer!” said Gania, the instant they were outside.

title: The Idiot
text: “What did she say?

title: The Idiot
text: Did you give the letter?

title: The Idiot
text: The prince silently held out the note.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania was struck motionless with amazement.

title: The Idiot
text: “How, what? my letter?” he cried.

title: The Idiot
text: “He never delivered it! I might have guessed it, oh! curse him! Of course she did not understand what I meant, naturally! Why—why—why didn’t you give her the note, you—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Excuse me; I was able to deliver it almost immediately after receiving your commission, and I gave it, too, just as you asked me to. It has come into my hands now because Aglaya Ivanovna has just returned it to me.”

title: The Idiot
text: “How? When?”

title: The Idiot
text: “As soon as I finished writing in her album for her, and when she asked me to come out of the room with her (you heard?), we went into the dining-room, and she gave me your letter to read, and then told me to return it.”

title: The Idiot
text: “To read?” cried Gania, almost at the top of his voice; “to read, and you read it?”

title: The Idiot
text: And again he stood like a log in the middle of the pavement; so amazed that his mouth remained open after the last word had left it.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, I have just read it.”

title: The Idiot
text: “And she gave it you to read herself—herself?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, herself; and you may believe me when I tell you that I would not have read it for anything without her permission.”

title: The Idiot
text: Gania was silent for a minute or two, as though thinking out some problem.

title: The Idiot
text: Suddenly he cried:

title: The Idiot
text: “It’s impossible, she cannot have given it to you to read! You are lying. You read it yourself!”

title: The Idiot
text: “I am telling you the truth,” said the prince in his former composed tone of voice; “and believe me, I am extremely sorry that the circumstance should have made such an unpleasant impression upon you!”

title: The Idiot
text: “But, you wretched man, at least she must have said something? There must be some answer from her!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, of course, she did say something!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Out with it then, damn it! Out with it at once!” and Gania stamped his foot twice on the pavement.

title: The Idiot
text: “As soon as I had finished reading it, she told me that you were fishing for her; that you wished to compromise her so far as to receive some hopes from her, trusting to which hopes you might break with the prospect of receiving a hundred thousand roubles. She said that if you had done this without bargaining with her, if you had broken with the money prospects without trying to force a guarantee out of her first, she might have been your friend. That’s all, I think. Oh no, when I asked her what I was to say, as I took the letter, she replied that ‘no answer is the best answer. I think that was it. Forgive me if I do not use her exact expressions. I tell you the sense as I understood it myself.”

title: The Idiot
text: Ungovernable rage and madness took entire possession of Gania, and his fury burst out without the least attempt at restraint.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh! that’s it, is it!” he yelled.

title: The Idiot
text: “She throws my letters out of the window, does she! Oh! and she does not condescend to bargain, while I do, eh? We shall see, we shall see! I shall pay her out for this.”

title: The Idiot
text: He twisted himself about with rage, and grew paler and paler; he shook his fist.

title: The Idiot
text: So the pair walked along a few steps.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania did not stand on ceremony with the prince; he behaved just as though he were alone in his room.

title: The Idiot
text: He clearly counted the latter as a nonentity.

title: The Idiot
text: But suddenly he seemed to have an idea, and recollected himself.

title: The Idiot
text: “But how was it?” he asked, “how was it that you (idiot that you are),” he added to himself, “were so very confidential a couple of hours after your first meeting with these people? How was that, eh?”

title: The Idiot
text: Up to this moment jealousy had not been one of his torments; now it suddenly gnawed at his heart.

title: The Idiot
text: “That is a thing I cannot undertake to explain,” replied the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania looked at him with angry contempt.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh! I suppose the present she wished to make to you, when she took you into the dining-room, was her confidence, eh?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I suppose that was it; I cannot explain it otherwise.”

title: The Idiot
text: “But why, why? Devil take it, what did you do in there? Why did they fancy you? Look here, can’t you remember exactly what you said to them, from the very beginning? Can’t you remember?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, we talked of a great many things. When first I went in we began to speak of Switzerland.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, the devil take Switzerland!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Then about executions.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Executions?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes—at least about one. Then I told the whole three years’ story of my life, and the history of a poor peasant girl—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, damn the peasant girl! go on, go on!” said Gania, impatiently.

title: The Idiot
text: “Then how Schneider told me about my childish nature, and—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, curse Schneider and his dirty opinions! Go on.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Then I began to talk about faces, at least about the expressions of faces, and said that Aglaya Ivanovna was nearly as lovely as Nastasia Philipovna. It was then I blurted out about the portrait—”

title: The Idiot
text: “But you didn’t repeat what you heard in the study? You didn’t repeat that—eh?”

title: The Idiot
text: “No, I tell you I did not.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Then how did they—look here! Did Aglaya show my letter to the old lady?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, there I can give you my fullest assurance that she did not. I was there all the while—she had no time to do it!”

title: The Idiot
text: “But perhaps you may not have observed it, oh, you damned idiot, you!” he shouted, quite beside himself with fury.

title: The Idiot
text: “You can’t even describe what went on.”

title: The Idiot
text: Gania having once descended to abuse, and receiving no check, very soon knew no bounds or limit to his licence, as is often the way in such cases.

title: The Idiot
text: His rage so blinded him that he had not even been able to detect that this “idiot,” whom he was abusing to such an extent, was very far from being slow of comprehension, and had a way of taking in an impression, and afterwards giving it out again, which was very un-idiotic indeed.

title: The Idiot
text: But something a little unforeseen now occurred.

title: The Idiot
text: “I think I ought to tell you, Gavrila Ardalionovitch,” said the prince, suddenly, “that though I once was so ill that I really was little better than an idiot, yet now I am almost recovered, and that, therefore, it is not altogether pleasant to be called an idiot to my face. Of course your anger is excusable, considering the treatment you have just experienced; but I must remind you that you have twice abused me rather rudely. I do not like this sort of thing, and especially so at the first time of meeting a man, and, therefore, as we happen to be at this moment standing at a crossroad, don’t you think we had better part, you to the left, homewards, and I to the right, here? I have twenty-five roubles, and I shall easily find a lodging.”

title: The Idiot
text: Gania was much confused, and blushed for shame “Do forgive me, prince!” he cried, suddenly changing his abusive tone for one of great courtesy.

title: The Idiot
text: “For Heaven’s sake, forgive me! You see what a miserable plight I am in, but you hardly know anything of the facts of the case as yet. If you did, I am sure you would forgive me, at least partially. Of course it was inexcusable of me, I know, but—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, dear me, I really do not require such profuse apologies,” replied the prince, hastily.

title: The Idiot
text: “I quite understand how unpleasant your position is, and that is what made you abuse me. So come along to your house, after all. I shall be delighted—”

title: The Idiot
text: “I am not going to let him go like this,” thought Gania, glancing angrily at the prince as they walked along.

title: The Idiot
text: “The fellow has sucked everything out of me, and now he takes off his mask—there’s something more than appears, here we shall see. It shall all be as clear as water by tonight, everything!”

title: The Idiot
text: But by this time they had reached Gania’s house.

title: The Idiot
text: The flat occupied by Gania and his family was on the third floor of the house.

title: The Idiot
text: It was reached by a clean light staircase, and consisted of seven rooms, a nice enough lodging, and one would have thought a little too good for a clerk on two thousand roubles a year.

title: The Idiot
text: But it was designed to accommodate a few lodgers on board terms, and had been taken a few months since, much to the disgust of Gania, at the urgent request of his mother and his sister, Varvara Ardalionovna, who longed to do something to increase the family income a little, and fixed their hopes upon letting lodgings.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania frowned upon the idea.

title: The Idiot
text: He thought it infra dig, and did not quite like appearing in society afterwards—that society in which he had been accustomed to pose up to now as a young man of rather brilliant prospects.

title: The Idiot
text: All these concessions and rebuffs of fortune, of late, had wounded his spirit severely, and his temper had become extremely irritable, his wrath being generally quite out of proportion to the cause.

title: The Idiot
text: But if he had made up his mind to put up with this sort of life for a while, it was only on the plain understanding with his inner self that he would very soon change it all, and have things as he chose again.

title: The Idiot
text: Yet the very means by which he hoped to make this change threatened to involve him in even greater difficulties than he had had before.

title: The Idiot
text: The flat was divided by a passage which led straight out of the entrance-hall.

title: The Idiot
text: Along one side of this corridor lay the three rooms which were designed for the accommodation of the “highly recommended” lodgers.

title: The Idiot
text: Besides these three rooms there was another small one at the end of the passage, close to the kitchen, which was allotted to General Ivolgin, the nominal master of the house, who slept on a wide sofa, and was obliged to pass into and out of his room through the kitchen, and up or down the back stairs.

title: The Idiot
text: Colia, Gania’s young brother, a school-boy of thirteen, shared this room with his father.

title: The Idiot
text: He, too, had to sleep on an old sofa, a narrow, uncomfortable thing with a torn rug over it; his chief duty being to look after his father, who needed to be watched more and more every day.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince was given the middle room of the three, the first being occupied by one Ferdishenko, while the third was empty.

title: The Idiot
text: But Gania first conducted the prince to the family apartments.

title: The Idiot
text: These consisted of a “salon,” which became the dining-room when required; a drawing-room, which was only a drawing-room in the morning, and became Gania’s study in the evening, and his bedroom at night; and lastly Nina Alexandrovna’s and Varvara’s bedroom, a small, close chamber which they shared together.

title: The Idiot
text: In a word, the whole place was confined, and a “tight fit” for the party.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania used to grind his teeth with rage over the state of affairs; though he was anxious to be dutiful and polite to his mother.

title: The Idiot
text: However, it was very soon apparent to anyone coming into the house, that Gania was the tyrant of the family.

title: The Idiot
text: Nina Alexandrovna and her daughter were both seated in the drawing-room, engaged in knitting, and talking to a visitor, Ivan Petrovitch Ptitsin.

title: The Idiot
text: The lady of the house appeared to be a woman of about fifty years of age, thin-faced, and with black lines under the eyes.

title: The Idiot
text: She looked ill and rather sad; but her face was a pleasant one for all that; and from the first word that fell from her lips, any stranger would at once conclude that she was of a serious and particularly sincere nature.

title: The Idiot
text: In spite of her sorrowful expression, she gave the idea of possessing considerable firmness and decision.

title: The Idiot
text: Her dress was modest and simple to a degree, dark and elderly in style; but both her face and appearance gave evidence that she had seen better days.

title: The Idiot
text: Varvara was a girl of some twenty-three summers, of middle height, thin, but possessing a face which, without being actually beautiful, had the rare quality of charm, and might fascinate even to the extent of passionate regard.

title: The Idiot
text: She was very like her mother: she even dressed like her, which proved that she had no taste for smart clothes.

title: The Idiot
text: The expression of her grey eyes was merry and gentle, when it was not, as lately, too full of thought and anxiety.

title: The Idiot
text: The same decision and firmness was to be observed in her face as in her mother’s, but her strength seemed to be more vigorous than that of Nina Alexandrovna.

title: The Idiot
text: She was subject to outbursts of temper, of which even her brother was a little afraid.

title: The Idiot
text: The present visitor, Ptitsin, was also afraid of her.

title: The Idiot
text: This was a young fellow of something under thirty, dressed plainly, but neatly.

title: The Idiot
text: His manners were good, but rather ponderously so.

title: The Idiot
text: His dark beard bore evidence to the fact that he was not in any government employ.

title: The Idiot
text: He could speak well, but preferred silence.

title: The Idiot
text: On the whole he made a decidedly agreeable impression.

title: The Idiot
text: He was clearly attracted by Varvara, and made no secret of his feelings.

title: The Idiot
text: She trusted him in a friendly way, but had not shown him any decided encouragement as yet, which fact did not quell his ardour in the least.

title: The Idiot
text: Nina Alexandrovna was very fond of him, and had grown quite confidential with him of late.

title: The Idiot
text: Ptitsin, as was well known, was engaged in the business of lending out money on good security, and at a good rate of interest.

title: The Idiot
text: He was a great friend of Gania’s.

title: The Idiot
text: After a formal introduction by Gania (who greeted his mother very shortly, took no notice of his sister, and immediately marched Ptitsin out of the room), Nina Alexandrovna addressed a few kind words to the prince and forthwith requested Colia, who had just appeared at the door, to show him to the “middle room.”

title: The Idiot
text: Colia was a nice-looking boy.

title: The Idiot
text: His expression was simple and confiding, and his manners were very polite and engaging.

title: The Idiot
text: “Where’s your luggage?” he asked, as he led the prince away to his room.

title: The Idiot
text: “I had a bundle; it’s in the entrance hall.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I’ll bring it you directly. We only have a cook and one maid, so I have to help as much as I can. Varia looks after things, generally, and loses her temper over it. Gania says you have only just arrived from Switzerland?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Is it jolly there?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Very.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Mountains?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I’ll go and get your bundle.”

title: The Idiot
text: Here Varvara joined them.

title: The Idiot
text: “The maid shall bring your bed-linen directly. Have you a portmanteau?”

title: The Idiot
text: “No; a bundle—your brother has just gone to the hall for it.”

title: The Idiot
text: “There’s nothing there except this,” said Colia, returning at this moment.

title: The Idiot
text: “Where did you put it?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh! but that’s all I have,” said the prince, taking it.

title: The Idiot
text: “Ah! I thought perhaps Ferdishenko had taken it.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Don’t talk nonsense,” said Varia, severely.

title: The Idiot
text: She seemed put out, and was only just polite with the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oho!” laughed the boy, “you can be nicer than that to me, you know—I’m not Ptitsin!”

title: The Idiot
text: “You ought to be whipped, Colia, you silly boy. If you want anything”

title: The Idiot
text: (to the prince)

title: The Idiot
text: “please apply to the servant. We dine at half-past four. You can take your dinner with us, or have it in your room, just as you please. Come along, Colia, don’t disturb the prince.”

title: The Idiot
text: At the door they met Gania coming in.

title: The Idiot
text: “Is father in?” he asked.

title: The Idiot
text: Colia whispered something in his ear and went out.

title: The Idiot
text: “Just a couple of words, prince, if you’ll excuse me. Don’t blab over there about what you may see here, or in this house as to all that about Aglaya and me, you know. Things are not altogether pleasant in this establishment—devil take it all! You’ll see. At all events keep your tongue to yourself for today.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I assure you I ‘blabbed’ a great deal less than you seem to suppose,” said the prince, with some annoyance.

title: The Idiot
text: Clearly the relations between Gania and himself were by no means improving.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh well; I caught it quite hot enough today, thanks to you. However, I forgive you.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I think you might fairly remember that I was not in any way bound, I had no reason to be silent about that portrait. You never asked me not to mention it.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Pfu! what a wretched room this is—dark, and the window looking into the yard. Your coming to our house is, in no respect, opportune. However, it’s not my affair. I don’t keep the lodgings.”

title: The Idiot
text: Ptitsin here looked in and beckoned to Gania, who hastily left the room, in spite of the fact that he had evidently wished to say something more and had only made the remark about the room to gain time.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince had hardly had time to wash and tidy himself a little when the door opened once more, and another figure appeared.

title: The Idiot
text: This was a gentleman of about thirty, tall, broad-shouldered, and red-haired; his face was red, too, and he possessed a pair of thick lips, a wide nose, small eyes, rather bloodshot, and with an ironical expression in them; as though he were perpetually winking at someone.

title: The Idiot
text: His whole appearance gave one the idea of impudence; his dress was shabby.

title: The Idiot
text: He opened the door just enough to let his head in.

title: The Idiot
text: His head remained so placed for a few seconds while he quietly scrutinized the room; the door then opened enough to admit his body; but still he did not enter.

title: The Idiot
text: He stood on the threshold and examined the prince carefully.

title: The Idiot
text: At last he gave the door a final shove, entered, approached the prince, took his hand and seated himself and the owner of the room on two chairs side by side.

title: The Idiot
text: “Ferdishenko,” he said, gazing intently and inquiringly into the prince’s eyes.

title: The Idiot
text: “Very well, what next?” said the latter, almost laughing in his face.

title: The Idiot
text: “A lodger here,” continued the other, staring as before.

title: The Idiot
text: “Do you wish to make acquaintance?” asked the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “Ah!” said the visitor, passing his fingers through his hair and sighing.

title: The Idiot
text: He then looked over to the other side of the room and around it.

title: The Idiot
text: “Got any money?” he asked, suddenly.

title: The Idiot
text: “Not much.”

title: The Idiot
text: “How much?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Twenty-five roubles.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Let’s see it.”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince took his banknote out and showed it to Ferdishenko.

title: The Idiot
text: The latter unfolded it and looked at it; then he turned it round and examined the other side; then he held it up to the light.

title: The Idiot
text: “How strange that it should have browned so,” he said, reflectively.

title: The Idiot
text: “These twenty-five rouble notes brown in a most extraordinary way, while other notes often grow paler. Take it.”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince took his note.

title: The Idiot
text: Ferdishenko rose.

title: The Idiot
text: “I came here to warn you,” he said.

title: The Idiot
text: “In the first place, don’t lend me any money, for I shall certainly ask you to.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Very well.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Shall you pay here?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, I intend to.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh! I don’t intend to. Thanks. I live here, next door to you; you noticed a room, did you? Don’t come to me very often; I shall see you here quite often enough. Have you seen the general?”

title: The Idiot
text: “No.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Nor heard him?”

title: The Idiot
text: “No; of course not.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, you’ll both hear and see him soon; he even tries to borrow money from me. Avis au lecteur. Good-bye; do you think a man can possibly live with a name like Ferdishenko?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Why not?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Good-bye.”

title: The Idiot
text: And so he departed.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince found out afterwards that this gentleman made it his business to amaze people with his originality and wit, but that it did not as a rule “come off.

title: The Idiot
text: He even produced a bad impression on some people, which grieved him sorely; but he did not change his ways for all that.

title: The Idiot
text: As he went out of the prince’s room, he collided with yet another visitor coming in.

title: The Idiot
text: Ferdishenko took the opportunity of making several warning gestures to the prince from behind the new arrival’s back, and left the room in conscious pride.

title: The Idiot
text: This next arrival was a tall red-faced man of about fifty-five, with greyish hair and whiskers, and large eyes which stood out of their sockets.

title: The Idiot
text: His appearance would have been distinguished had it not been that he gave the idea of being rather dirty.

title: The Idiot
text: He was dressed in an old coat, and he smelled of vodka when he came near.

title: The Idiot
text: His walk was effective, and he clearly did his best to appear dignified, and to impress people by his manner.

title: The Idiot
text: This gentleman now approached the prince slowly, and with a most courteous smile; silently took his hand and held it in his own, as he examined the prince’s features as though searching for familiar traits therein.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘Tis he, ‘tis he!” he said at last, quietly, but with much solemnity.

title: The Idiot
text: “As though he were alive once more. I heard the familiar name—the dear familiar name—and, oh! how it reminded me of the irrevocable past—Prince Muishkin, I believe?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Exactly so.”

title: The Idiot
text: “General Ivolgin—retired and unfortunate. May I ask your Christian and generic names?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Lef Nicolaievitch.”

title: The Idiot
text: “So, so—the son of my old, I may say my childhood’s friend, Nicolai Petrovitch.”

title: The Idiot
text: “My father’s name was Nicolai Lvovitch.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Lvovitch,” repeated the general without the slightest haste, and with perfect confidence, just as though he had not committed himself the least in the world, but merely made a little slip of the tongue.

title: The Idiot
text: He sat down, and taking the prince’s hand, drew him to a seat next to himself.

title: The Idiot
text: “I carried you in my arms as a baby,” he observed.

title: The Idiot
text: “Really?” asked the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “Why, it’s twenty years since my father died.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, yes—twenty years and three months. We were educated together; I went straight into the army, and he—”

title: The Idiot
text: “My father went into the army, too. He was a sub-lieutenant in the Vasiliefsky regiment.”

title: The Idiot
text: “No, sir—in the Bielomirsky; he changed into the latter shortly before his death. I was at his bedside when he died, and gave him my blessing for eternity. Your mother—”

title: The Idiot
text: The general paused, as though overcome with emotion.

title: The Idiot
text: “She died a few months later, from a cold,” said the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, not cold—believe an old man—not from a cold, but from grief for her prince. Oh—your mother, your mother! heigh-ho! Youth—youth! Your father and I—old friends as we were—nearly murdered each other for her sake.”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince began to be a little incredulous.

title: The Idiot
text: “I was passionately in love with her when she was engaged—engaged to my friend. The prince noticed the fact and was furious. He came and woke me at seven o’clock one morning. I rise and dress in amazement; silence on both sides. I understand it all. He takes a couple of pistols out of his pocket—across a handkerchief—without witnesses. Why invite witnesses when both of us would be walking in eternity in a couple of minutes? The pistols are loaded; we stretch the handkerchief and stand opposite one another. We aim the pistols at each other’s hearts. Suddenly tears start to our eyes, our hands shake; we weep, we embrace—the battle is one of self-sacrifice now!
