text: “That’s the sort of woman for me! Which of you would think of doing a thing like that, you blackguards, eh?” he yelled.

title: The Idiot
text: He was hopelessly and wildly beside himself with ecstasy.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince watched the whole scene, silent and dejected.

title: The Idiot
text: “I’ll pull it out with my teeth for one thousand,” said Ferdishenko.

title: The Idiot
text: “So would I,” said another, from behind, “with pleasure. Devil take the thing!” he added, in a tempest of despair, “it will all be burnt up in a minute—It’s burning, it’s burning!”

title: The Idiot
text: “It’s burning, it’s burning!” cried all, thronging nearer and nearer to the fire in their excitement.

title: The Idiot
text: “Gania, don’t be a fool! I tell you for the last time.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Get on, quick!” shrieked Ferdishenko, rushing wildly up to Gania, and trying to drag him to the fire by the sleeve of his coat.

title: The Idiot
text: “Get it, you dummy, it’s burning away fast! Oh—damn the thing!”

title: The Idiot
text: Gania hurled Ferdishenko from him; then he turned sharp round and made for the door.

title: The Idiot
text: But he had not gone a couple of steps when he tottered and fell to the ground.

title: The Idiot
text: “He’s fainted!” the cry went round.

title: The Idiot
text: “And the money’s burning still,” Lebedeff lamented.

title: The Idiot
text: “Burning for nothing,” shouted others.

title: The Idiot
text: “Katia-Pasha! Bring him some water!” cried Nastasia Philipovna.

title: The Idiot
text: Then she took the tongs and fished out the packet.

title: The Idiot
text: Nearly the whole of the outer covering was burned away, but it was soon evident that the contents were hardly touched.

title: The Idiot
text: The packet had been wrapped in a threefold covering of newspaper, and the notes were safe.

title: The Idiot
text: All breathed more freely.

title: The Idiot
text: “Some dirty little thousand or so may be touched,” said Lebedeff, immensely relieved, “but there’s very little harm done, after all.”

title: The Idiot
text: “It’s all his—the whole packet is for him, do you hear—all of you?” cried Nastasia Philipovna, placing the packet by the side of Gania.

title: The Idiot
text: “He restrained himself, and didn’t go after it; so his self-respect is greater than his thirst for money. All right—he’ll come to directly—he must have the packet or he’ll cut his throat afterwards. There! He’s coming to himself. General, Totski, all of you, did you hear me? The money is all Gania’s. I give it to him, fully conscious of my action, as recompense for—well, for anything he thinks best. Tell him so. Let it lie here beside him. Off we go, Rogojin! Goodbye, prince. I have seen a man for the first time in my life. Goodbye, Afanasy Ivanovitch—and thanks!”

title: The Idiot
text: The Rogojin gang followed their leader and Nastasia Philipovna to the entrance-hall, laughing and shouting and whistling.

title: The Idiot
text: In the hall the servants were waiting, and handed her her fur cloak.

title: The Idiot
text: Martha, the cook, ran in from the kitchen.

title: The Idiot
text: Nastasia kissed them all round.

title: The Idiot
text: “Are you really throwing us all over, little mother? Where, where are you going to? And on your birthday, too!” cried the four girls, crying over her and kissing her hands.

title: The Idiot
text: “I am going out into the world, Katia; perhaps I shall be a laundress. I don’t know. No more of Afanasy Ivanovitch, anyhow. Give him my respects. Don’t think badly of me, girls.”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince hurried down to the front gate where the party were settling into the troikas, all the bells tinkling a merry accompaniment the while.

title: The Idiot
text: The general caught him up on the stairs:

title: The Idiot
text: “Prince, prince!” he cried, seizing hold of his arm, “recollect yourself! Drop her, prince! You see what sort of a woman she is. I am speaking to you like a father.”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince glanced at him, but said nothing.

title: The Idiot
text: He shook himself free, and rushed on downstairs.

title: The Idiot
text: The general was just in time to see the prince take the first sledge he could get, and, giving the order to Ekaterinhof, start off in pursuit of the troikas.

title: The Idiot
text: Then the general’s fine grey horse dragged that worthy home, with some new thoughts, and some new hopes and calculations developing in his brain, and with the pearls in his pocket, for he had not forgotten to bring them along with him, being a man of business.

title: The Idiot
text: Amid his new thoughts and ideas there came, once or twice, the image of Nastasia Philipovna.

title: The Idiot
text: The general sighed.

title: The Idiot
text: “I’m sorry, really sorry,” he muttered.

title: The Idiot
text: “She’s a ruined woman. Mad! mad! However, the prince is not for Nastasia Philipovna now,—perhaps it’s as well.”

title: The Idiot
text: Two more of Nastasia’s guests, who walked a short distance together, indulged in high moral sentiments of a similar nature.

title: The Idiot
text: “Do you know, Totski, this is all very like what they say goes on among the Japanese?” said Ptitsin.

title: The Idiot
text: “The offended party there, they say, marches off to his insulter and says to him, ‘You insulted me, so I have come to rip myself open before your eyes;’ and with these words he does actually rip his stomach open before his enemy, and considers, doubtless, that he is having all possible and necessary satisfaction and revenge. There are strange characters in the world, sir!”

title: The Idiot
text: “H’m! and you think there was something of this sort here, do you? Dear me—a very remarkable comparison, you know! But you must have observed, my dear Ptitsin, that I did all I possibly could. I could do no more than I did. And you must admit that there are some rare qualities in this woman. I felt I could not speak in that Bedlam, or I should have been tempted to cry out, when she reproached me, that she herself was my best justification. Such a woman could make anyone forget all reason—everything! Even that moujik, Rogojin, you saw, brought her a hundred thousand roubles! Of course, all that happened tonight was ephemeral, fantastic, unseemly—yet it lacked neither colour nor originality. My God! What might not have been made of such a character combined with such beauty! Yet in spite of all efforts—in spite of all education, even—all those gifts are wasted! She is an uncut diamond.... I have often said so.”

title: The Idiot
text: And Afanasy Ivanovitch heaved a deep sigh.

title: The Idiot
text: Two days after the strange conclusion to Nastasia Philipovna’s birthday party, with the record of which we concluded the first part of this story, Prince Muishkin hurriedly left St. Petersburg for Moscow, in order to see after some business connected with the receipt of his unexpected fortune.

title: The Idiot
text: It was said that there were other reasons for his hurried departure; but as to this, and as to his movements in Moscow, and as to his prolonged absence from St. Petersburg, we are able to give very little information.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince was away for six months, and even those who were most interested in his destiny were able to pick up very little news about him all that while.

title: The Idiot
text: True, certain rumours did reach his friends, but these were both strange and rare, and each one contradicted the last.

title: The Idiot
text: Of course the Epanchin family was much interested in his movements, though he had not had time to bid them farewell before his departure.

title: The Idiot
text: The general, however, had had an opportunity of seeing him once or twice since the eventful evening, and had spoken very seriously with him; but though he had seen the prince, as I say, he told his family nothing about the circumstance.

title: The Idiot
text: In fact, for a month or so after his departure it was considered not the thing to mention the prince’s name in the Epanchin household.

title: The Idiot
text: Only Mrs. Epanchin, at the commencement of this period, had announced that she had been “cruelly mistaken in the prince!” and a day or two after, she had added, evidently alluding to him, but not mentioning his name, that it was an unalterable characteristic of hers to be mistaken in people.

title: The Idiot
text: Then once more, ten days later, after some passage of arms with one of her daughters, she had remarked sententiously.

title: The Idiot
text: “We have had enough of mistakes.

title: The Idiot
text: I shall be more careful in future!

title: The Idiot
text: However, it was impossible to avoid remarking that there was some sense of oppression in the household—something unspoken, but felt; something strained.

title: The Idiot
text: All the members of the family wore frowning looks.

title: The Idiot
text: The general was unusually busy; his family hardly ever saw him.

title: The Idiot
text: As to the girls, nothing was said openly, at all events; and probably very little in private.

title: The Idiot
text: They were proud damsels, and were not always perfectly confidential even among themselves.

title: The Idiot
text: But they understood each other thoroughly at the first word on all occasions; very often at the first glance, so that there was no need of much talking as a rule.

title: The Idiot
text: One fact, at least, would have been perfectly plain to an outsider, had any such person been on the spot; and that was, that the prince had made a very considerable impression upon the family, in spite of the fact that he had but once been inside the house, and then only for a short time.

title: The Idiot
text: Of course, if analyzed, this impression might have proved to be nothing more than a feeling of curiosity; but be it what it might, there it undoubtedly was.

title: The Idiot
text: Little by little, the rumours spread about town became lost in a maze of uncertainty.

title: The Idiot
text: It was said that some foolish young prince, name unknown, had suddenly come into possession of a gigantic fortune, and had married a French ballet dancer.

title: The Idiot
text: This was contradicted, and the rumour circulated that it was a young merchant who had come into the enormous fortune and married the great ballet dancer, and that at the wedding the drunken young fool had burned seventy thousand roubles at a candle out of pure bravado.

title: The Idiot
text: However, all these rumours soon died down, to which circumstance certain facts largely contributed.

title: The Idiot
text: For instance, the whole of the Rogojin troop had departed, with him at their head, for Moscow.

title: The Idiot
text: This was exactly a week after a dreadful orgy at the Ekaterinhof gardens, where Nastasia Philipovna had been present.

title: The Idiot
text: It became known that after this orgy Nastasia Philipovna had entirely disappeared, and that she had since been traced to Moscow; so that the exodus of the Rogojin band was found consistent with this report.

title: The Idiot
text: There were rumours current as to Gania, too; but circumstances soon contradicted these.

title: The Idiot
text: He had fallen seriously ill, and his illness precluded his appearance in society, and even at business, for over a month.

title: The Idiot
text: As soon as he had recovered, however, he threw up his situation in the public company under General Epanchin’s direction, for some unknown reason, and the post was given to another.

title: The Idiot
text: He never went near the Epanchins’ house at all, and was exceedingly irritable and depressed.

title: The Idiot
text: Varvara Ardalionovna married Ptitsin this winter, and it was said that the fact of Gania’s retirement from business was the ultimate cause of the marriage, since Gania was now not only unable to support his family, but even required help himself.

title: The Idiot
text: We may mention that Gania was no longer mentioned in the Epanchin household any more than the prince was; but that a certain circumstance in connection with the fatal evening at Nastasia’s house became known to the general, and, in fact, to all the family the very next day.

title: The Idiot
text: This fact was that Gania had come home that night, but had refused to go to bed.

title: The Idiot
text: He had awaited the prince’s return from Ekaterinhof with feverish impatience.

title: The Idiot
text: On the latter’s arrival, at six in the morning, Gania had gone to him in his room, bringing with him the singed packet of money, which he had insisted that the prince should return to Nastasia Philipovna without delay.

title: The Idiot
text: It was said that when Gania entered the prince’s room, he came with anything but friendly feelings, and in a condition of despair and misery; but that after a short conversation, he had stayed on for a couple of hours with him, sobbing continuously and bitterly the whole time.

title: The Idiot
text: They had parted upon terms of cordial friendship.

title: The Idiot
text: The Epanchins heard about this, as well as about the episode at Nastasia Philipovna’s.

title: The Idiot
text: It was strange, perhaps, that the facts should become so quickly, and fairly accurately, known.

title: The Idiot
text: As far as Gania was concerned, it might have been supposed that the news had come through Varvara Ardalionovna, who had suddenly become a frequent visitor of the Epanchin girls, greatly to their mother’s surprise.

title: The Idiot
text: But though Varvara had seen fit, for some reason, to make friends with them, it was not likely that she would have talked to them about her brother.

title: The Idiot
text: She had plenty of pride, in spite of the fact that in thus acting she was seeking intimacy with people who had practically shown her brother the door.

title: The Idiot
text: She and the Epanchin girls had been acquainted in childhood, although of late they had met but rarely.

title: The Idiot
text: Even now Varvara hardly ever appeared in the drawing-room, but would slip in by a back way.

title: The Idiot
text: Lizabetha Prokofievna, who disliked Varvara, although she had a great respect for her mother, was much annoyed by this sudden intimacy, and put it down to the general “contrariness” of her daughters, who were “always on the lookout for some new way of opposing her.

title: The Idiot
text: Nevertheless, Varvara continued her visits.

title: The Idiot
text: A month after Muishkin’s departure, Mrs. Epanchin received a letter from her old friend Princess Bielokonski (who had lately left for Moscow), which letter put her into the greatest good humour.

title: The Idiot
text: She did not divulge its contents either to her daughters or the general, but her conduct towards the former became affectionate in the extreme.

title: The Idiot
text: She even made some sort of confession to them, but they were unable to understand what it was about.

title: The Idiot
text: She actually relaxed towards the general a little—he had been long disgraced—and though she managed to quarrel with them all the next day, yet she soon came round, and from her general behaviour it was to be concluded that she had had good news of some sort, which she would like, but could not make up her mind, to disclose.

title: The Idiot
text: However, a week later she received another letter from the same source, and at last resolved to speak.

title: The Idiot
text: She solemnly announced that she had heard from old Princess Bielokonski, who had given her most comforting news about “that queer young prince.

title: The Idiot
text: Her friend had hunted him up, and found that all was going well with him.

title: The Idiot
text: He had since called in person upon her, making an extremely favourable impression, for the princess had received him each day since, and had introduced him into several good houses.

title: The Idiot
text: The girls could see that their mother concealed a great deal from them, and left out large pieces of the letter in reading it to them.

title: The Idiot
text: However, the ice was broken, and it suddenly became possible to mention the prince’s name again.

title: The Idiot
text: And again it became evident how very strong was the impression the young man had made in the household by his one visit there.

title: The Idiot
text: Mrs. Epanchin was surprised at the effect which the news from Moscow had upon the girls, and they were no less surprised that after solemnly remarking that her most striking characteristic was “being mistaken in people” she should have troubled to obtain for the prince the favour and protection of so powerful an old lady as the Princess Bielokonski.

title: The Idiot
text: As soon as the ice was thus broken, the general lost no time in showing that he, too, took the greatest interest in the subject.

title: The Idiot
text: He admitted that he was interested, but said that it was merely in the business side of the question.

title: The Idiot
text: It appeared that, in the interests of the prince, he had made arrangements in Moscow for a careful watch to be kept upon the prince’s business affairs, and especially upon Salaskin.

title: The Idiot
text: All that had been said as to the prince being an undoubted heir to a fortune turned out to be perfectly true; but the fortune proved to be much smaller than was at first reported.

title: The Idiot
text: The estate was considerably encumbered with debts; creditors turned up on all sides, and the prince, in spite of all advice and entreaty, insisted upon managing all matters of claim himself—which, of course, meant satisfying everybody all round, although half the claims were absolutely fraudulent.

title: The Idiot
text: Mrs. Epanchin confirmed all this.

title: The Idiot
text: She said the princess had written to much the same effect, and added that there was no curing a fool.

title: The Idiot
text: But it was plain, from her expression of face, how strongly she approved of this particular young fool’s doings.

title: The Idiot
text: In conclusion, the general observed that his wife took as great an interest in the prince as though he were her own son; and that she had commenced to be especially affectionate towards Aglaya was a self-evident fact.

title: The Idiot
text: All this caused the general to look grave and important.

title: The Idiot
text: But, alas! this agreeable state of affairs very soon changed once more.

title: The Idiot
text: A couple of weeks went by, and suddenly the general and his wife were once more gloomy and silent, and the ice was as firm as ever.

title: The Idiot
text: The fact was, the general, who had heard first, how Nastasia Philipovna had fled to Moscow and had been discovered there by Rogojin; that she had then disappeared once more, and been found again by Rogojin, and how after that she had almost promised to marry him, now received news that she had once more disappeared, almost on the very day fixed for her wedding, flying somewhere into the interior of Russia this time, and that Prince Muishkin had left all his affairs in the hands of Salaskin and disappeared also—but whether he was with Nastasia, or had only set off in search of her, was unknown.

title: The Idiot
text: Lizabetha Prokofievna received confirmatory news from the princess—and alas, two months after the prince’s first departure from St. Petersburg, darkness and mystery once more enveloped his whereabouts and actions, and in the Epanchin family the ice of silence once more formed over the subject.

title: The Idiot
text: Varia, however, informed the girls of what had happened, she having received the news from Ptitsin, who generally knew more than most people.

title: The Idiot
text: To make an end, we may say that there were many changes in the Epanchin household in the spring, so that it was not difficult to forget the prince, who sent no news of himself.

title: The Idiot
text: The Epanchin family had at last made up their minds to spend the summer abroad, all except the general, who could not waste time in “travelling for enjoyment,” of course.

title: The Idiot
text: This arrangement was brought about by the persistence of the girls, who insisted that they were never allowed to go abroad because their parents were too anxious to marry them off.

title: The Idiot
text: Perhaps their parents had at last come to the conclusion that husbands might be found abroad, and that a summer’s travel might bear fruit.

title: The Idiot
text: The marriage between Alexandra and Totski had been broken off.

title: The Idiot
text: Since the prince’s departure from St. Petersburg no more had been said about it; the subject had been dropped without ceremony, much to the joy of Mrs. General, who, announced that she was “ready to cross herself with both hands” in gratitude for the escape.

title: The Idiot
text: The general, however, regretted Totski for a long while.

title: The Idiot
text: “Such a fortune!” he sighed, “and such a good, easy-going fellow!”

title: The Idiot
text: After a time it became known that Totski had married a French marquise, and was to be carried off by her to Paris, and then to Brittany.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, well,” thought the general, “he’s lost to us for good, now.”

title: The Idiot
text: So the Epanchins prepared to depart for the summer.

title: The Idiot
text: But now another circumstance occurred, which changed all the plans once more, and again the intended journey was put off, much to the delight of the general and his spouse.

title: The Idiot
text: A certain Prince S—— arrived in St. Petersburg from Moscow, an eminent and honourable young man.

title: The Idiot
text: He was one of those active persons who always find some good work with which to employ themselves.

title: The Idiot
text: Without forcing himself upon the public notice, modest and unobtrusive, this young prince was concerned with much that happened in the world in general.

title: The Idiot
text: He had served, at first, in one of the civil departments, had then attended to matters connected with the local government of provincial towns, and had of late been a corresponding member of several important scientific societies.

title: The Idiot
text: He was a man of excellent family and solid means, about thirty-five years of age.

title: The Idiot
text: Prince S—— made the acquaintance of the general’s family, and Adelaida, the second girl, made a great impression upon him.

title: The Idiot
text: Towards the spring he proposed to her, and she accepted him.

title: The Idiot
text: The general and his wife were delighted.

title: The Idiot
text: The journey abroad was put off, and the wedding was fixed for a day not very distant.

title: The Idiot
text: The trip abroad might have been enjoyed later on by Mrs. Epanchin and her two remaining daughters, but for another circumstance.

title: The Idiot
text: It so happened that Prince S—— introduced a distant relation of his own into the Epanchin family—one Evgenie Pavlovitch, a young officer of about twenty-eight years of age, whose conquests among the ladies in Moscow had been proverbial.

title: The Idiot
text: This young gentleman no sooner set eyes on Aglaya than he became a frequent visitor at the house.

title: The Idiot
text: He was witty, well-educated, and extremely wealthy, as the general very soon discovered.

title: The Idiot
text: His past reputation was the only thing against him.

title: The Idiot
text: Nothing was said; there were not even any hints dropped; but still, it seemed better to the parents to say nothing more about going abroad this season, at all events.

title: The Idiot
text: Aglaya herself perhaps was of a different opinion.

title: The Idiot
text: All this happened just before the second appearance of our hero upon the scene.

title: The Idiot
text: By this time, to judge from appearances, poor Prince Muishkin had been quite forgotten in St. Petersburg.

title: The Idiot
text: If he had appeared suddenly among his acquaintances, he would have been received as one from the skies; but we must just glance at one more fact before we conclude this preface.

title: The Idiot
text: Colia Ivolgin, for some time after the prince’s departure, continued his old life.

title: The Idiot
text: That is, he went to school, looked after his father, helped Varia in the house, and ran her errands, and went frequently to see his friend, Hippolyte.

title: The Idiot
text: The lodgers had disappeared very quickly—Ferdishenko soon after the events at Nastasia Philipovna’s, while the prince went to Moscow, as we know.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania and his mother went to live with Varia and Ptitsin immediately after the latter’s wedding, while the general was housed in a debtor’s prison by reason of certain IOU’s given to the captain’s widow under the impression that they would never be formally used against him.

title: The Idiot
text: This unkind action much surprised poor Ardalion Alexandrovitch, the victim, as he called himself, of an “unbounded trust in the nobility of the human heart.”

title: The Idiot
text: When he signed those notes of hand he never dreamt that they would be a source of future trouble.

title: The Idiot
text: The event showed that he was mistaken.

title: The Idiot
text: “Trust in anyone after this! Have the least confidence in man or woman!” he cried in bitter tones, as he sat with his new friends in prison, and recounted to them his favourite stories of the siege of Kars, and the resuscitated soldier.

title: The Idiot
text: On the whole, he accommodated himself very well to his new position.

title: The Idiot
text: Ptitsin and Varia declared that he was in the right place, and Gania was of the same opinion.

title: The Idiot
text: The only person who deplored his fate was poor Nina Alexandrovna, who wept bitter tears over him, to the great surprise of her household, and, though always in feeble health, made a point of going to see him as often as possible.

title: The Idiot
text: Since the general’s “mishap,” as Colia called it, and the marriage of his sister, the boy had quietly possessed himself of far more freedom.

title: The Idiot
text: His relations saw little of him, for he rarely slept at home.

title: The Idiot
text: He made many new friends; and was moreover, a frequent visitor at the debtor’s prison, to which he invariably accompanied his mother.

title: The Idiot
text: Varia, who used to be always correcting him, never spoke to him now on the subject of his frequent absences, and the whole household was surprised to see Gania, in spite of his depression, on quite friendly terms with his brother.

title: The Idiot
text: This was something new, for Gania had been wont to look upon Colia as a kind of errand-boy, treating him with contempt, threatening to “pull his ears,” and in general driving him almost wild with irritation.

title: The Idiot
text: It seemed now that Gania really needed his brother, and the latter, for his part, felt as if he could forgive Gania much since he had returned the hundred thousand roubles offered to him by Nastasia Philipovna.

title: The Idiot
text: Three months after the departure of the prince, the Ivolgin family discovered that Colia had made acquaintance with the Epanchins, and was on very friendly terms with the daughters.

title: The Idiot
text: Varia heard of it first, though Colia had not asked her to introduce him.

title: The Idiot
text: Little by little the family grew quite fond of him.

title: The Idiot
text: Madame Epanchin at first looked on him with disdain, and received him coldly, but in a short time he grew to please her, because, as she said, he “was candid and no flatterer”—a very true description.

title: The Idiot
text: From the first he put himself on an equality with his new friends, and though he sometimes read newspapers and books to the mistress of the house, it was simply because he liked to be useful.

title: The Idiot
text: One day, however, he and Lizabetha Prokofievna quarrelled seriously about the “woman question,” in the course of a lively discussion on that burning subject.

title: The Idiot
text: He told her that she was a tyrant, and that he would never set foot in her house again.

title: The Idiot
text: It may seem incredible, but a day or two after, Madame Epanchin sent a servant with a note begging him to return, and Colia, without standing on his dignity, did so at once.

title: The Idiot
text: Aglaya was the only one of the family whose good graces he could not gain, and who always spoke to him haughtily, but it so happened that the boy one day succeeded in giving the proud maiden a surprise.

title: The Idiot
text: It was about Easter, when, taking advantage of a momentary tête-à-tête Colia handed Aglaya a letter, remarking that he “had orders to deliver it to her privately.

title: The Idiot
text: She stared at him in amazement, but he did not wait to hear what she had to say, and went out.

title: The Idiot
text: Aglaya broke the seal, and read as follows:

title: The Idiot
text: “Once you did me the honour of giving me your confidence.

title: The Idiot
text: Perhaps you have quite forgotten me now!

title: The Idiot
text: How is it that I am writing to you?

title: The Idiot
text: I do not know; but I am conscious of an irresistible desire to remind you of my existence, especially you.

title: The Idiot
text: How many times I have needed all three of you; but only you have dwelt always in my mind’s eye.

title: The Idiot
text: I need you—I need you very much.

title: The Idiot
text: I will not write about myself.

title: The Idiot
text: I have nothing to tell you.

title: The Idiot
text: But I long for you to be happy.

title: The Idiot
text: Are you happy?

title: The Idiot
text: That is all I wished to say to you—Your brother,

title: The Idiot
text: “Pr. L. Muishkin.”

title: The Idiot
text: On reading this short and disconnected note, Aglaya suddenly blushed all over, and became very thoughtful.

title: The Idiot
text: It would be difficult to describe her thoughts at that moment.

title: The Idiot
text: One of them was, “Shall I show it to anyone?

title: The Idiot
text: But she was ashamed to show it.

title: The Idiot
text: So she ended by hiding it in her table drawer, with a very strange, ironical smile upon her lips.

title: The Idiot
text: Next day, she took it out, and put it into a large book, as she usually did with papers which she wanted to be able to find easily.

title: The Idiot
text: She laughed when, about a week later, she happened to notice the name of the book, and saw that it was Don Quixote, but it would be difficult to say exactly why.

title: The Idiot
text: I cannot say, either, whether she showed the letter to her sisters.

title: The Idiot
text: But when she had read it herself once more, it suddenly struck her that surely that conceited boy, Colia, had not been the one chosen correspondent of the prince all this while.

title: The Idiot
text: She determined to ask him, and did so with an exaggerated show of carelessness.

title: The Idiot
text: He informed her haughtily that though he had given the prince his permanent address when the latter left town, and had offered his services, the prince had never before given him any commission to perform, nor had he written until the following lines arrived, with Aglaya’s letter.

title: The Idiot
text: Aglaya took the note, and read it.

title: The Idiot
text: “DEAR COLIA,—Please be so kind as to give the enclosed sealed letter to Aglaya Ivanovna.

title: The Idiot
text: Keep well—Ever your loving,

title: The Idiot
text: “Pr. L. Muishkin.”

title: The Idiot
text: “It seems absurd to trust a little pepper-box like you,” said Aglaya, as she returned the note, and walked past the “pepper-box” with an expression of great contempt.

title: The Idiot
text: This was more than Colia could bear.

title: The Idiot
text: He had actually borrowed Gania’s new green tie for the occasion, without saying why he wanted it, in order to impress her.

title: The Idiot
text: He was very deeply mortified.

title: The Idiot
text: It was the beginning of June, and for a whole week the weather in St. Petersburg had been magnificent.

title: The Idiot
text: The Epanchins had a luxurious country-house at Pavlofsk, [One of the fashionable summer resorts near St. Petersburg.] and to this spot Mrs. Epanchin determined to proceed without further delay.

title: The Idiot
text: In a couple of days all was ready, and the family had left town.

title: The Idiot
text: A day or two after this removal to Pavlofsk, Prince Muishkin arrived in St. Petersburg by the morning train from Moscow.

title: The Idiot
text: No one met him; but, as he stepped out of the carriage, he suddenly became aware of two strangely glowing eyes fixed upon him from among the crowd that met the train.

title: The Idiot
text: On endeavouring to re-discover the eyes, and see to whom they belonged, he could find nothing to guide him.

title: The Idiot
text: It must have been a hallucination.

title: The Idiot
text: But the disagreeable impression remained, and without this, the prince was sad and thoughtful already, and seemed to be much preoccupied.

title: The Idiot
text: His cab took him to a small and bad hotel near the Litaynaya.

title: The Idiot
text: Here he engaged a couple of rooms, dark and badly furnished.

title: The Idiot
text: He washed and changed, and hurriedly left the hotel again, as though anxious to waste no time.

title: The Idiot
text: Anyone who now saw him for the first time since he left Petersburg would judge that he had improved vastly so far as his exterior was concerned.

title: The Idiot
text: His clothes certainly were very different; they were more fashionable, perhaps even too much so, and anyone inclined to mockery might have found something to smile at in his appearance.

title: The Idiot
text: But what is there that people will not smile at?

title: The Idiot
text: The prince took a cab and drove to a street near the Nativity, where he soon discovered the house he was seeking.

title: The Idiot
text: It was a small wooden villa, and he was struck by its attractive and clean appearance; it stood in a pleasant little garden, full of flowers.

title: The Idiot
text: The windows looking on the street were open, and the sound of a voice, reading aloud or making a speech, came through them.

title: The Idiot
text: It rose at times to a shout, and was interrupted occasionally by bursts of laughter.

title: The Idiot
text: Prince Muishkin entered the court-yard, and ascended the steps.

title: The Idiot
text: A cook with her sleeves turned up to the elbows opened the door.

title: The Idiot
text: The visitor asked if Mr. Lebedeff were at home.

title: The Idiot
text: “He is in there,” said she, pointing to the salon.

title: The Idiot
text: The room had a blue wall-paper, and was well, almost pretentiously, furnished, with its round table, its divan, and its bronze clock under a glass shade.

title: The Idiot
text: There was a narrow pier-glass against the wall, and a chandelier adorned with lustres hung by a bronze chain from the ceiling.

title: The Idiot
text: When the prince entered, Lebedeff was standing in the middle of the room, his back to the door.

title: The Idiot
text: He was in his shirt-sleeves, on account of the extreme heat, and he seemed to have just reached the peroration of his speech, and was impressively beating his breast.

title: The Idiot
text: His audience consisted of a youth of about fifteen years of age with a clever face, who had a book in his hand, though he was not reading; a young lady of twenty, in deep mourning, stood near him with an infant in her arms; another girl of thirteen, also in black, was laughing loudly, her mouth wide open; and on the sofa lay a handsome young man, with black hair and eyes, and a suspicion of beard and whiskers.

title: The Idiot
text: He frequently interrupted the speaker and argued with him, to the great delight of the others.

title: The Idiot
text: “Lukian Timofeyovitch! Lukian Timofeyovitch! Here’s someone to see you! Look here!... a gentleman to speak to you!... Well, it’s not my fault!” and the cook turned and went away red with anger.

title: The Idiot
text: Lebedeff started, and at sight of the prince stood like a statue for a moment.

title: The Idiot
text: Then he moved up to him with an ingratiating smile, but stopped short again.

title: The Idiot
text: “Prince! ex-ex-excellency!” he stammered.

title: The Idiot
text: Then suddenly he ran towards the girl with the infant, a movement so unexpected by her that she staggered and fell back, but next moment he was threatening the other child, who was standing, still laughing, in the doorway.

title: The Idiot
text: She screamed, and ran towards the kitchen.

title: The Idiot
text: Lebedeff stamped his foot angrily; then, seeing the prince regarding him with amazement, he murmured apologetically—“Pardon to show respect!... he-he!”

title: The Idiot
text: “You are quite wrong...” began the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “At once... at once... in one moment!”

title: The Idiot
text: He rushed like a whirlwind from the room, and Muishkin looked inquiringly at the others.

title: The Idiot
text: They were all laughing, and the guest joined in the chorus.

title: The Idiot
text: “He has gone to get his coat,” said the boy.

title: The Idiot
text: “How annoying!” exclaimed the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “I thought... Tell me, is he...”

title: The Idiot
text: “You think he is drunk?” cried the young man on the sofa.

title: The Idiot
text: “Not in the least. He’s only had three or four small glasses, perhaps five; but what is that? The usual thing!”

title: The Idiot
text: As the prince opened his mouth to answer, he was interrupted by the girl, whose sweet face wore an expression of absolute frankness.

title: The Idiot
text: “He never drinks much in the morning; if you have come to talk business with him, do it now. It is the best time. He sometimes comes back drunk in the evening; but just now he passes the greater part of the evening in tears, and reads passages of Holy Scripture aloud, because our mother died five weeks ago.”

title: The Idiot
text: “No doubt he ran off because he did not know what to say to you,” said the youth on the divan.

title: The Idiot
text: “I bet he is trying to cheat you, and is thinking how best to do it.”

title: The Idiot
text: Just then Lebedeff returned, having put on his coat.

title: The Idiot
text: “Five weeks!” said he, wiping his eyes.

title: The Idiot
text: “Only five weeks! Poor orphans!”

title: The Idiot
text: “But why wear a coat in holes,” asked the girl, “when your new one is hanging behind the door? Did you not see it?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Hold your tongue, dragon-fly!” he scolded.

title: The Idiot
text: “What a plague you are!

title: The Idiot
text: He stamped his foot irritably, but she only laughed, and answered:

title: The Idiot
text: “Are you trying to frighten me? I am not Tania, you know, and I don’t intend to run away. Look, you are waking Lubotchka, and she will have convulsions again. Why do you shout like that?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, well! I won’t again,” said the master of the house, his anxiety getting the better of his temper.

title: The Idiot
text: He went up to his daughter, and looked at the child in her arms, anxiously making the sign of the cross over her three times.

title: The Idiot
text: “God bless her! God bless her!” he cried with emotion.

title: The Idiot
text: “This little creature is my daughter Luboff,” addressing the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “My wife, Helena, died—at her birth; and this is my big daughter Vera, in mourning, as you see; and this, this, oh, this,” pointing to the young man on the divan...

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, go on! never mind me!” mocked the other.

title: The Idiot
text: “Don’t be afraid!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Excellency! Have you read that account of the murder of the Zemarin family, in the newspaper?” cried Lebedeff, all of a sudden.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes,” said Muishkin, with some surprise.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, that is the murderer! It is he—in fact—”

title: The Idiot
text: “What do you mean?” asked the visitor.

title: The Idiot
text: “I am speaking allegorically, of course; but he will be the murderer of a Zemarin family in the future. He is getting ready. ...”

title: The Idiot
text: They all laughed, and the thought crossed the prince’s mind that perhaps Lebedeff was really trifling in this way because he foresaw inconvenient questions, and wanted to gain time.

title: The Idiot
text: “He is a traitor! a conspirator!” shouted Lebedeff, who seemed to have lost all control over himself.

title: The Idiot
text: “A monster! a slanderer! Ought I to treat him as a nephew, the son of my sister Anisia?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh! do be quiet! You must be drunk! He has taken it into his head to play the lawyer, prince, and he practices speechifying, and is always repeating his eloquent pleadings to his children. And who do you think was his last client? An old woman who had been robbed of five hundred roubles, her all, by some rogue of a usurer, besought him to take up her case, instead of which he defended the usurer himself, a Jew named Zeidler, because this Jew promised to give him fifty roubles....”

title: The Idiot
text: “It was to be fifty if I won the case, only five if I lost,” interrupted Lebedeff, speaking in a low tone, a great contrast to his earlier manner.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well! naturally he came to grief: the law is not administered as it used to be, and he only got laughed at for his pains. But he was much pleased with himself in spite of that. ‘Most learned judge!’ said he, ‘picture this unhappy man, crippled by age and infirmities, who gains his living by honourable toil—picture him, I repeat, robbed of his all, of his last mouthful; remember, I entreat you, the words of that learned legislator, “Let mercy and justice alike rule the courts of law. Now, would you believe it, excellency, every morning he recites this speech to us from beginning to end, exactly as he spoke it before the magistrate. To-day we have heard it for the fifth time. He was just starting again when you arrived, so much does he admire it. He is now preparing to undertake another case. I think, by the way, that you are Prince Muishkin? Colia tells me you are the cleverest man he has ever known....”

title: The Idiot
text: “The cleverest in the world,” interrupted his uncle hastily.

title: The Idiot
text: “I do not pay much attention to that opinion,” continued the young man calmly.

title: The Idiot
text: “Colia is very fond of you, but he,” pointing to Lebedeff, “is flattering you. I can assure you I have no intention of flattering you, or anyone else, but at least you have some common-sense. Well, will you judge between us? Shall we ask the prince to act as arbitrator?” he went on, addressing his uncle.

title: The Idiot
text: “I am so glad you chanced to come here, prince.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I agree,” said Lebedeff, firmly, looking round involuntarily at his daughter, who had come nearer, and was listening attentively to the conversation.

title: The Idiot
text: “What is it all about?” asked the prince, frowning.

title: The Idiot
text: His head ached, and he felt sure that Lebedeff was trying to cheat him in some way, and only talking to put off the explanation that he had come for.

title: The Idiot
text: “I will tell you all the story. I am his nephew; he did speak the truth there, although he is generally telling lies. I am at the University, and have not yet finished my course. I mean to do so, and I shall, for I have a determined character. I must, however, find something to do for the present, and therefore I have got employment on the railway at twenty-four roubles a month. I admit that my uncle has helped me once or twice before. Well, I had twenty roubles in my pocket, and I gambled them away. Can you believe that I should be so low, so base, as to lose money in that way?”

title: The Idiot
text: “And the man who won it is a rogue, a rogue whom you ought not to have paid!” cried Lebedeff.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, he is a rogue, but I was obliged to pay him,” said the young man.

title: The Idiot
text: “As to his being a rogue, he is assuredly that, and I am not saying it because he beat you. He is an ex-lieutenant, prince, dismissed from the service, a teacher of boxing, and one of Rogojin’s followers. They are all lounging about the pavements now that Rogojin has turned them off. Of course, the worst of it is that, knowing he was a rascal, and a card-sharper, I none the less played palki with him, and risked my last rouble. To tell the truth, I thought to myself, ‘If I lose, I will go to my uncle, and I am sure he will not refuse to help me. Now that was base—cowardly and base!”

title: The Idiot
text: “That is so,” observed Lebedeff quietly; “cowardly and base.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, wait a bit, before you begin to triumph,” said the nephew viciously; for the words seemed to irritate him.

title: The Idiot
text: “He is delighted! I came to him here and told him everything: I acted honourably, for I did not excuse myself. I spoke most severely of my conduct, as everyone here can witness. But I must smarten myself up before I take up my new post, for I am really like a tramp. Just look at my boots! I cannot possibly appear like this, and if I am not at the bureau at the time appointed, the job will be given to someone else; and I shall have to try for another. Now I only beg for fifteen roubles, and I give my word that I will never ask him for anything again. I am also ready to promise to repay my debt in three months’ time, and I will keep my word, even if I have to live on bread and water. My salary will amount to seventy-five roubles in three months. The sum I now ask, added to what I have borrowed already, will make a total of about thirty-five roubles, so you see I shall have enough to pay him and confound him! if he wants interest, he shall have that, too! Haven’t I always paid back the money he lent me before? Why should he be so mean now? He grudges my having paid that lieutenant; there can be no other reason! That’s the kind he is—a dog in the manger!”

title: The Idiot
text: “And he won’t go away!” cried Lebedeff.

title: The Idiot
text: “He has installed himself here, and here he remains!”

title: The Idiot
text: “I have told you already, that I will not go away until I have got what I ask. Why are you smiling, prince? You look as if you disapproved of me.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I am not smiling, but I really think you are in the wrong, somewhat,” replied Muishkin, reluctantly.

title: The Idiot
text: “Don’t shuffle! Say plainly that you think that I am quite wrong, without any ‘somewhat’! Why ‘somewhat’?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I will say you are quite wrong, if you wish.”

title: The Idiot
text: “If I wish! That’s good, I must say! Do you think I am deceived as to the flagrant impropriety of my conduct? I am quite aware that his money is his own, and that my action—is much like an attempt at extortion. But you-you don’t know what life is! If people don’t learn by experience, they never understand. They must be taught. My intentions are perfectly honest; on my conscience he will lose nothing, and I will pay back the money with interest. Added to which he has had the moral satisfaction of seeing me disgraced. What does he want more? and what is he good for if he never helps anyone? Look what he does himself! just ask him about his dealings with others, how he deceives people! How did he manage to buy this house? You may cut off my head if he has not let you in for something—and if he is not trying to cheat you again. You are smiling. You don’t believe me?”

title: The Idiot
text: “It seems to me that all this has nothing to do with your affairs,” remarked the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “I have lain here now for three days,” cried the young man without noticing, “and I have seen a lot! Fancy! he suspects his daughter, that angel, that orphan, my cousin—he suspects her, and every evening he searches her room, to see if she has a lover hidden in it! He comes here too on tiptoe, creeping softly—oh, so softly—and looks under the sofa—my bed, you know. He is mad with suspicion, and sees a thief in every corner. He runs about all night long; he was up at least seven times last night, to satisfy himself that the windows and doors were barred, and to peep into the oven. That man who appears in court for scoundrels, rushes in here in the night and prays, lying prostrate, banging his head on the ground by the half-hour—and for whom do you think he prays? Who are the sinners figuring in his drunken petitions? I have heard him with my own ears praying for the repose of the soul of the Countess du Barry! Colia heard it too. He is as mad as a March hare!”

title: The Idiot
text: “You hear how he slanders me, prince,” said Lebedeff, almost beside himself with rage.

title: The Idiot
text: “I may be a drunkard, an evil-doer, a thief, but at least I can say one thing for myself. He does not know—how should he, mocker that he is?—that when he came into the world it was I who washed him, and dressed him in his swathing-bands, for my sister Anisia had lost her husband, and was in great poverty. I was very little better off than she, but I sat up night after night with her, and nursed both mother and child; I used to go downstairs and steal wood for them from the house-porter. How often did I sing him to sleep when I was half dead with hunger! In short, I was more than a father to him, and now—now he jeers at me! Even if I did cross myself, and pray for the repose of the soul of the Comtesse du Barry, what does it matter? Three days ago, for the first time in my life, I read her biography in an historical dictionary. Do you know who she was? You there!” addressing his nephew.

title: The Idiot
text: “Speak! do you know?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Of course no one knows anything about her but you,” muttered the young man in a would-be jeering tone.

title: The Idiot
text: “She was a Countess who rose from shame to reign like a Queen. An Empress wrote to her, with her own hand, as ‘Ma chère cousine. At a lever-du-roi one morning (do you know what a lever-du-roi was?)—a Cardinal, a Papal legate, offered to put on her stockings; a high and holy person like that looked on it as an honour! Did you know this? I see by your expression that you did not! Well, how did she die? Answer!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh! do stop—you are too absurd!”

title: The Idiot
text: “This is how she died. After all this honour and glory, after having been almost a Queen, she was guillotined by that butcher, Samson. She was quite innocent, but it had to be done, for the satisfaction of the fishwives of Paris. She was so terrified, that she did not understand what was happening. But when Samson seized her head, and pushed her under the knife with his foot, she cried out: ‘Wait a moment! wait a moment, monsieur! Well, because of that moment of bitter suffering, perhaps the Saviour will pardon her other faults, for one cannot imagine a greater agony. As I read the story my heart bled for her. And what does it matter to you, little worm, if I implored the Divine mercy for her, great sinner as she was, as I said my evening prayer? I might have done it because I doubted if anyone had ever crossed himself for her sake before. It may be that in the other world she will rejoice to think that a sinner like herself has cried to heaven for the salvation of her soul. Why are you laughing? You believe nothing, atheist! And your story was not even correct! If you had listened to what I was saying, you would have heard that I did not only pray for the Comtesse du Barry. I said, ‘Oh Lord! give rest to the soul of that great sinner, the Comtesse du Barry, and to all unhappy ones like her. You see that is quite a different thing, for how many sinners there are, how many women, who have passed through the trials of this life, are now suffering and groaning in purgatory! I prayed for you, too, in spite of your insolence and impudence, also for your fellows, as it seems that you claim to know how I pray...”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh! that’s enough in all conscience! Pray for whom you choose, and the devil take them and you! We have a scholar here; you did not know that, prince?” he continued, with a sneer.

title: The Idiot
text: “He reads all sorts of books and memoirs now.”

title: The Idiot
text: “At any rate, your uncle has a kind heart,” remarked the prince, who really had to force himself to speak to the nephew, so much did he dislike him.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, now you are going to praise him! He will be set up! He puts his hand on his heart, and he is delighted! I never said he was a man without heart, but he is a rascal—that’s the pity of it. And then, he is addicted to drink, and his mind is unhinged, like that of most people who have taken more than is good for them for years. He loves his children—oh, I know that well enough! He respected my aunt, his late wife... and he even has a sort of affection for me. He has remembered me in his will.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I shall leave you nothing!” exclaimed his uncle angrily.

title: The Idiot
text: “Listen to me, Lebedeff,” said the prince in a decided voice, turning his back on the young man.

title: The Idiot
text: “I know by experience that when you choose, you can be business-like... I have very little time to spare, and if you... By the way—excuse me—what is your Christian name? I have forgotten it.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Ti-Ti-Timofey.”

title: The Idiot
text: “And?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Lukianovitch.”

title: The Idiot
text: Everyone in the room began to laugh.

title: The Idiot
text: “He is telling lies!” cried the nephew.

title: The Idiot
text: “Even now he cannot speak the truth. He is not called Timofey Lukianovitch, prince, but Lukian Timofeyovitch. Now do tell us why you must needs lie about it? Lukian or Timofey, it is all the same to you, and what difference can it make to the prince? He tells lies without the least necessity, simply by force of habit, I assure you.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Is that true?” said the prince impatiently.

title: The Idiot
text: “My name really is Lukian Timofeyovitch,” acknowledged Lebedeff, lowering his eyes, and putting his hand on his heart.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, for God’s sake, what made you say the other?”

title: The Idiot
text: “To humble myself,” murmured Lebedeff.

title: The Idiot
text: “What on earth do you mean? Oh I if only I knew where Colia was at this moment!” cried the prince, standing up, as if to go.

title: The Idiot
text: “I can tell you all about Colia,” said the young man

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh! no, no!” said Lebedeff, hurriedly.

title: The Idiot
text: “Colia spent the night here, and this morning went after his father, whom you let out of prison by paying his debts—Heaven only knows why! Yesterday the general promised to come and lodge here, but he did not appear. Most probably he slept at the hotel close by. No doubt Colia is there, unless he has gone to Pavlofsk to see the Epanchins. He had a little money, and was intending to go there yesterday. He must be either at the hotel or at Pavlofsk.”

title: The Idiot
text: “At Pavlofsk! He is at Pavlofsk, undoubtedly!” interrupted Lebedeff....

title: The Idiot
text: “But come—let us go into the garden—we will have coffee there....

title: The Idiot
text: And Lebedeff seized the prince’s arm, and led him from the room.

title: The Idiot
text: They went across the yard, and found themselves in a delightful little garden with the trees already in their summer dress of green, thanks to the unusually fine weather.

title: The Idiot
text: Lebedeff invited his guest to sit down on a green seat before a table of the same colour fixed in the earth, and took a seat facing him.

title: The Idiot
text: In a few minutes the coffee appeared, and the prince did not refuse it.

title: The Idiot
text: The host kept his eyes fixed on Muishkin, with an expression of passionate servility.

title: The Idiot
text: “I knew nothing about your home before,” said the prince absently, as if he were thinking of something else.

title: The Idiot
text: “Poor orphans,” began Lebedeff, his face assuming a mournful air, but he stopped short, for the other looked at him inattentively, as if he had already forgotten his own remark.

title: The Idiot
text: They waited a few minutes in silence, while Lebedeff sat with his eyes fixed mournfully on the young man’s face.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well!” said the latter, at last rousing himself.

title: The Idiot
text: “Ah! yes! You know why I came, Lebedeff. Your letter brought me. Speak! Tell me all about it.”

title: The Idiot
text: The clerk, rather confused, tried to say something, hesitated, began to speak, and again stopped.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince looked at him gravely.

title: The Idiot
text: “I think I understand, Lukian Timofeyovitch: you were not sure that I should come. You did not think I should start at the first word from you, and you merely wrote to relieve your conscience. However, you see now that I have come, and I have had enough of trickery. Give up serving, or trying to serve, two masters. Rogojin has been here these three weeks. Have you managed to sell her to him as you did before? Tell me the truth.”

title: The Idiot
text: “He discovered everything, the monster... himself......”

title: The Idiot
text: “Don’t abuse him; though I dare say you have something to complain of....”

title: The Idiot
text: “He beat me, he thrashed me unmercifully!” replied Lebedeff vehemently.

title: The Idiot
text: “He set a dog on me in Moscow, a bloodhound, a terrible beast that chased me all down the street.”

title: The Idiot
text: “You seem to take me for a child, Lebedeff. Tell me, is it a fact that she left him while they were in Moscow?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, it is a fact, and this time, let me tell you, on the very eve of their marriage!

title: The Idiot
text: It was a question of minutes when she slipped off to Petersburg.

title: The Idiot
text: She came to me directly she arrived—‘Save me, Lukian! find me some refuge, and say nothing to the prince!

title: The Idiot
text: She is afraid of you, even more than she is of him, and in that she shows her wisdom!

title: The Idiot
text: And Lebedeff slily put his finger to his brow as he said the last words.

title: The Idiot
text: “And now it is you who have brought them together again?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Excellency, how could I, how could I prevent it?”

title: The Idiot
text: “That will do. I can find out for myself. Only tell me, where is she now? At his house? With him?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh no! Certainly not! ‘I am free,’ she says; you know how she insists on that point. ‘I am entirely free. She repeats it over and over again. She is living in Petersburgskaia, with my sister-in-law, as I told you in my letter.”

title: The Idiot
text: “She is there at this moment?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, unless she has gone to Pavlofsk: the fine weather may have tempted her, perhaps, into the country, with Daria Alexeyevna. ‘I am quite free,’ she says. Only yesterday she boasted of her freedom to Nicolai Ardalionovitch—a bad sign,” added Lebedeff, smiling.

title: The Idiot
text: “Colia goes to see her often, does he not?”

title: The Idiot
text: “He is a strange boy, thoughtless, and inclined to be indiscreet.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Is it long since you saw her?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I go to see her every day, every day.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Then you were there yesterday?”

title: The Idiot
text: “N-no: I have not been these three last days.”

title: The Idiot
text: “It is a pity you have taken too much wine, Lebedeff I want to ask you something... but...”

title: The Idiot
text: “All right! all right! I am not drunk,” replied the clerk, preparing to listen.

title: The Idiot
text: “Tell me, how was she when you left her?”

title: The Idiot
text: “She is a woman who is seeking...”

title: The Idiot
text: “Seeking?”

title: The Idiot
text: “She seems always to be searching about, as if she had lost something. The mere idea of her coming marriage disgusts her; she looks on it as an insult. She cares as much for him as for a piece of orange-peel—not more. Yet I am much mistaken if she does not look on him with fear and trembling. She forbids his name to be mentioned before her, and they only meet when unavoidable. He understands, well enough! But it must be gone through. She is restless, mocking, deceitful, violent....”

title: The Idiot
text: “Deceitful and violent?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, violent. I can give you a proof of it. A few days ago she tried to pull my hair because I said something that annoyed her. I tried to soothe her by reading the Apocalypse aloud.”

title: The Idiot
text: “What?” exclaimed the prince, thinking he had not heard aright.

title: The Idiot
text: “By reading the Apocalypse. The lady has a restless imagination, he-he! She has a liking for conversation on serious subjects, of any kind; in fact they please her so much, that it flatters her to discuss them. Now for fifteen years at least I have studied the Apocalypse, and she agrees with me in thinking that the present is the epoch represented by the third horse, the black one whose rider holds a measure in his hand. It seems to me that everything is ruled by measure in our century; all men are clamouring for their rights; ‘a measure of wheat for a penny, and three measures of barley for a penny. But, added to this, men desire freedom of mind and body, a pure heart, a healthy life, and all God’s good gifts. Now by pleading their rights alone, they will never attain all this, so the white horse, with his rider Death, comes next, and is followed by Hell. We talked about this matter when we met, and it impressed her very much.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Do you believe all this?” asked Muishkin, looking curiously at his companion.

title: The Idiot
text: “I both believe it and explain it. I am but a poor creature, a beggar, an atom in the scale of humanity. Who has the least respect for Lebedeff? He is a target for all the world, the butt of any fool who chooses to kick him. But in interpreting revelation I am the equal of anyone, great as he may be! Such is the power of the mind and the spirit. I have made a lordly personage tremble, as he sat in his armchair... only by talking to him of things concerning the spirit. Two years ago, on Easter Eve, His Excellency Nil Alexeyovitch, whose subordinate I was then, wished to hear what I had to say, and sent a message by Peter Zakkaritch to ask me to go to his private room. ‘They tell me you expound the prophecies relating to Antichrist,’ said he, when we were alone. ‘Is that so? ‘Yes,’ I answered unhesitatingly, and I began to give some comments on the Apostle’s allegorical vision. At first he smiled, but when we reached the numerical computations and correspondences, he trembled, and turned pale. Then he begged me to close the book, and sent me away, promising to put my name on the reward list. That took place as I said on the eve of Easter, and eight days later his soul returned to God.”

title: The Idiot
text: “What?”

title: The Idiot
text: “It is the truth. One evening after dinner he stumbled as he stepped out of his carriage. He fell, and struck his head on the curb, and died immediately. He was seventy-three years of age, and had a red face, and white hair; he deluged himself with scent, and was always smiling like a child. Peter Zakkaritch recalled my interview with him, and said, ‘you foretold his death.’”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince rose from his seat, and Lebedeff, surprised to see his guest preparing to go so soon, remarked: “You are not interested?” in a respectful tone.

title: The Idiot
text: “I am not very well, and my head aches. Doubtless the effect of the journey,” replied the prince, frowning.

title: The Idiot
text: “You should go into the country,” said Lebedeff timidly.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince seemed to be considering the suggestion.

title: The Idiot
text: “You see, I am going into the country myself in three days, with my children and belongings. The little one is delicate; she needs change of air; and during our absence this house will be done up. I am going to Pavlofsk.”

title: The Idiot
text: “You are going to Pavlofsk too?” asked the prince sharply.

title: The Idiot
text: “Everybody seems to be going there. Have you a house in that neighbourhood?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I don’t know of many people going to Pavlofsk, and as for the house, Ivan Ptitsin has let me one of his villas rather cheaply. It is a pleasant place, lying on a hill surrounded by trees, and one can live there for a mere song. There is good music to be heard, so no wonder it is popular. I shall stay in the lodge. As to the villa itself...”

title: The Idiot
text: “Have you let it?”

title: The Idiot
text: “N-no—not exactly.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Let it to me,” said the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: Now this was precisely what Lebedeff had made up his mind to do in the last three minutes.

title: The Idiot
text: Not that he had any difficulty in finding a tenant; in fact the house was occupied at present by a chance visitor, who had told Lebedeff that he would perhaps take it for the summer months.

title: The Idiot
text: The clerk knew very well that this “perhaps” meant “certainly,” but as he thought he could make more out of a tenant like the prince, he felt justified in speaking vaguely about the present inhabitant’s intentions.

title: The Idiot
text: “This is quite a coincidence,” thought he, and when the subject of price was mentioned, he made a gesture with his hand, as if to waive away a question of so little importance.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh well, as you like!” said Muishkin.

title: The Idiot
text: “I will think it over. You shall lose nothing!”

title: The Idiot
text: They were walking slowly across the garden.

title: The Idiot
text: “But if you... I could...” stammered Lebedeff, “if... if you please, prince, tell you something on the subject which would interest you, I am sure.

title: The Idiot
text: He spoke in wheedling tones, and wriggled as he walked along.

title: The Idiot
text: Muishkin stopped short.

title: The Idiot
text: “Daria Alexeyevna also has a villa at Pavlofsk.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well?”

title: The Idiot
text: “A certain person is very friendly with her, and intends to visit her pretty often.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Aglaya Ivanovna...”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh stop, Lebedeff!” interposed Muishkin, feeling as if he had been touched on an open wound.

title: The Idiot
text: “That... that has nothing to do with me. I should like to know when you are going to start. The sooner the better as far as I am concerned, for I am at an hotel.”

title: The Idiot
text: They had left the garden now, and were crossing the yard on their way to the gate.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, leave your hotel at once and come here; then we can all go together to Pavlofsk the day after tomorrow.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I will think about it,” said the prince dreamily, and went off.

title: The Idiot
text: The clerk stood looking after his guest, struck by his sudden absent-mindedness.

title: The Idiot
text: He had not even remembered to say goodbye, and Lebedeff was the more surprised at the omission, as he knew by experience how courteous the prince usually was.

title: The Idiot
text: It was now close on twelve o’clock.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince knew that if he called at the Epanchins’ now he would only find the general, and that the latter might probably carry him straight off to Pavlofsk with him; whereas there was one visit he was most anxious to make without delay.

title: The Idiot
text: So at the risk of missing General Epanchin altogether, and thus postponing his visit to Pavlofsk for a day, at least, the prince decided to go and look for the house he desired to find.

title: The Idiot
text: The visit he was about to pay was, in some respects, a risky one.

title: The Idiot
text: He was in two minds about it, but knowing that the house was in the Gorohovaya, not far from the Sadovaya, he determined to go in that direction, and to try to make up his mind on the way.

title: The Idiot
text: Arrived at the point where the Gorohovaya crosses the Sadovaya, he was surprised to find how excessively agitated he was.

title: The Idiot
text: He had no idea that his heart could beat so painfully.

title: The Idiot
text: One house in the Gorohovaya began to attract his attention long before he reached it, and the prince remembered afterwards that he had said to himself: “That is the house, I’m sure of it.

title: The Idiot
text: He came up to it quite curious to discover whether he had guessed right, and felt that he would be disagreeably impressed to find that he had actually done so.

title: The Idiot
text: The house was a large gloomy-looking structure, without the slightest claim to architectural beauty, in colour a dirty green.

title: The Idiot
text: There are a few of these old houses, built towards the end of the last century, still standing in that part of St. Petersburg, and showing little change from their original form and colour.

title: The Idiot
text: They are solidly built, and are remarkable for the thickness of their walls, and for the fewness of their windows, many of which are covered by gratings.

title: The Idiot
text: On the ground-floor there is usually a money-changer’s shop, and the owner lives over it.

title: The Idiot
text: Without as well as within, the houses seem inhospitable and mysterious—an impression which is difficult to explain, unless it has something to do with the actual architectural style.

title: The Idiot
text: These houses are almost exclusively inhabited by the merchant class.

title: The Idiot
text: Arrived at the gate, the prince looked up at the legend over it, which ran:

title: The Idiot
text: “House of Rogojin, hereditary and honourable citizen.”

title: The Idiot
text: He hesitated no longer; but opened the glazed door at the bottom of the outer stairs and made his way up to the second storey.

title: The Idiot
text: The place was dark and gloomy-looking; the walls of the stone staircase were painted a dull red.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin and his mother and brother occupied the whole of the second floor.

title: The Idiot
text: The servant who opened the door to Muishkin led him, without taking his name, through several rooms and up and down many steps until they arrived at a door, where he knocked.

title: The Idiot
text: Parfen Rogojin opened the door himself.

title: The Idiot
text: On seeing the prince he became deadly white, and apparently fixed to the ground, so that he was more like a marble statue than a human being.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince had expected some surprise, but Rogojin evidently considered his visit an impossible and miraculous event.

title: The Idiot
text: He stared with an expression almost of terror, and his lips twisted into a bewildered smile.

title: The Idiot
text: “Parfen! perhaps my visit is ill-timed. I—I can go away again if you like,” said Muishkin at last, rather embarrassed.

title: The Idiot
text: “No, no; it’s all right, come in,” said Parfen, recollecting himself.

title: The Idiot
text: They were evidently on quite familiar terms.

title: The Idiot
text: In Moscow they had had many occasions of meeting; indeed, some few of those meetings were but too vividly impressed upon their memories.

title: The Idiot
text: They had not met now, however, for three months.

title: The Idiot
text: The deathlike pallor, and a sort of slight convulsion about the lips, had not left Rogojin’s face.

title: The Idiot
text: Though he welcomed his guest, he was still obviously much disturbed.

title: The Idiot
text: As he invited the prince to sit down near the table, the latter happened to turn towards him, and was startled by the strange expression on his face.

title: The Idiot
text: A painful recollection flashed into his mind.

title: The Idiot
text: He stood for a time, looking straight at Rogojin, whose eyes seemed to blaze like fire.

title: The Idiot
text: At last Rogojin smiled, though he still looked agitated and shaken.

title: The Idiot
text: “What are you staring at me like that for?” he muttered.

title: The Idiot
text: “Sit down.”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince took a chair.

title: The Idiot
text: “Parfen,” he said, “tell me honestly, did you know that I was coming to Petersburg or no?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, I supposed you were coming,” the other replied, smiling sarcastically, “and I was right in my supposition, you see; but how was I to know that you would come today?”

title: The Idiot
text: A certain strangeness and impatience in his manner impressed the prince very forcibly.

title: The Idiot
text: “And if you had known that I was coming today, why be so irritated about it?” he asked, in quiet surprise.

title: The Idiot
text: “Why did you ask me?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Because when I jumped out of the train this morning, two eyes glared at me just as yours did a moment since.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Ha! and whose eyes may they have been?” said Rogojin, suspiciously.

title: The Idiot
text: It seemed to the prince that he was trembling.

title: The Idiot
text: “I don’t know; I thought it was a hallucination. I often have hallucinations nowadays. I feel just as I did five years ago when my fits were about to come on.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, perhaps it was a hallucination, I don’t know,” said Parfen.

title: The Idiot
text: He tried to give the prince an affectionate smile, and it seemed to the latter as though in this smile of his something had broken, and that he could not mend it, try as he would.

title: The Idiot
text: “Shall you go abroad again then?” he asked, and suddenly added, “Do you remember how we came up in the train from Pskoff together? You and your cloak and leggings, eh?”

title: The Idiot
text: And Rogojin burst out laughing, this time with unconcealed malice, as though he were glad that he had been able to find an opportunity for giving vent to it.

title: The Idiot
text: “Have you quite taken up your quarters here?” asked the prince

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, I’m at home. Where else should I go to?”

title: The Idiot
text: “We haven’t met for some time. Meanwhile I have heard things about you which I should not have believed to be possible.”

title: The Idiot
text: “What of that? People will say anything,” said Rogojin drily.

title: The Idiot
text: “At all events, you’ve disbanded your troop—and you are living in your own house instead of being fast and loose about the place; that’s all very good. Is this house all yours, or joint property?”

title: The Idiot
text: “It is my mother’s. You get to her apartments by that passage.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Where’s your brother?”

title: The Idiot
text: “In the other wing.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Is he married?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Widower. Why do you want to know all this?”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince looked at him, but said nothing.

title: The Idiot
text: He had suddenly relapsed into musing, and had probably not heard the question at all.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin did not insist upon an answer, and there was silence for a few moments.

title: The Idiot
text: “I guessed which was your house from a hundred yards off,” said the prince at last.

title: The Idiot
text: “Why so?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I don’t quite know. Your house has the aspect of yourself and all your family; it bears the stamp of the Rogojin life; but ask me why I think so, and I can tell you nothing. It is nonsense, of course. I am nervous about this kind of thing troubling me so much. I had never before imagined what sort of a house you would live in, and yet no sooner did I set eyes on this one than I said to myself that it must be yours.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Really!” said Rogojin vaguely, not taking in what the prince meant by his rather obscure remarks.

title: The Idiot
text: The room they were now sitting in was a large one, lofty but dark, well furnished, principally with writing-tables and desks covered with papers and books.

title: The Idiot
text: A wide sofa covered with red morocco evidently served Rogojin for a bed.

title: The Idiot
text: On the table beside which the prince had been invited to seat himself lay some books; one containing a marker where the reader had left off, was a volume of Solovieff’s History.

title: The Idiot
text: Some oil-paintings in worn gilded frames hung on the walls, but it was impossible to make out what subjects they represented, so blackened were they by smoke and age.

title: The Idiot
text: One, a life-sized portrait, attracted the prince’s attention.

title: The Idiot
text: It showed a man of about fifty, wearing a long riding-coat of German cut.

title: The Idiot
text: He had two medals on his breast; his beard was white, short and thin; his face yellow and wrinkled, with a sly, suspicious expression in the eyes.

title: The Idiot
text: “That is your father, is it not?” asked the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, it is,” replied Rogojin with an unpleasant smile, as if he had expected his guest to ask the question, and then to make some disagreeable remark.

title: The Idiot
text: “Was he one of the Old Believers?”

title: The Idiot
text: “No, he went to church, but to tell the truth he really preferred the old religion. This was his study and is now mine. Why did you ask if he were an Old Believer?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Are you going to be married here?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Ye-yes!” replied Rogojin, starting at the unexpected question.

title: The Idiot
text: “Soon?”

title: The Idiot
text: “You know yourself it does not depend on me.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Parfen, I am not your enemy, and I do not intend to oppose your intentions in any way.

title: The Idiot
text: I repeat this to you now just as I said it to you once before on a very similar occasion.

title: The Idiot
text: When you were arranging for your projected marriage in Moscow, I did not interfere with you—you know I did not.

title: The Idiot
text: That first time she fled to me from you, from the very altar almost, and begged me to ‘save her from you. Afterwards she ran away from me again, and you found her and arranged your marriage with her once more; and now, I hear, she has run away from you and come to Petersburg. Is it true? Lebedeff wrote me to this effect, and that’s why I came here.

title: The Idiot
text: That you had once more arranged matters with Nastasia Philipovna I only learned last night in the train from a friend of yours, Zaleshoff—if you wish to know.

title: The Idiot
text: “I confess I came here with an object.

title: The Idiot
text: I wished to persuade Nastasia to go abroad for her health; she requires it.

title: The Idiot
text: Both mind and body need a change badly.

title: The Idiot
text: I did not intend to take her abroad myself.

title: The Idiot
text: I was going to arrange for her to go without me.

title: The Idiot
text: Now I tell you honestly, Parfen, if it is true that all is made up between you, I will not so much as set eyes upon her, and I will never even come to see you again.

title: The Idiot
