text: However, in a very few minutes he decided that to run away was impossible; that it would be cowardly; that great problems lay before him, and that he had no right to leave them unsolved, or at least to refuse to give all his energy and strength to the attempt to solve them.

title: The Idiot
text: Having come to this determination, he turned and went home, his walk having lasted less than a quarter of an hour.

title: The Idiot
text: At that moment he was thoroughly unhappy.

title: The Idiot
text: Lebedeff had not returned, so towards evening Keller managed to penetrate into the prince’s apartments.

title: The Idiot
text: He was not drunk, but in a confidential and talkative mood.

title: The Idiot
text: He announced that he had come to tell the story of his life to Muishkin, and had only remained at Pavlofsk for that purpose.

title: The Idiot
text: There was no means of turning him out; nothing short of an earthquake would have removed him.

title: The Idiot
text: In the manner of one with long hours before him, he began his history; but after a few incoherent words he jumped to the conclusion, which was that “having ceased to believe in God Almighty, he had lost every vestige of morality, and had gone so far as to commit a theft. “Could you imagine such a thing?” said he.

title: The Idiot
text: “Listen to me, Keller,” returned the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “If I were in your place, I should not acknowledge that unless it were absolutely necessary for some reason. But perhaps you are making yourself out to be worse than you are, purposely?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I should tell it to no one but yourself, prince, and I only name it now as a help to my soul’s evolution. When I die, that secret will die with me! But, excellency, if you knew, if you only had the least idea, how difficult it is to get money nowadays! Where to find it is the question. Ask for a loan, the answer is always the same: ‘Give us gold, jewels, or diamonds, and it will be quite easy. Exactly what one has not got! Can you picture that to yourself? I got angry at last, and said, ‘I suppose you would accept emeralds? ‘Certainly, we accept emeralds with pleasure. Yes! ‘Well, that’s all right,’ said I. ‘Go to the devil, you den of thieves! And with that I seized my hat, and walked out.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Had you any emeralds?” asked the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “What? I have emeralds? Oh, prince! with what simplicity, with what almost pastoral simplicity, you look upon life!”

title: The Idiot
text: Could not something be made of this man under good influences?

title: The Idiot
text: asked the prince of himself, for he began to feel a kind of pity for his visitor.

title: The Idiot
text: He thought little of the value of his own personal influence, not from a sense of humility, but from his peculiar way of looking at things in general.

title: The Idiot
text: Imperceptibly the conversation grew more animated and more interesting, so that neither of the two felt anxious to bring it to a close.

title: The Idiot
text: Keller confessed, with apparent sincerity, to having been guilty of many acts of such a nature that it astonished the prince that he could mention them, even to him.

title: The Idiot
text: At every fresh avowal he professed the deepest repentance, and described himself as being “bathed in tears”; but this did not prevent him from putting on a boastful air at times, and some of his stories were so absurdly comical that both he and the prince laughed like madmen.

title: The Idiot
text: “One point in your favour is that you seem to have a child-like mind, and extreme truthfulness,” said the prince at last.

title: The Idiot
text: “Do you know that that atones for much?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I am assuredly noble-minded, and chivalrous to a degree!” said Keller, much softened.

title: The Idiot
text: “But, do you know, this nobility of mind exists in a dream, if one may put it so? It never appears in practice or deed. Now, why is that? I can never understand.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Do not despair. I think we may say without fear of deceiving ourselves, that you have now given a fairly exact account of your life. I, at least, think it would be impossible to add much to what you have just told me.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Impossible?” cried Keller, almost pityingly.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh prince, how little you really seem to understand human nature!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Is there really much more to be added?” asked the prince, with mild surprise.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, what is it you really want of me? Speak out; tell me why you came to make your confession to me?”

title: The Idiot
text: “What did I want? Well, to begin with, it is good to meet a man like you. It is a pleasure to talk over my faults with you. I know you for one of the best of men... and then... then...”

title: The Idiot
text: He hesitated, and appeared so much embarrassed that the prince helped him out.

title: The Idiot
text: “Then you wanted me to lend you money?”

title: The Idiot
text: The words were spoken in a grave tone, and even somewhat shyly.

title: The Idiot
text: Keller started, gave an astonished look at the speaker, and thumped the table with his fist.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, prince, that’s enough to knock me down! It astounds me! Here you are, as simple and innocent as a knight of the golden age, and yet... yet... you read a man’s soul like a psychologist! Now, do explain it to me, prince, because I... I really do not understand!... Of course, my aim was to borrow money all along, and you... you asked the question as if there was nothing blameable in it—as if you thought it quite natural.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes... from you it is quite natural.”

title: The Idiot
text: “And you are not offended?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Why should I be offended?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, just listen, prince. I remained here last evening, partly because I have a great admiration for the French archbishop Bourdaloue. I enjoyed a discussion over him till three o’clock in the morning, with Lebedeff; and then... then—I swear by all I hold sacred that I am telling you the truth—then I wished to develop my soul in this frank and heartfelt confession to you. This was my thought as I was sobbing myself to sleep at dawn. Just as I was losing consciousness, tears in my soul, tears on my face (I remember how I lay there sobbing), an idea from hell struck me. ‘Why not, after confessing, borrow money from him? You see, this confession was a kind of masterstroke; I intended to use it as a means to your good grace and favour—and then—then I meant to walk off with a hundred and fifty roubles. Now, do you not call that base?”

title: The Idiot
text: “It is hardly an exact statement of the case,” said the prince in reply.

title: The Idiot
text: “You have confused your motives and ideas, as I need scarcely say too often happens to myself. I can assure you, Keller, I reproach myself bitterly for it sometimes. When you were talking just now I seemed to be listening to something about myself. At times I have imagined that all men were the same,” he continued earnestly, for he appeared to be much interested in the conversation, “and that consoled me in a certain degree, for a double motive is a thing most difficult to fight against.

title: The Idiot
text: I have tried, and I know.

title: The Idiot
text: God knows whence they arise, these ideas that you speak of as base.

title: The Idiot
text: I fear these double motives more than ever just now, but I am not your judge, and in my opinion it is going too far to give the name of baseness to it—what do you think?

title: The Idiot
text: You were going to employ your tears as a ruse in order to borrow money, but you also say—in fact, you have sworn to the fact—that independently of this your confession was made with an honourable motive.

title: The Idiot
text: As for the money, you want it for drink, do you not?

title: The Idiot
text: After your confession, that is weakness, of course; but, after all, how can anyone give up a bad habit at a moment’s notice?

title: The Idiot
text: It is impossible.

title: The Idiot
text: What can we do?

title: The Idiot
text: It is best, I think, to leave the matter to your own conscience.

title: The Idiot
text: How does it seem to you?

title: The Idiot
text: As he concluded the prince looked curiously at Keller; evidently this problem of double motives had often been considered by him before.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, how anybody can call you an idiot after that, is more than I can understand!” cried the boxer.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince reddened slightly.

title: The Idiot
text: “Bourdaloue, the archbishop, would not have spared a man like me,” Keller continued, “but you, you have judged me with humanity. To show how grateful I am, and as a punishment, I will not accept a hundred and fifty roubles. Give me twenty-five—that will be enough; it is all I really need, for a fortnight at least. I will not ask you for more for a fortnight. I should like to have given Agatha a present, but she does not really deserve it. Oh, my dear prince, God bless you!”

title: The Idiot
text: At this moment Lebedeff appeared, having just arrived from Petersburg.

title: The Idiot
text: He frowned when he saw the twenty-five rouble note in Keller’s hand, but the latter, having got the money, went away at once.

title: The Idiot
text: Lebedeff began to abuse him.

title: The Idiot
text: “You are unjust; I found him sincerely repentant,” observed the prince, after listening for a time.

title: The Idiot
text: “What is the good of repentance like that? It is the same exactly as mine yesterday, when I said, ‘I am base, I am base,’—words, and nothing more!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Then they were only words on your part? I thought, on the contrary...”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, I don’t mind telling you the truth—you only! Because you see through a man somehow. Words and actions, truth and falsehood, are all jumbled up together in me, and yet I am perfectly sincere. I feel the deepest repentance, believe it or not, as you choose; but words and lies come out in the infernal craving to get the better of other people. It is always there—the notion of cheating people, and of using my repentant tears to my own advantage! I assure you this is the truth, prince! I would not tell any other man for the world! He would laugh and jeer at me—but you, you judge a man humanely.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Why, Keller said the same thing to me nearly word for word a few minutes ago!” cried Muishkin.

title: The Idiot
text: “And you both seem inclined to boast about it! You astonish me, but I think he is more sincere than you, for you make a regular trade of it. Oh, don’t put on that pathetic expression, and don’t put your hand on your heart! Have you anything to say to me? You have not come for nothing...”

title: The Idiot
text: Lebedeff grinned and wriggled.

title: The Idiot
text: “I have been waiting all day for you, because I want to ask you a question; and, for once in your life, please tell me the truth at once. Had you anything to do with that affair of the carriage yesterday?”

title: The Idiot
text: Lebedeff began to grin again, rubbed his hands, sneezed, but spoke not a word in reply.

title: The Idiot
text: “I see you had something to do with it.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Indirectly, quite indirectly! I am speaking the truth—I am indeed! I merely told a certain person that I had people in my house, and that such and such personages might be found among them.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I am aware that you sent your son to that house—he told me so himself just now, but what is this intrigue?” said the prince, impatiently.

title: The Idiot
text: “It is not my intrigue!” cried Lebedeff, waving his hand.

title: The Idiot
text: “It was engineered by other people, and is, properly speaking, rather a fantasy than an intrigue!”

title: The Idiot
text: “But what is it all about? Tell me, for Heaven’s sake! Cannot you understand how nearly it touches me? Why are they blackening Evgenie Pavlovitch’s reputation?”

title: The Idiot
text: Lebedeff grimaced and wriggled again.

title: The Idiot
text: “Prince!” said he.

title: The Idiot
text: “Excellency! You won’t let me tell you the whole truth; I have tried to explain; more than once I have begun, but you have not allowed me to go on...”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince gave no answer, and sat deep in thought.

title: The Idiot
text: Evidently he was struggling to decide.

title: The Idiot
text: “Very well! Tell me the truth,” he said, dejectedly.

title: The Idiot
text: “Aglaya Ivanovna...” began Lebedeff, promptly.

title: The Idiot
text: “Be silent! At once!” interrupted the prince, red with indignation, and perhaps with shame, too.

title: The Idiot
text: “It is impossible and absurd! All that has been invented by you, or fools like you! Let me never hear you say a word again on that subject!”

title: The Idiot
text: Late in the evening Colia came in with a whole budget of Petersburg and Pavlofsk news.

title: The Idiot
text: He did not dwell much on the Petersburg part of it, which consisted chiefly of intelligence about his friend Hippolyte, but passed quickly to the Pavlofsk tidings.

title: The Idiot
text: He had gone straight to the Epanchins’ from the station.

title: The Idiot
text: “There’s the deuce and all going on there!” he said.

title: The Idiot
text: “First of all about the row last night, and I think there must be something new as well, though I didn’t like to ask. Not a word about you, prince, the whole time! The most interesting fact was that Aglaya had been quarrelling with her people about Gania. Colia did not know any details, except that it had been a terrible quarrel! Also Evgenie Pavlovitch had called, and met with an excellent reception all round. And another curious thing: Mrs. Epanchin was so angry that she called Varia to her—Varia was talking to the girls—and turned her out of the house ‘once for all’ she said. I heard it from Varia herself—Mrs. Epanchin was quite polite, but firm; and when Varia said good-bye to the girls, she told them nothing about it, and they didn’t know they were saying goodbye for the last time. I’m sorry for Varia, and for Gania too; he isn’t half a bad fellow, in spite of his faults, and I shall never forgive myself for not liking him before! I don’t know whether I ought to continue to go to the Epanchins’ now,” concluded Colia—“I like to be quite independent of others, and of other people’s quarrels if I can; but I must think over it.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I don’t think you need break your heart over Gania,” said the prince; “for if what you say is true, he must be considered dangerous in the Epanchin household, and if so, certain hopes of his must have been encouraged.”

title: The Idiot
text: “What? What hopes?” cried Colia; “you surely don’t mean Aglaya?—oh, no!—”

title: The Idiot
text: “You’re a dreadful sceptic, prince,” he continued, after a moment’s silence.

title: The Idiot
text: “I have observed of late that you have grown sceptical about everything. You don’t seem to believe in people as you did, and are always attributing motives and so on—am I using the word ‘sceptic’ in its proper sense?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I believe so; but I’m not sure.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, I’ll change it, right or wrong; I’ll say that you are not sceptical, but jealous.

title: The Idiot
text: There! you are deadly jealous of Gania, over a certain proud damsel!

title: The Idiot
text: Come!

title: The Idiot
text: Colia jumped up, with these words, and burst out laughing.

title: The Idiot
text: He laughed as he had perhaps never laughed before, and still more when he saw the prince flushing up to his temples.

title: The Idiot
text: He was delighted that the prince should be jealous about Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: However, he stopped immediately on seeing that the other was really hurt, and the conversation continued, very earnestly, for an hour or more.

title: The Idiot
text: Next day the prince had to go to town, on business.

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: The latter seized his hand, glancing around nervously, as if he were afraid of being caught in wrong-doing, and dragged him into a first-class compartment.

title: The Idiot
text: He was burning to speak about something of importance.

title: The Idiot
text: “In the first place, my dear prince, don’t be angry with me. I would have come to see you yesterday, but I didn’t know how Lizabetha Prokofievna would take it. My dear fellow, my house is simply a hell just now, a sort of sphinx has taken up its abode there. We live in an atmosphere of riddles; I can’t make head or tail of anything. As for you, I feel sure you are the least to blame of any of us, though you certainly have been the cause of a good deal of trouble. You see, it’s all very pleasant to be a philanthropist; but it can be carried too far. Of course I admire kind-heartedness, and I esteem my wife, but—”

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: She’s an extraordinary woman, you see, an eccentric woman; I tell you I am so frightened of that woman that I can’t sleep.

title: The Idiot
text: What a carriage that was, and where did it come from, eh?

title: The Idiot
text: I declare, I was base enough to suspect Evgenie at first; but it seems certain that that cannot be the case, and if so, why is she interfering here?

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: Is it to keep Evgenie to herself?

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: It’s quite clear we must treat the impudent creature’s attempt with disdain, and redouble our courtesy towards Evgenie.

title: The Idiot

I blush at the very idea. And now she turns up again like this, when I thought she had finally disappeared! Where’s Rogojin all this time? I thought she was Mrs. Rogojin, long ago.”

title: The Idiot
text: The old man was in a state of great mental perturbation.

title: The Idiot
text: The whole of the journey, which occupied nearly an hour, he continued in this strain, putting questions and answering them himself, shrugging his shoulders, pressing the prince’s hand, and assuring the latter that, at all events, he had no suspicion whatever of him.

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: And it was not until the third day that the formal reconciliation between the prince and the Epanchins took place, as said before.

title: The Idiot
text: It was seven in the evening, and the prince was just preparing to go out for a walk in the park, when suddenly Mrs. Epanchin appeared on the terrace.

title: The Idiot
text: “In the first place, don’t dare to suppose,” she began, “that I am going to apologize. Nonsense! You were entirely to blame.”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince remained silent.

title: The Idiot
text: “Were you to blame, or not?”

title: The Idiot
text: “No, certainly not, no more than yourself, though at first I thought I was.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, very well, let’s sit down, at all events, for I don’t intend to stand up all day. And remember, if you say, one word about ‘mischievous urchins,’ I shall go away and break with you altogether. Now then, did you, or did you not, send a letter to Aglaya, a couple of months or so ago, about Easter-tide?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes!”

title: The Idiot
text: “What for?

title: The Idiot
text: What was your object?

title: The Idiot
text: Show me the letter.

title: The Idiot
text: Mrs. Epanchin’s eyes flashed; she was almost trembling with impatience.

title: The Idiot
text: “I have not got the letter,” said the prince, timidly, extremely surprised at the turn the conversation had taken.

title: The Idiot
text: “If anyone has it, if it still exists, Aglaya Ivanovna must have it.”

title: The Idiot
text: “No finessing, please. What did you write about?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I am not finessing, and I am not in the least afraid of telling you; but I don’t see the slightest reason why I should not have written.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Be quiet, you can talk afterwards! What was the letter about? Why are you blushing?”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince was silent.

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: “I don’t understand your thoughts, Lizabetha Prokofievna; but I can see that the fact of my having written is for some reason repugnant to you. You must admit that I have a perfect right to refuse to answer your questions; but, in order to show you that I am neither ashamed of the letter, nor sorry that I wrote it, and that I am not in the least inclined to blush about it” (here the prince’s blushes redoubled), “I will repeat the substance of my letter, for I think I know it almost by heart.”

title: The Idiot
text: So saying, the prince repeated the letter almost word for word, as he had written it.

title: The Idiot
text: “My goodness, what utter twaddle, and what may all this nonsense have signified, pray? If it had any meaning at all!” said Mrs. Epanchin, cuttingly, after having listened with great attention.

title: The Idiot
text: “I really don’t absolutely know myself; I know my feeling was very sincere. I had moments at that time full of life and hope.”

title: The Idiot
text: “What sort of hope?”

title: The Idiot
text: “It is difficult to explain, but certainly not the hopes you have in your mind. Hopes—well, in a word, hopes for the future, and a feeling of joy that there, at all events, I was not entirely a stranger and a foreigner. I felt an ecstasy in being in my native land once more; and one sunny morning I took up a pen and wrote her that letter, but why to her, I don’t quite know. Sometimes one longs to have a friend near, and I evidently felt the need of one then,” added the prince, and paused.

title: The Idiot
text: “Are you in love with her?”

title: The Idiot
text: “N-no! I wrote to her as to a sister; I signed myself her brother.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh yes, of course, on purpose! I quite understand.”

title: The Idiot
text: “It is very painful to me to answer these questions, Lizabetha Prokofievna.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I dare say it is; but that’s no affair of mine. Now then, assure me truly as before Heaven, are you lying to me or not?”

title: The Idiot
text: “No, I am not lying.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Are you telling the truth when you say you are not in love?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I believe it is the absolute truth.”

title: The Idiot
text: “‘I believe,’ indeed! Did that mischievous urchin give it to her?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I asked Nicolai Ardalionovitch...”

title: The Idiot
text: “The urchin! the urchin!” interrupted Lizabetha Prokofievna in an angry voice.

title: The Idiot
text: “I do not want to know if it were Nicolai Ardalionovitch! The urchin!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Nicolai Ardalionovitch...”

title: The Idiot
text: “The urchin, I tell you!”

title: The Idiot
text: “No, it was not the urchin: it was Nicolai Ardalionovitch,” said the prince very firmly, but without raising his voice.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, all right! All right, my dear! I shall put that down to your account.”

title: The Idiot
text: She was silent a moment to get breath, and to recover her composure.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well!—and what’s the meaning of the ‘poor knight,’ eh?”

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, that’s a comfort, at all events. You don’t suppose she could take any interest in you, do you? Why, she called you an ‘idiot’ herself.”

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: “Don’t be angry; she is a wilful, mad, spoilt girl. If she likes a person she will pitch into him, and chaff him. I used to be just such another. title: The Idiot
text: “Lizabetha Prokofievna, what are you thinking of?” cried the prince, almost leaping to his feet in amazement.

title: The Idiot
text: “Why? You very nearly were, anyhow.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes—I nearly was,” whispered the prince, hanging his head.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well then, have you come here for her? Are you in love with her? With that creature?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I did not come to marry at all,” replied the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “Is there anything you hold sacred?”

title: The Idiot
text: “There is.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Then swear by it that you did not come here to marry her!”

title: The Idiot
text: “I’ll swear it by whatever you please.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I believe you. You may kiss me; I breathe freely at last. But you must know, my dear friend, Aglaya does not love you, and she shall never be your wife while I am out of my grave. So be warned in time. Do you hear me?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, I hear.”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince flushed up so much that he could not look her in the face.

title: The Idiot
text: “I have waited for you with the greatest impatience (not that you were worth it). Every night I have drenched my pillow with tears, not for you, my friend, not for you, don’t flatter yourself! I have my own grief, always the same, always the same. But I’ll tell you why I have been awaiting you so impatiently, because I believe that Providence itself sent you to be a friend and a brother to me. I haven’t a friend in the world except Princess Bielokonski, and she is growing as stupid as a sheep from old age. Now then, tell me, yes or no? Do you know why she called out from her carriage the other night?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I give you my word of honour that I had nothing to do with the matter and know nothing about it.”

title: The Idiot

There does not, and there has never existed such a one, because all socialists are derived from the two classes—the landed proprietors, and the seminarists. All our eminent socialists are merely old liberals of the class of landed proprietors, men who were liberals in the days of serfdom. Why do you laugh? Give me their books, give me their studies, their memoirs, and though I am not a literary critic, yet I will prove as clear as day that every chapter and every word of their writings has been the work of a former landed proprietor of the old school. You’ll find that all their raptures, all their generous transports are proprietary, all their woes and their tears, proprietary; all proprietary or seminarist! You are laughing again, and you, prince, are smiling too. Don’t you agree with me?”

title: The Idiot
text: It was true enough that everybody was laughing, the prince among them.

title: The Idiot
text: “I cannot tell you on the instant whether I agree with you or not,” said the latter, suddenly stopping his laughter, and starting like a schoolboy caught at mischief.

title: The Idiot
text: “But, I assure you, I am listening to you with extreme gratification.”

title: The Idiot
text: So saying, he almost panted with agitation, and a cold sweat stood upon his forehead.

title: The Idiot
text: These were his first words since he had entered the house; he tried to lift his eyes, and look around, but dared not; Evgenie Pavlovitch noticed his confusion, and smiled.

title: The Idiot
text: “I’ll just tell you one fact, ladies and gentlemen,” continued the latter, with apparent seriousness and even exaltation of manner, but with a suggestion of “chaff” behind every word, as though he were laughing in his sleeve at his own nonsense—“a fact, the discovery of which, I believe, I may claim to have made by myself alone.

title: The Idiot
text: At all events, no other has ever said or written a word about it; and in this fact is expressed the whole essence of Russian liberalism of the sort which I am now considering.

title: The Idiot
text: “In the first place, what is liberalism, speaking generally, but an attack (whether mistaken or reasonable, is quite another question) upon the existing order of things? Is this so? Yes. Very well. Then my ‘fact’ consists in this, that Russian liberalism is not an attack upon the existing order of things, but an attack upon the very essence of things themselves—indeed, on the things themselves; not an attack on the Russian order of things, but on Russia itself. My Russian liberal goes so far as to reject Russia; that is, he hates and strikes his own mother. Every misfortune and mishap of the mother-country fills him with mirth, and even with ecstasy. He hates the national customs, Russian history, and everything. If he has a justification, it is that he does not know what he is doing, and believes that his hatred of Russia is the grandest and most profitable kind of liberalism. (You will often find a liberal who is applauded and esteemed by his fellows, but who is in reality the dreariest, blindest, dullest of conservatives, and is not aware of the fact.) This hatred for Russia has been mistaken by some of our ‘Russian liberals’ for sincere love of their country, and they boast that they see better than their neighbours what real love of one’s country should consist in. But of late they have grown, more candid and are ashamed of the expression ‘love of country,’ and have annihilated the very spirit of the words as something injurious and petty and undignified. This is the truth, and I hold by it; but at the same time it is a phenomenon which has not been repeated at any other time or place; and therefore, though I hold to it as a fact, yet I recognize that it is an accidental phenomenon, and may likely enough pass away. There can be no such thing anywhere else as a liberal who really hates his country; and how is this fact to be explained among us? By my original statement that a Russian liberal is not a Russian liberal—that’s the only explanation that I can see.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I take all that you have said as a joke,” said Prince S. seriously.

title: The Idiot
text: “I have not seen all kinds of liberals, and cannot, therefore, set myself up as a judge,” said Alexandra, “but I have heard all you have said with indignation. You have taken some accidental case and twisted it into a universal law, which is unjust.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Accidental case!” said Evgenie Pavlovitch.

title: The Idiot
text: “Do you consider it an accidental case, prince?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I must also admit,” said the prince, “that I have not seen much, or been very far into the question; but I cannot help thinking that you are more or less right, and that Russian liberalism—that phase of it which you are considering, at least—really is sometimes inclined to hate Russia itself, and not only its existing order of things in general. Of course this is only partially the truth; you cannot lay down the law for all...”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince blushed and broke off, without finishing what he meant to say.

title: The Idiot
text: In spite of his shyness and agitation, he could not help being greatly interested in the conversation.

title: The Idiot
text: A special characteristic of his was the naive candour with which he always listened to arguments which interested him, and with which he answered any questions put to him on the subject at issue.

title: The Idiot
text: In the very expression of his face this naivete was unmistakably evident, this disbelief in the insincerity of others, and unsuspecting disregard of irony or humour in their words.

title: The Idiot
text: But though Evgenie Pavlovitch had put his questions to the prince with no other purpose but to enjoy the joke of his simple-minded seriousness, yet now, at his answer, he was surprised into some seriousness himself, and looked gravely at Muishkin as though he had not expected that sort of answer at all.

title: The Idiot
text: “Why, how strange!” he ejaculated.

title: The Idiot
text: “You didn’t answer me seriously, surely, did you?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Did not you ask me the question seriously” inquired the prince, in amazement.

title: The Idiot
text: Everybody laughed.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, trust him for that!” said Adelaida.

title: The Idiot
text: “Evgenie Pavlovitch turns everything and everybody he can lay hold of to ridicule. You should hear the things he says sometimes, apparently in perfect seriousness.”

title: The Idiot
text: “In my opinion the conversation has been a painful one throughout, and we ought never to have begun it,” said Alexandra.

title: The Idiot
text: “We were all going for a walk—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Come along then,” said Evgenie; “it’s a glorious evening. But, to prove that this time I was speaking absolutely seriously, and especially to prove this to the prince (for you, prince, have interested me exceedingly, and I swear to you that I am not quite such an ass as I like to appear sometimes, although I am rather an ass, I admit), and—well, ladies and gentlemen, will you allow me to put just one more question to the prince, out of pure curiosity? It shall be the last. This question came into my mind a couple of hours since (you see, prince, I do think seriously at times), and I made my own decision upon it; now I wish to hear what the prince will say to it.”

title: The Idiot
text: “We have just used the expression ‘accidental case. This is a significant phrase; we often hear it. Well, not long since everyone was talking and reading about that terrible murder of six people on the part of a—young fellow, and of the extraordinary speech of the counsel for the defence, who observed that in the poverty-stricken condition of the criminal it must have come naturally into his head to kill these six people. I do not quote his words, but that is the sense of them, or something very like it. Now, in my opinion, the barrister who put forward this extraordinary plea was probably absolutely convinced that he was stating the most liberal, the most humane, the most enlightened view of the case that could possibly be brought forward in these days. Now, was this distortion, this capacity for a perverted way of viewing things, a special or accidental case, or is such a general rule?”

title: The Idiot
text: Everyone laughed at this.

title: The Idiot
text: “A special case—accidental, of course!” cried Alexandra and Adelaida.

title: The Idiot
text: “Let me remind you once more, Evgenie,” said Prince S., “that your joke is getting a little threadbare.”

title: The Idiot
text: “What do you think about it, prince?” asked Evgenie, taking no notice of the last remark, and observing Muishkin’s serious eyes fixed upon his face.

title: The Idiot
text: “What do you think—was it a special or a usual case—the rule, or an exception? I confess I put the question especially for you.”

title: The Idiot
text: “No, I don’t think it was a special case,” said the prince, quietly, but firmly.

title: The Idiot
text: “My dear fellow!” cried Prince S., with some annoyance, “don’t you see that he is chaffing you? He is simply laughing at you, and wants to make game of you.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I thought Evgenie Pavlovitch was talking seriously,” said the prince, blushing and dropping his eyes.

title: The Idiot
text: “My dear prince,” continued Prince S. “remember what you and I were saying two or three months ago. We spoke of the fact that in our newly opened Law Courts one could already lay one’s finger upon so many talented and remarkable young barristers. How pleased you were with the state of things as we found it, and how glad I was to observe your delight! We both said it was a matter to be proud of; but this clumsy defence that Evgenie mentions, this strange argument can, of course, only be an accidental case—one in a thousand!”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince reflected a little, but very soon he replied, with absolute conviction in his tone, though he still spoke somewhat shyly and timidly:

title: The Idiot
text: “I only wished to say that this ‘distortion,’ as Evgenie Pavlovitch expressed it, is met with very often, and is far more the general rule than the exception, unfortunately for Russia. So much so, that if this distortion were not the general rule, perhaps these dreadful crimes would be less frequent.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Dreadful crimes? But I can assure you that crimes just as dreadful, and probably more horrible, have occurred before our times, and at all times, and not only here in Russia, but everywhere else as well. And in my opinion it is not at all likely that such murders will cease to occur for a very long time to come. The only difference is that in former times there was less publicity, while now everyone talks and writes freely about such things—which fact gives the impression that such crimes have only now sprung into existence. That is where your mistake lies—an extremely natural mistake, I assure you, my dear fellow!” said Prince S.

title: The Idiot
text: “I know that there were just as many, and just as terrible, crimes before our times. Not long since I visited a convict prison and made acquaintance with some of the criminals. There were some even more dreadful criminals than this one we have been speaking of—men who have murdered a dozen of their fellow-creatures, and feel no remorse whatever. But what I especially noticed was this, that the very most hopeless and remorseless murderer—however hardened a criminal he may be—still knows that he is a criminal; that is, he is conscious that he has acted wickedly, though he may feel no remorse whatever. And they were all like this. Those of whom Evgenie Pavlovitch has spoken, do not admit that they are criminals at all; they think they had a right to do what they did, and that they were even doing a good deed, perhaps. I consider there is the greatest difference between the two cases. And recollect—it was a youth, at the particular age which is most helplessly susceptible to the distortion of ideas!”

title: The Idiot
text: Prince S. was now no longer smiling; he gazed at the prince in bewilderment.

title: The Idiot
text: Alexandra, who had seemed to wish to put in her word when the prince began, now sat silent, as though some sudden thought had caused her to change her mind about speaking.

title: The Idiot
text: Evgenie Pavlovitch gazed at him in real surprise, and this time his expression of face had no mockery in it whatever.

title: The Idiot
text: “What are you looking so surprised about, my friend?” asked Mrs. Epanchin, suddenly.

title: The Idiot
text: “Did you suppose he was stupider than yourself, and was incapable of forming his own opinions, or what?”

title: The Idiot
text: “No! Oh no! Not at all!” said Evgenie.

title: The Idiot
text: “But—how is it, prince, that you—(excuse the question, will you?)—if you are capable of observing and seeing things as you evidently do, how is it that you saw nothing distorted or perverted in that claim upon your property, which you acknowledged a day or two since; and which was full of arguments founded upon the most distorted views of right and wrong?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I’ll tell you what, my friend,” cried Mrs. Epanchin, of a sudden, “here are we all sitting here and imagining we are very clever, and perhaps laughing at the prince, some of us, and meanwhile he has received a letter this very day in which that same claimant renounces his claim, and begs the prince’s pardon. There! we don’t often get that sort of letter; and yet we are not ashamed to walk with our noses in the air before him.”

title: The Idiot
text: “And Hippolyte has come down here to stay,” said Colia, suddenly.

title: The Idiot
text: “What! has he arrived?” said the prince, starting up.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, I brought him down from town just after you had left the house.”

title: The Idiot
text: “There now! It’s just like him,” cried Lizabetha Prokofievna, boiling over once more, and entirely oblivious of the fact that she had just taken the prince’s part.

title: The Idiot
text: “I dare swear that you went up to town yesterday on purpose to get the little wretch to do you the great honour of coming to stay at your house. You did go up to town, you know you did—you said so yourself! Now then, did you, or did you not, go down on your knees and beg him to come, confess!”

title: The Idiot
text: “No, he didn’t, for I saw it all myself,” said Colia.

title: The Idiot
text: “On the contrary, Hippolyte kissed his hand twice and thanked him; and all the prince said was that he thought Hippolyte might feel better here in the country!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Don’t, Colia,—what is the use of saying all that?” cried the prince, rising and taking his hat.

title: The Idiot
text: “Where are you going to now?” cried Mrs. Epanchin.

title: The Idiot
text: “Never mind about him now, prince,” said Colia.

title: The Idiot
text: “He is all right and taking a nap after the journey. He is very happy to be here; but I think perhaps it would be better if you let him alone for today,—he is very sensitive now that he is so ill—and he might be embarrassed if you show him too much attention at first. He is decidedly better today, and says he has not felt so well for the last six months, and has coughed much less, too.”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince observed that Aglaya came out of her corner and approached the table at this point.

title: The Idiot
text: He did not dare look at her, but he was conscious, to the very tips of his fingers, that she was gazing at him, perhaps angrily; and that she had probably flushed up with a look of fiery indignation in her black eyes.

title: The Idiot
text: “It seems to me, Mr. Colia, that you were very foolish to bring your young friend down—if he is the same consumptive boy who wept so profusely, and invited us all to his own funeral,” remarked Evgenie Pavlovitch.

title: The Idiot
text: “He talked so eloquently about the blank wall outside his bedroom window, that I’m sure he will never support life here without it.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I think so too,” said Mrs. Epanchin; “he will quarrel with you, and be off,” and she drew her workbox towards her with an air of dignity, quite oblivious of the fact that the family was about to start for a walk in the park.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, I remember he boasted about the blank wall in an extraordinary way,” continued Evgenie, “and I feel that without that blank wall he will never be able to die eloquently; and he does so long to die eloquently!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, you must forgive him the blank wall,” said the prince, quietly.

title: The Idiot
text: “He has come down to see a few trees now, poor fellow.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, I forgive him with all my heart; you may tell him so if you like,” laughed Evgenie.

title: The Idiot
text: “I don’t think you should take it quite like that,” said the prince, quietly, and without removing his eyes from the carpet.

title: The Idiot
text: “I think it is more a case of his forgiving you.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Forgiving me! why so? What have I done to need his forgiveness?”

title: The Idiot
text: “If you don’t understand, then—but of course, you do understand. He wished—he wished to bless you all round and to have your blessing—before he died—that’s all.”

title: The Idiot
text: “My dear prince,” began Prince S., hurriedly, exchanging glances with some of those present, “you will not easily find heaven on earth, and yet you seem to expect to. Heaven is a difficult thing to find anywhere, prince; far more difficult than appears to that good heart of yours. Better stop this conversation, or we shall all be growing quite disturbed in our minds, and—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Let’s go and hear the band, then,” said Lizabetha Prokofievna, angrily rising from her place.

title: The Idiot
text: The rest of the company followed her example.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince suddenly approached Evgenie Pavlovitch.

title: The Idiot
text: “Evgenie Pavlovitch,” he said, with strange excitement and seizing the latter’s hand in his own, “be assured that I esteem you as a generous and honourable man, in spite of everything. Be assured of that.”

title: The Idiot
text: Evgenie Pavlovitch fell back a step in astonishment.

title: The Idiot
text: For one moment it was all he could do to restrain himself from bursting out laughing; but, looking closer, he observed that the prince did not seem to be quite himself; at all events, he was in a very curious state.

title: The Idiot
text: “I wouldn’t mind betting, prince,” he cried, “that you did not in the least mean to say that, and very likely you meant to address someone else altogether. What is it? Are you feeling unwell or anything?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Very likely, extremely likely, and you must be a very close observer to detect the fact that perhaps I did not intend to come up to you at all.”

title: The Idiot
text: So saying he smiled strangely; but suddenly and excitedly he began again:

title: The Idiot
text: “Don’t remind me of what I have done or said. Don’t! I am very much ashamed of myself, I—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Why, what have you done? I don’t understand you.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I see you are ashamed of me, Evgenie Pavlovitch; you are blushing for me; that’s a sign of a good heart. Don’t be afraid; I shall go away directly.”

title: The Idiot
text: “What’s the matter with him? Do his fits begin like that?” said Lizabetha Prokofievna, in a high state of alarm, addressing Colia.

title: The Idiot
text: “No, no, Lizabetha Prokofievna, take no notice of me. I am not going to have a fit. I will go away directly; but I know I am afflicted. I was twenty-four years an invalid, you see—the first twenty-four years of my life—so take all I do and say as the sayings and actions of an invalid. I’m going away directly, I really am—don’t be afraid. I am not blushing, for I don’t think I need blush about it, need I? But I see that I am out of place in society—society is better without me. It’s not vanity, I assure you. I have thought over it all these last three days, and I have made up my mind that I ought to unbosom myself candidly before you at the first opportunity. There are certain things, certain great ideas, which I must not so much as approach, as Prince S. has just reminded me, or I shall make you all laugh. I have no sense of proportion, I know; my words and gestures do not express my ideas—they are a humiliation and abasement of the ideas, and therefore, I have no right—and I am too sensitive. Still, I believe I am beloved in this household, and esteemed far more than I deserve. But I can’t help knowing that after twenty-four years of illness there must be some trace left, so that it is impossible for people to refrain from laughing at me sometimes; don’t you think so?”

title: The Idiot
text: He seemed to pause for a reply, for some verdict, as it were, and looked humbly around him.

title: The Idiot
text: All present stood rooted to the earth with amazement at this unexpected and apparently uncalled-for outbreak; but the poor prince’s painful and rambling speech gave rise to a strange episode.

title: The Idiot
text: “Why do you say all this here?” cried Aglaya, suddenly.

title: The Idiot
text: “Why do you talk like this to them?”

title: The Idiot
text: She appeared to be in the last stages of wrath and irritation; her eyes flashed.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince stood dumbly and blindly before her, and suddenly grew pale.

title: The Idiot
text: “There is not one of them all who is worthy of these words of yours,” continued Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: “Not one of them is worth your little finger, not one of them has heart or head to compare with yours! You are more honest than all, and better, nobler, kinder, wiser than all. There are some here who are unworthy to bend and pick up the handkerchief you have just dropped. Why do you humiliate yourself like this, and place yourself lower than these people? Why do you debase yourself before them? Why have you no pride?”

title: The Idiot
text: “My God! Who would ever have believed this?” cried Mrs. Epanchin, wringing her hands.

title: The Idiot
text: “Hurrah for the ‘poor knight’!” cried Colia.

title: The Idiot
text: “Be quiet! How dare they laugh at me in your house?” said Aglaya, turning sharply on her mother in that hysterical frame of mind that rides recklessly over every obstacle and plunges blindly through proprieties.

title: The Idiot
text: “Why does everyone, everyone worry and torment me? Why have they all been bullying me these three days about you, prince? I will not marry you—never, and under no circumstances! Know that once and for all; as if anyone could marry an absurd creature like you! Just look in the glass and see what you look like, this very moment! Why, why do they torment me and say I am going to marry you? You must know it; you are in the plot with them!”

title: The Idiot
text: “No one ever tormented you on the subject,” murmured Adelaida, aghast.

title: The Idiot
text: “No one ever thought of such a thing! There has never been a word said about it!” cried Alexandra.

title: The Idiot
text: “Who has been annoying her? Who has been tormenting the child? Who could have said such a thing to her? Is she raving?” cried Lizabetha Prokofievna, trembling with rage, to the company in general.

title: The Idiot
text: “Every one of them has been saying it—every one of them—all these three days! And I will never, never marry him!”

title: The Idiot
text: So saying, Aglaya burst into bitter tears, and, hiding her face in her handkerchief, sank back into a chair.

title: The Idiot
text: “But he has never even—”

title: The Idiot
text: “I have never asked you to marry me, Aglaya Ivanovna!” said the prince, of a sudden.

title: The Idiot
text: “What?” cried Mrs. Epanchin, raising her hands in horror.

title: The Idiot
text: “What’s that?”

title: The Idiot
text: She could not believe her ears.

title: The Idiot
text: “I meant to say—I only meant to say,” said the prince, faltering, “I merely meant to explain to Aglaya Ivanovna—to have the honour to explain, as it were—that I had no intention—never had—to ask the honour of her hand. I assure you I am not guilty, Aglaya Ivanovna, I am not, indeed. I never did wish to—I never thought of it at all—and never shall—you’ll see it yourself—you may be quite assured of it. Some wicked person has been maligning me to you; but it’s all right. Don’t worry about it.”

title: The Idiot
text: So saying, the prince approached Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: She took the handkerchief from her face, glanced keenly at him, took in what he had said, and burst out laughing—such a merry, unrestrained laugh, so hearty and gay, that Adelaida could not contain herself.

title: The Idiot
text: She, too, glanced at the prince’s panic-stricken countenance, then rushed at her sister, threw her arms round her neck, and burst into as merry a fit of laughter as Aglaya’s own.

title: The Idiot
text: They laughed together like a couple of school-girls.

title: The Idiot
text: Hearing and seeing this, the prince smiled happily, and in accents of relief and joy, he exclaimed “Well, thank God—thank God!”

title: The Idiot
text: Alexandra now joined in, and it looked as though the three sisters were going to laugh on for ever.

title: The Idiot
text: “They are insane,” muttered Lizabetha Prokofievna.

title: The Idiot
text: “Either they frighten one out of one’s wits, or else—”

title: The Idiot
text: But Prince S. was laughing now, too, so was Evgenie Pavlovitch, so was Colia, and so was the prince himself, who caught the infection as he looked round radiantly upon the others.

title: The Idiot
text: “Come along, let’s go out for a walk!” cried Adelaida.

title: The Idiot
text: “We’ll all go together, and the prince must absolutely go with us. You needn’t go away, you dear good fellow! Isn’t he a dear, Aglaya? Isn’t he, mother? I must really give him a kiss for—for his explanation to Aglaya just now. Mother, dear, I may kiss him, mayn’t I? Aglaya, may I kiss your prince?” cried the young rogue, and sure enough she skipped up to the prince and kissed his forehead.

title: The Idiot
text: He seized her hands, and pressed them so hard that Adelaida nearly cried out; he then gazed with delight into her eyes, and raising her right hand to his lips with enthusiasm, kissed it three times.

title: The Idiot
text: “Come along,” said Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: “Prince, you must walk with me. May he, mother? This young cavalier, who won’t have me? You said you would never have me, didn’t you, prince? No—no, not like that; that’s not the way to give your arm. Don’t you know how to give your arm to a lady yet? There—so. Now, come along, you and I will lead the way. Would you like to lead the way with me alone, tête-à-tête?”

title: The Idiot
text: She went on talking and chatting without a pause, with occasional little bursts of laughter between.

title: The Idiot
text: “Thank God—thank God!” said Lizabetha Prokofievna to herself, without quite knowing why she felt so relieved.

title: The Idiot
text: “What extraordinary people they are!” thought Prince S., for perhaps the hundredth time since he had entered into intimate relations with the family; but—he liked these “extraordinary people,” all the same.

title: The Idiot
text: As for Prince Lef Nicolaievitch himself, Prince S. did not seem quite to like him, somehow.

title: The Idiot
text: He was decidedly preoccupied and a little disturbed as they all started off.

title: The Idiot
text: Evgenie Pavlovitch seemed to be in a lively humour.

title: The Idiot
text: He made Adelaida and Alexandra laugh all the way to the Vauxhall; but they both laughed so very readily and promptly that the worthy Evgenie began at last to suspect that they were not listening to him at all.

title: The Idiot
text: At this idea, he burst out laughing all at once, in quite unaffected mirth, and without giving any explanation.

title: The Idiot
text: The sisters, who also appeared to be in high spirits, never tired of glancing at Aglaya and the prince, who were walking in front.

title: The Idiot
text: It was evident that their younger sister was a thorough puzzle to them both.

title: The Idiot
text: Prince S. tried hard to get up a conversation with Mrs. Epanchin upon outside subjects, probably with the good intention of distracting and amusing her; but he bored her dreadfully.

title: The Idiot
text: She was absent-minded to a degree, and answered at cross purposes, and sometimes not at all.

title: The Idiot
text: But the puzzle and mystery of Aglaya was not yet over for the evening.

title: The Idiot
text: The last exhibition fell to the lot of the prince alone.

title: The Idiot
text: When they had proceeded some hundred paces or so from the house, Aglaya said to her obstinately silent cavalier in a quick half-whisper:

title: The Idiot
text: “Look to the right!”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince glanced in the direction indicated.

title: The Idiot
text: “Look closer. Do you see that bench, in the park there, just by those three big trees—that green bench?”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince replied that he saw it.

title: The Idiot
text: “Do you like the position of it? Sometimes of a morning early, at seven o’clock, when all the rest are still asleep, I come out and sit there alone.”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince muttered that the spot was a lovely one.

title: The Idiot
text: “Now, go away, I don’t wish to have your arm any longer; or perhaps, better, continue to give me your arm, and walk along beside me, but don’t speak a word to me. I wish to think by myself.”

title: The Idiot
text: The warning was certainly unnecessary; for the prince would not have said a word all the rest of the time whether forbidden to speak or not.

title: The Idiot
text: His heart beat loud and painfully when Aglaya spoke of the bench; could she—but no! he banished the thought, after an instant’s deliberation.

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: Out of its trunk, about a couple of inches below its head, came two legs at an angle of forty-five degrees, each about three inches long, so that the beast looked like a trident from above.

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: I was dreadfully afraid it would sting me; somebody had told me, I thought, that it was venomous; but what tormented me most of all was the wondering and wondering as to who had sent it into my room, and what was the mystery which I felt it contained.

title: The Idiot
text: “It hid itself under the cupboard and under the chest of drawers, and crawled into the corners.

title: The Idiot
text: I sat on a chair and kept my legs tucked under me.

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: “Suddenly I heard behind me, and about on a level with my head, a sort of rattling sound.

title: The Idiot
text: I turned sharp round and saw that the brute had crawled up the wall as high as the level of my face, and that its horrible tail, which was moving incredibly fast from side to side, was actually touching my hair!

title: The Idiot
text: I jumped up—and it disappeared.

title: The Idiot
text: I did not dare lie down on my bed for fear it should creep under my pillow.

title: The Idiot
text: My mother came into the room, and some friends of hers.

title: The Idiot
text: They began to hunt for the reptile and were more composed than I was; they did not seem to be afraid of it.

title: The Idiot
text: But they did not understand as I did.

title: The Idiot
text: “Suddenly the monster reappeared; it crawled slowly across the room and made for the door, as though with some fixed intention, and with a slow movement that was more horrible than ever.

title: The Idiot
text: “Then my mother opened the door and called my dog, Norma.

title: The Idiot
text: Norma was a great Newfoundland, and died five years ago.

title: The Idiot
text: “She sprang forward and stood still in front of the reptile as if she had been turned to stone.

title: The Idiot
text: The beast stopped too, but its tail and claws still moved about.

title: The Idiot
text: I believe animals are incapable of feeling supernatural fright—if I have been rightly informed,—but at this moment there appeared to me to be something more than ordinary about Norma’s terror, as though it must be supernatural; and as though she felt, just as I did myself, that this reptile was connected with some mysterious secret, some fatal omen.

title: The Idiot
text: “Norma backed slowly and carefully away from the brute, which followed her, creeping deliberately after her as though it intended to make a sudden dart and sting her.

title: The Idiot
text: “In spite of Norma’s terror she looked furious, though she trembled in all her limbs. At length she slowly bared her terrible teeth, opened her great red jaws, hesitated—took courage, and seized the beast in her mouth. It seemed to try to dart out of her jaws twice, but Norma caught at it and half swallowed it as it was escaping. The shell cracked in her teeth; and the tail and legs stuck out of her mouth and shook about in a horrible manner. Suddenly Norma gave a piteous whine; the reptile had bitten her tongue. She opened her mouth wide with the pain, and I saw the beast lying across her tongue, and out of its body, which was almost bitten in two, came a hideous white-looking substance, oozing out into Norma’s mouth; it was of the consistency of a crushed black-beetle. Just then I awoke and the prince entered the room.”

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: I confess I might well have resented that blind, deaf fate, which, with no apparent reason, seemed to have decided to crush me like a fly; but why did I not stop at resentment?

title: The Idiot
text: Why did I begin to live, knowing that it was not worthwhile to begin?

title: The Idiot
text: Why did I attempt to do what I knew to be an impossibility?

title: The Idiot
text: And yet I could not even read a book to the end; I had given up reading.

title: The Idiot
text: What is the good of reading, what is the good of learning anything, for just six months?

title: The Idiot
text: That thought has made me throw aside a book more than once.

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

text: I used to wait for Colia’s arrival impatiently, for I was so ill myself, then, that I could not leave the house.

title: The Idiot
text: I so threw myself into every little detail of news, and took so much interest in every report and rumour, that I believe I became a regular gossip!

title: The Idiot
text: I could not understand, among other things, how all these people—with so much life in and before them—do not become rich—and I don’t understand it now.

title: The Idiot
text: I remember being told of a poor wretch I once knew, who had died of hunger.

title: The Idiot
text: I was almost beside myself with rage!

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: I could not bear to see all those preoccupied, anxious-looking creatures continuously surging along the streets past me!

title: The Idiot
text: Why are they always anxious?

title: The Idiot
text: What is the meaning of their eternal care and worry?

title: The Idiot
text: It is their wickedness, their perpetual detestable malice—that’s what it is—they are all full of malice, malice!

title: The Idiot
text: “Whose fault is it that they are all miserable, that they don’t know how to live, though they have fifty or sixty years of life before them?

title: The Idiot
text: Why did that fool allow himself to die of hunger with sixty years of unlived life before him?

title: The Idiot
text: “And everyone of them shows his rags, his toil-worn hands, and yells in his wrath: ‘Here are we, working like cattle all our lives, and always as hungry as dogs, and there are others who do not work, and are fat and rich! title: The Idiot
text: Oh!

title: The Idiot
text: I have no pity and no patience for these fools of people.

title: The Idiot
text: Why can’t they be Rothschilds?

title: The Idiot
text: Whose fault is it that a man has not got millions of money like Rothschild?

title: The Idiot
text: If he has life, all this must be in his power!

title: The Idiot
text: Whose fault is it that he does not know how to live his life?

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh! it’s all the same to me now—now!

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: My mother dared not disobey me; she kept the children quiet, for my sake, and beat them if they dared to make any noise and disturb me. I so often complained of them that I should think they must be very fond, indeed, of me by this time.

title: The Idiot
text: I think I must have tormented ‘my faithful Colia’ (as I called him) a good deal too.

title: The Idiot

He seemed to have taken it into his head to imitate the prince in Christian meekness! Surikoff, who lived above us, annoyed me, too. He was so miserably poor, and I used to prove to him that he had no one to blame but himself for his poverty. I used to be so angry that I think I frightened him eventually, for he stopped coming to see me. He was a most meek and humble fellow, was Surikoff. (N.B.—They say that meekness is a great power. I must ask the prince about this, for the expression is his.) But I remember one day in March, when I went up to his lodgings to see whether it was true that one of his children had been starved and frozen to death, I began to hold forth to him about his poverty being his own fault, and, in the course of my remarks, I accidentally smiled at the corpse of his child. title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: When I entered the room, the man, who had entered but a moment before me, and was still unpacking his parcels, was saying something to his wife in an excited manner.

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: “The gentleman before me gazed at me for some seconds in amazement, and his wife in terror; as though there was something alarmingly extraordinary in the fact that anyone could come to see them.

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: “Of course he was delighted to get hold of someone upon whom to vent his rage against things in general.

title: The Idiot
text: “For a moment I thought he would assault me; he grew so pale that he looked like a woman about to have hysterics; his wife was dreadfully alarmed.

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: Of course nobody would listen to him for a long time; he would come and tell his story one day and be refused promptly; another day he would be fed on false promises; again he would be treated harshly; then he would be told to sign some documents; then he would sign the paper and hand it in, and they would refuse to receive it, and tell him to file a formal petition.

title: The Idiot
text: In a word he had been driven about from office to office for five months and had spent every farthing he had; his wife’s last rags had just been pawned; and meanwhile a child had been born to them and—and today I have a final refusal to my petition, and I have hardly a crumb of bread left—I have nothing left; my wife has had a baby lately—and I—I—’

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: “‘If only they would allow me to explain all to his excellency! If I could but be permitted to tell my tale to him!” he cried, trembling with feverish agitation, and his eyes flashing with excitement.

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: “‘In Moscow,’ I said, ‘there was an old state counsellor, a civil general, who, all his life, had been in the habit of visiting the prisons and speaking to criminals. Every party of convicts on its way to Siberia knew beforehand that on the Vorobeef Hills the “old general” would pay them a visit.

title: The Idiot
text: He did all he undertook seriously and devotedly.

title: The Idiot
text: He would walk down the rows of the unfortunate prisoners, stop before each individual and ask after his needs—he never sermonized them; he spoke kindly to them—he gave them money; he brought them all sorts of necessaries for the journey, and gave them devotional books, choosing those who could read, under the firm conviction that they would read to those who could not, as they went along.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘He scarcely ever talked about the particular crimes of any of them, but listened if any volunteered information on that point.

title: The Idiot
text: All the convicts were equal for him, and he made no distinction.

title: The Idiot
text: He spoke to all as to brothers, and every one of them looked upon him as a father.

title: The Idiot
text: When he observed among the exiles some poor woman with a child, he would always come forward and fondle the little one, and make it laugh.

title: The Idiot
text: He continued these acts of mercy up to his very death; and by that time all the criminals, all over Russia and Siberia, knew him!

title: The Idiot
text: “‘A man I knew who had been to Siberia and returned, told me that he himself had been a witness of how the very most hardened criminals remembered the old general, though, in point of fact, he could never, of course, have distributed more than a few pence to each member of a party.

title: The Idiot
text: Their recollection of him was not sentimental or particularly devoted.

title: The Idiot
text: Some wretch, for instance, who had been a murderer—cutting the throat of a dozen fellow-creatures, for instance; or stabbing six little children for his own amusement (there have been such men!)—would perhaps, without rhyme or reason, suddenly give a sigh and say, “I wonder whether that old general is alive still!

title: The Idiot
text: Although perhaps he had not thought of mentioning him for a dozen years before!

title: The Idiot
text: How can one say what seed of good may have been dropped into his soul, never to die?

title: The Idiot
text: “I continued in that strain for a long while, pointing out to Bachmatoff how impossible it is to follow up the effects of any isolated good deed one may do, in all its influences and subtle workings upon the heart and after-actions of others.

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: He shrugged his shoulders, but quite agreed with me; and we parted better friends than I had expected.

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: And for the climax I needed greater determination than I yet possessed.

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: Ten days ago Rogojin called upon me about certain business of his own with which I have nothing to do at present.

title: The Idiot
