title: The Idiot
text: “It’s a good thing that you take it philosophically, at all events,” said Varia.

title: The Idiot
text: “I’m really very glad of it.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, it’s off our hands—off yours, I should say.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I think I have served you faithfully. I never even asked you what happiness you expected to find with Aglaya.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Did I ever expect to find happiness with Aglaya?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Come, come, don’t overdo your philosophy. Of course you did. Now it’s all over, and a good thing, too; pair of fools that we have been! I confess I have never been able to look at it seriously. I busied myself in it for your sake, thinking that there was no knowing what might happen with a funny girl like that to deal with. There were ninety to one chances against it. To this moment I can’t make out why you wished for it.”

title: The Idiot
text: “H’m! now, I suppose, you and your husband will never weary of egging me on to work again. You’ll begin your lectures about perseverance and strength of will, and all that. I know it all by heart,” said Gania, laughing.

title: The Idiot
text: “He’s got some new idea in his head,” thought Varia.

title: The Idiot
text: “Are they pleased over there—the parents?” asked Gania, suddenly.

title: The Idiot
text: “N-no, I don’t think they are. You can judge for yourself. I think the general is pleased enough; her mother is a little uneasy. She always loathed the idea of the prince as a husband; everybody knows that.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Of course, naturally. The bridegroom is an impossible and ridiculous one. I mean, has she given her formal consent?”

title: The Idiot
text: “She has not said ‘no,’ up to now, and that’s all. It was sure to be so with her. You know what she is like. You know how absurdly shy she is. You remember how she used to hide in a cupboard as a child, so as to avoid seeing visitors, for hours at a time. She is just the same now; but, do you know, I think there is something serious in the matter, even from her side; I feel it, somehow. She laughs at the prince, they say, from morn to night in order to hide her real feelings; but you may be sure she finds occasion to say something or other to him on the sly, for he himself is in a state of radiant happiness. He walks in the clouds; they say he is extremely funny just now; I heard it from themselves. They seemed to be laughing at me in their sleeves—those elder girls—I don’t know why.”

title: The Idiot
text: Gania had begun to frown, and probably Varia added this last sentence in order to probe his thought.

title: The Idiot
text: However, at this moment, the noise began again upstairs.

title: The Idiot
text: “I’ll turn him out!” shouted Gania, glad of the opportunity of venting his vexation.

title: The Idiot
text: “I shall just turn him out—we can’t have this.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, and then he’ll go about the place and disgrace us as he did yesterday.”

title: The Idiot
text: “How ‘as he did yesterday’? What do you mean? What did he do yesterday?” asked Gania, in alarm.

title: The Idiot
text: “Why, goodness me, don’t you know?

title: The Idiot
text: Varia stopped short.

title: The Idiot
text: “What? You don’t mean to say that he went there yesterday!” cried Gania, flushing red with shame and anger.

title: The Idiot
text: “Good heavens, Varia!

title: The Idiot
text: Speak!

title: The Idiot
text: You have just been there.

title: The Idiot
text: Was he there or not, quick?

title: The Idiot
text: And Gania rushed for the door.

title: The Idiot
text: Varia followed and caught him by both hands.

title: The Idiot
text: “What are you doing? Where are you going to? You can’t let him go now; if you do he’ll go and do something worse.”

title: The Idiot
text: “What did he do there? What did he say?”

title: The Idiot
text: “They couldn’t tell me themselves; they couldn’t make head or tail of it; but he frightened them all. He came to see the general, who was not at home; so he asked for Lizabetha Prokofievna. First of all, he begged her for some place, or situation, for work of some kind, and then he began to complain about us, about me and my husband, and you, especially you; he said a lot of things.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh! couldn’t you find out?” muttered Gania, trembling hysterically.

title: The Idiot
text: “No—nothing more than that. Why, they couldn’t understand him themselves; and very likely didn’t tell me all.”

title: The Idiot
text: Gania seized his head with both hands and tottered to the window; Varia sat down at the other window.

title: The Idiot
text: “Funny girl, Aglaya,” she observed, after a pause.

title: The Idiot
text: “When she left me she said, ‘Give my special and personal respects to your parents; I shall certainly find an opportunity to see your father one day,’ and so serious over it. She’s a strange creature.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Wasn’t she joking? She was speaking sarcastically!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Not a bit of it; that’s just the strange part of it.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Does she know about father, do you think—or not?”

title: The Idiot
text: “That they do not know about it in the house is quite certain, the rest of them, I mean; but you have given me an idea. Aglaya perhaps knows. She alone, though, if anyone; for the sisters were as astonished as I was to hear her speak so seriously. If she knows, the prince must have told her.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh! it’s not a great matter to guess who told her. A thief! A thief in our family, and the head of the family, too!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh! nonsense!” cried Varia, angrily.

title: The Idiot
text: “That was nothing but a drunkard’s tale. Nonsense! Why, who invented the whole thing—Lebedeff and the prince—a pretty pair! Both were probably drunk.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Father is a drunkard and a thief; I am a beggar, and the husband of my sister is a usurer,” continued Gania, bitterly.

title: The Idiot
text: “There was a pretty list of advantages with which to enchant the heart of Aglaya.”

title: The Idiot
text: “That same husband of your sister, the usurer—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Feeds me? Go on. Don’t stand on ceremony, pray.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Don’t lose your temper. You are just like a schoolboy. You think that all this sort of thing would harm you in Aglaya’s eyes, do you? You little know her character. She is capable of refusing the most brilliant party, and running away and starving in a garret with some wretched student; that’s the sort of girl she is. You never could or did understand how interesting you would have seen in her eyes if you had come firmly and proudly through our misfortunes. The prince has simply caught her with hook and line; firstly, because he never thought of fishing for her, and secondly, because he is an idiot in the eyes of most people. It’s quite enough for her that by accepting him she puts her family out and annoys them all round—that’s what she likes. You don’t understand these things.”

title: The Idiot
text: “We shall see whether I understand or no!” said Gania, enigmatically.

title: The Idiot
text: “But I shouldn’t like her to know all about father, all the same. I thought the prince would manage to hold his tongue about this, at least. He prevented Lebedeff spreading the news—he wouldn’t even tell me all when I asked him—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Then you must see that he is not responsible. What does it matter to you now, in any case? What are you hoping for still? If you have a hope left, it is that your suffering air may soften her heart towards you.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, she would funk a scandal like anyone else. You are all tarred with one brush!”

title: The Idiot
text: “What! Aglaya would have funked? You are a chicken-hearted fellow, Gania!” said Varia, looking at her brother with contempt.

title: The Idiot
text: “Not one of us is worth much. Aglaya may be a wild sort of a girl, but she is far nobler than any of us, a thousand times nobler!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well—come! there’s nothing to get cross about,” said Gania.

title: The Idiot
text: “All I’m afraid of is—mother. I’m afraid this scandal about father may come to her ears; perhaps it has already. I am dreadfully afraid.”

title: The Idiot
text: “It undoubtedly has already!” observed Gania.

title: The Idiot
text: Varia had risen from her place and had started to go upstairs to her mother; but at this observation of Gania’s she turned and gazed at him attentively.

title: The Idiot
text: “Who could have told her?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Hippolyte, probably. He would think it the most delightful amusement in the world to tell her of it the instant he moved over here; I haven’t a doubt of it.”

title: The Idiot
text: “But how could he know anything of it? Tell me that. Lebedeff and the prince determined to tell no one—even Colia knows nothing.”

title: The Idiot
text: “What, Hippolyte? He found it out himself, of course. Why, you have no idea what a cunning little animal he is; dirty little gossip! He has the most extraordinary nose for smelling out other people’s secrets, or anything approaching to scandal. Believe it or not, but I’m pretty sure he has got round Aglaya. If he hasn’t, he soon will. Rogojin is intimate with him, too. How the prince doesn’t notice it, I can’t understand. The little wretch considers me his enemy now and does his best to catch me tripping. What on earth does it matter to him, when he’s dying? However, you’ll see; I shall catch him tripping yet, and not he me.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Why did you get him over here, if you hate him so? And is it really worth your while to try to score off him?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Why, it was yourself who advised me to bring him over!”

title: The Idiot
text: “I thought he might be useful. You know he is in love with Aglaya himself, now, and has written to her; he has even written to Lizabetha Prokofievna!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh! he’s not dangerous there!” cried Gania, laughing angrily.

title: The Idiot
text: “However, I believe there is something of that sort in the air; he is very likely to be in love, for he is a mere boy. But he won’t write anonymous letters to the old lady; that would be too audacious a thing for him to attempt; but I dare swear the very first thing he did was to show me up to Aglaya as a base deceiver and intriguer. I confess I was fool enough to attempt something through him at first. I thought he would throw himself into my service out of revengeful feelings towards the prince, the sly little beast! But I know him better now. As for the theft, he may have heard of it from the widow in Petersburg, for if the old man committed himself to such an act, he can have done it for no other object but to give the money to her. Hippolyte said to me, without any prelude, that the general had promised the widow four hundred roubles. Of course I understood, and the little wretch looked at me with a nasty sort of satisfaction. I know him; you may depend upon it he went and told mother too, for the pleasure of wounding her. And why doesn’t he die, I should like to know? He undertook to die within three weeks, and here he is getting fatter. His cough is better, too. It was only yesterday that he said that was the second day he hadn’t coughed blood.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, turn him out!”

title: The Idiot
text: “I don’t hate, I despise him,” said Gania, grandly.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, I do hate him, if you like!” he added, with a sudden access of rage, “and I’ll tell him so to his face, even when he’s dying! If you had but read his confession—good Lord! what refinement of impudence! Oh, but I’d have liked to whip him then and there, like a schoolboy, just to see how surprised he would have been! Now he hates everybody because he—Oh, I say, what on earth are they doing there! Listen to that noise! I really can’t stand this any longer. Ptitsin!” he cried, as the latter entered the room, “what in the name of goodness are we coming to? Listen to that—”

title: The Idiot
text: But the noise came rapidly nearer, the door burst open, and old General Ivolgin, raging, furious, purple-faced, and trembling with anger, rushed in.

title: The Idiot
text: He was followed by Nina Alexandrovna, Colia, and behind the rest, Hippolyte.

title: The Idiot
text: Hippolyte had now been five days at the Ptitsins’.

title: The Idiot
text: His flitting from the prince’s to these new quarters had been brought about quite naturally and without many words.

title: The Idiot
text: He did not quarrel with the prince—in fact, they seemed to part as friends.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania, who had been hostile enough on that eventful evening, had himself come to see him a couple of days later, probably in obedience to some sudden impulse.

title: The Idiot
text: For some reason or other, Rogojin too had begun to visit the sick boy.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince thought it might be better for him to move away from his (the prince’s) house.

title: The Idiot
text: Hippolyte informed him, as he took his leave, that Ptitsin “had been kind enough to offer him a corner,” and did not say a word about Gania, though Gania had procured his invitation, and himself came to fetch him away.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania noticed this at the time, and put it to Hippolyte’s debit on account.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania was right when he told his sister that Hippolyte was getting better; that he was better was clear at the first glance.

title: The Idiot
text: He entered the room now last of all, deliberately, and with a disagreeable smile on his lips.

title: The Idiot
text: Nina Alexandrovna came in, looking frightened.

title: The Idiot
text: She had changed much since we last saw her, half a year ago, and had grown thin and pale.

title: The Idiot
text: Colia looked worried and perplexed.

title: The Idiot
text: He could not understand the vagaries of the general, and knew nothing of the last achievement of that worthy, which had caused so much commotion in the house.

title: The Idiot
text: But he could see that his father had of late changed very much, and that he had begun to behave in so extraordinary a fashion both at home and abroad that he was not like the same man.

title: The Idiot
text: What perplexed and disturbed him as much as anything was that his father had entirely given up drinking during the last few days.

title: The Idiot
text: Colia knew that he had quarrelled with both Lebedeff and the prince, and had just bought a small bottle of vodka and brought it home for his father.

title: The Idiot
text: “Really, mother,” he had assured Nina Alexandrovna upstairs, “really you had better let him drink. He has not had a drop for three days; he must be suffering agonies—” The general now entered the room, threw the door wide open, and stood on the threshold trembling with indignation.

title: The Idiot
text: “Look here, my dear sir,” he began, addressing Ptitsin in a very loud tone of voice; “if you have really made up your mind to sacrifice an old man—your father too or at all events father of your wife—an old man who has served his emperor—to a wretched little atheist like this, all I can say is, sir, my foot shall cease to tread your floors. Make your choice, sir; make your choice quickly, if you please! Me or this—screw! Yes, screw, sir; I said it accidentally, but let the word stand—this screw, for he screws and drills himself into my soul—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Hadn’t you better say corkscrew?” said Hippolyte.

title: The Idiot
text: “No, sir, not corkscrew. I am a general, not a bottle, sir. Make your choice, sir—me or him.”

title: The Idiot
text: Here Colia handed him a chair, and he subsided into it, breathless with rage.

title: The Idiot
text: “Hadn’t you better—better—take a nap?” murmured the stupefied Ptitsin.

title: The Idiot
text: “A nap?” shrieked the general.

title: The Idiot
text: “I am not drunk, sir; you insult me! I see,” he continued, rising, “I see that all are against me here. Enough—I go; but know, sirs—know that—”

title: The Idiot
text: He was not allowed to finish his sentence.

title: The Idiot
text: Somebody pushed him back into his chair, and begged him to be calm.

title: The Idiot
text: Nina Alexandrovna trembled, and cried quietly.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania retired to the window in disgust.

title: The Idiot
text: “But what have I done? What is his grievance?” asked Hippolyte, grinning.

title: The Idiot
text: “What have you done, indeed?” put in Nina Alexandrovna.

title: The Idiot
text: “You ought to be ashamed of yourself, teasing an old man like that—and in your position, too.”

title: The Idiot
text: “And pray what is my position, madame? I have the greatest respect for you, personally; but—”

title: The Idiot
text: “He’s a little screw,” cried the general; “he drills holes in my heart and soul. He wishes me to be a pervert to atheism. Know, you young greenhorn, that I was covered with honours before ever you were born; and you are nothing better than a wretched little worm, torn in two with coughing, and dying slowly of your own malice and unbelief. What did Gavrila bring you over here for? They’re all against me, even to my own son—all against me.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, come—nonsense!” cried Gania; “if you did not go shaming us all over the town, things might be better for all parties.”

title: The Idiot
text: “What—shame you? I?—what do you mean, you young calf? I shame you? I can only do you honour, sir; I cannot shame you.”

title: The Idiot
text: He jumped up from his chair in a fit of uncontrollable rage.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania was very angry too.

title: The Idiot
text: “Honour, indeed!” said the latter, with contempt.

title: The Idiot
text: “What do you say, sir?” growled the general, taking a step towards him.

title: The Idiot
text: “I say that I have but to open my mouth, and you—”

title: The Idiot
text: Gania began, but did not finish.

title: The Idiot
text: The two—father and son—stood before one another, both unspeakably agitated, especially Gania.

title: The Idiot
text: “Gania, Gania, reflect!” cried his mother, hurriedly.

title: The Idiot
text: “It’s all nonsense on both sides,” snapped out Varia.

title: The Idiot
text: “Let them alone, mother.”

title: The Idiot
text: “It’s only for mother’s sake that I spare him,” said Gania, tragically.

title: The Idiot
text: “Speak!” said the general, beside himself with rage and excitement; “speak—under the penalty of a father’s curse!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, father’s curse be hanged—you don’t frighten me that way!” said Gania.

title: The Idiot
text: “Whose fault is it that you have been as mad as a March hare all this week? It is just a week—you see, I count the days. Take care now; don’t provoke me too much, or I’ll tell all. Why did you go to the Epanchins’ yesterday—tell me that? And you call yourself an old man, too, with grey hair, and father of a family! H’m—nice sort of a father.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Be quiet, Gania,” cried Colia.

title: The Idiot
text: “Shut up, you fool!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, but how have I offended him?” repeated Hippolyte, still in the same jeering voice.

title: The Idiot
text: “Why does he call me a screw? You all heard it. He came to me himself and began telling me about some Captain Eropegoff. I don’t wish for your company, general. I always avoided you—you know that. What have I to do with Captain Eropegoff? All I did was to express my opinion that probably Captain Eropegoff never existed at all!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Of course he never existed!

title: The Idiot
text: Gania interrupted.

title: The Idiot
text: But the general only stood stupefied and gazed around in a dazed way.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania’s speech had impressed him, with its terrible candour.

title: The Idiot
text: For the first moment or two he could find no words to answer him, and it was only when Hippolyte burst out laughing, and said:

title: The Idiot
text: “There, you see! Even your own son supports my statement that there never was such a person as Captain Eropegoff!” that the old fellow muttered confusedly:

title: The Idiot
text: “Kapiton Eropegoff—not Captain Eropegoff!—Kapiton—major retired—Eropegoff—Kapiton.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Kapiton didn’t exist either!” persisted Gania, maliciously.

title: The Idiot
text: “What? Didn’t exist?” cried the poor general, and a deep blush suffused his face.

title: The Idiot
text: “That’ll do, Gania!” cried Varia and Ptitsin.

title: The Idiot
text: “Shut up, Gania!” said Colia.

title: The Idiot
text: But this intercession seemed to rekindle the general.

title: The Idiot
text: “What did you mean, sir, that he didn’t exist? Explain yourself,” he repeated, angrily.

title: The Idiot
text: “Because he didn’t exist—never could and never did—there! You’d better drop the subject, I warn you!”

title: The Idiot
text: “And this is my son—my own son—whom I—oh, gracious Heaven! Eropegoff—Eroshka Eropegoff didn’t exist!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Ha, ha! it’s Eroshka now,” laughed Hippolyte.

title: The Idiot
text: “No, sir, Kapitoshka—not Eroshka. I mean, Kapiton Alexeyevitch—retired major—married Maria Petrovna Lu—Lu—he was my friend and companion—Lutugoff—from our earliest beginnings. I closed his eyes for him—he was killed. Kapiton Eropegoff never existed! tfu!”

title: The Idiot
text: The general shouted in his fury; but it was to be concluded that his wrath was not kindled by the expressed doubt as to Kapiton’s existence.

title: The Idiot
text: This was his scapegoat; but his excitement was caused by something quite different.

title: The Idiot
text: As a rule he would have merely shouted down the doubt as to Kapiton, told a long yarn about his friend, and eventually retired upstairs to his room.

title: The Idiot
text: But today, in the strange uncertainty of human nature, it seemed to require but so small an offence as this to make his cup to overflow.

title: The Idiot
text: The old man grew purple in the face, he raised his hands.

title: The Idiot
text: “Enough of this!” he yelled.

title: The Idiot
text: “My curse—away, out of the house I go!

title: The Idiot
text: Colia, bring my bag away!

title: The Idiot
text: He left the room hastily and in a paroxysm of rage.

title: The Idiot
text: His wife, Colia, and Ptitsin ran out after him.

title: The Idiot
text: “What have you done now?” said Varia to Gania.

title: The Idiot
text: “He’ll probably be making off there again! What a disgrace it all is!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, he shouldn’t steal,” cried Gania, panting with fury.

title: The Idiot
text: And just at this moment his eye met Hippolyte’s.

title: The Idiot
text: “As for you, sir,” he cried, “you should at least remember that you are in a strange house and—receiving hospitality; you should not take the opportunity of tormenting an old man, sir, who is too evidently out of his mind.”

title: The Idiot
text: Hippolyte looked furious, but he restrained himself.

title: The Idiot
text: “I don’t quite agree with you that your father is out of his mind,” he observed, quietly.

title: The Idiot
text: “On the contrary, I cannot help thinking he has been less demented of late. Don’t you think so? He has grown so cunning and careful, and weighs his words so deliberately; he spoke to me about that Kapiton fellow with an object, you know! Just fancy—he wanted me to—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, devil take what he wanted you to do! Don’t try to be too cunning with me, young man!” shouted Gania.

title: The Idiot
text: “If you are aware of the real reason for my father’s present condition (and you have kept such an excellent spying watch during these last few days that you are sure to be aware of it)—you had no right whatever to torment the—unfortunate man, and to worry my mother by your exaggerations of the affair; because the whole business is nonsense—simply a drunken freak, and nothing more, quite unproved by any evidence, and I don’t believe that much of it!” (he snapped his fingers).

title: The Idiot
text: “But you must needs spy and watch over us all, because you are a—a—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Screw!” laughed Hippolyte.

title: The Idiot
text: “Because you are a humbug, sir; and thought fit to worry people for half an hour, and tried to frighten them into believing that you would shoot yourself with your little empty pistol, pirouetting about and playing at suicide! I gave you hospitality, you have fattened on it, your cough has left you, and you repay all this—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Excuse me—two words! I am Varvara Ardalionovna’s guest, not yours; you have extended no hospitality to me. On the contrary, if I am not mistaken, I believe you are yourself indebted to Mr. Ptitsin’s hospitality. Four days ago I begged my mother to come down here and find lodgings, because I certainly do feel better here, though I am not fat, nor have I ceased to cough. I am today informed that my room is ready for me; therefore, having thanked your sister and mother for their kindness to me, I intend to leave the house this evening. I beg your pardon—I interrupted you—I think you were about to add something?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh—if that is the state of affairs—” began Gania.

title: The Idiot
text: “Excuse me—I will take a seat,” interrupted Hippolyte once more, sitting down deliberately; “for I am not strong yet. Now then, I am ready to hear you. Especially as this is the last chance we shall have of a talk, and very likely the last meeting we shall ever have at all.”

title: The Idiot
text: Gania felt a little guilty.

title: The Idiot
text: “I assure you I did not mean to reckon up debits and credits,” he began, “and if you—”

title: The Idiot
text: “I don’t understand your condescension,” said Hippolyte.

title: The Idiot
text: “As for me, I promised myself, on the first day of my arrival in this house, that I would have the satisfaction of settling accounts with you in a very thorough manner before I said good-bye to you. I intend to perform this operation now, if you like; after you, though, of course.”

title: The Idiot
text: “May I ask you to be so good as to leave this room?”

title: The Idiot
text: “You’d better speak out. You’ll be sorry afterwards if you don’t.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Hippolyte, stop, please! It’s so dreadfully undignified,” said Varia.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, only for the sake of a lady,” said Hippolyte, laughing.

title: The Idiot
text: “I am ready to put off the reckoning, but only put it off, Varvara Ardalionovna, because an explanation between your brother and myself has become an absolute necessity, and I could not think of leaving the house without clearing up all misunderstandings first.”

title: The Idiot
text: “In a word, you are a wretched little scandal-monger,” cried Gania, “and you cannot go away without a scandal!”

title: The Idiot
text: “You see,” said Hippolyte, coolly, “you can’t restrain yourself. You’ll be dreadfully sorry afterwards if you don’t speak out now. Come, you shall have the first say. I’ll wait.”

title: The Idiot
text: Gania was silent and merely looked contemptuously at him.

title: The Idiot
text: “You won’t? Very well. I shall be as short as possible, for my part. Two or three times to-day I have had the word ‘hospitality’ pushed down my throat; this is not fair. In inviting me here you yourself entrapped me for your own use; you thought I wished to revenge myself upon the prince. You heard that Aglaya Ivanovna had been kind to me and read my confession. Making sure that I should give myself up to your interests, you hoped that you might get some assistance out of me. I will not go into details. I ought to tell you that I never in my life met a man anything like him for noble simplicity of mind and for boundless trustfulness. title: The Idiot

You imagined that you were doing an heroic action! How could you spare any love for him, when you love your own vanity to such an extent? Why could you not simply go away from here, instead of writing me those absurd letters? Why do you not now marry that generous man who loves you, and has done you the honour of offering you his hand? It is plain enough why; if you marry Rogojin you lose your grievance; you will have nothing more to complain of. You will be receiving too much honour. title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, me, of course! Of course you were afraid of me, or you would not have decided to come. You cannot despise one you fear. And to think that I have actually esteemed you up to this very moment! Do you know why you are afraid of me, and what is your object now? You wished to satisfy yourself with your own eyes as to which he loves best, myself or you, because you are fearfully jealous.”

title: The Idiot
text: “He has told me already that he hates you,” murmured Aglaya, scarcely audibly.

title: The Idiot

I am ready to forgive you, in consideration of your position; but I confess I thought better of you. I thought you were wiser, and more beautiful, too; I did, indeed! Well, take your treasure! See, he is gazing at you, he can’t recollect himself. Take him, but on one condition; go away at once, this instant!”

title: The Idiot
text: She fell back into a chair, and burst into tears.

Heavens! what a fool I have been to humiliate myself before them! Why, prince, you yourself gave me your word that you would marry me whatever happened, and would never abandon me. You said you loved me and would forgive me all, and—and resp—yes, you even said that! I only ran away from you in order to set you free, and now I don’t care to let you go again. Will you go again now that she has insulted me, before your eyes, too; turn away from me and lead her away, arm-in-arm? May you be accursed too, for you were the only one I trusted among them all! Go away, Rogojin, I don’t want you,” she continued, blind with fury, and forcing the words out with dry lips and distorted features, evidently not believing a single word of her own tirade, but, at the same time, doing her utmost to prolong the moment of self-deception.

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: A fortnight had passed since the events recorded in the last chapter, and the position of the actors in our story had become so changed that it is almost impossible for us to continue the tale without some few explanations.

title: The Idiot
text: Yet we feel that we ought to limit ourselves to the simple record of facts, without much attempt at explanation, for a very patent reason: because we ourselves have the greatest possible difficulty in accounting for the facts to be recorded.

title: The Idiot
text: Such a statement on our part may appear strange to the reader.

title: The Idiot
text: How is anyone to tell a story which he cannot understand himself?

title: The Idiot
text: In order to keep clear of a false position, we had perhaps better give an example of what we mean; and probably the intelligent reader will soon understand the difficulty.

title: The Idiot
text: More especially are we inclined to take this course since the example will constitute a distinct march forward of our story, and will not hinder the progress of the events remaining to be recorded.

title: The Idiot
text: During the next fortnight—that is, through the early part of July—the history of our hero was circulated in the form of strange, diverting, most unlikely-sounding stories, which passed from mouth to mouth, through the streets and villas adjoining those inhabited by Lebedeff, Ptitsin, Nastasia Philipovna and the Epanchins; in fact, pretty well through the whole town and its environs.

title: The Idiot
text: All society—both the inhabitants of the place and those who came down of an evening for the music—had got hold of one and the same story, in a thousand varieties of detail—as to how a certain young prince had raised a terrible scandal in a most respectable household, had thrown over a daughter of the family, to whom he was engaged, and had been captured by a woman of shady reputation whom he was determined to marry at once—breaking off all old ties for the satisfaction of his insane idea; and, in spite of the public indignation roused by his action, the marriage was to take place in Pavlofsk openly and publicly, and the prince had announced his intention of going through with it with head erect and looking the whole world in the face.

title: The Idiot
text: The story was so artfully adorned with scandalous details, and persons of so great eminence and importance were apparently mixed up in it, while, at the same time, the evidence was so circumstantial, that it was no wonder the matter gave food for plenty of curiosity and gossip.

title: The Idiot
text: According to the reports of the most talented gossip-mongers—those who, in every class of society, are always in haste to explain every event to their neighbours—the young gentleman concerned was of good family—a prince—fairly rich—weak of intellect, but a democrat and a dabbler in the Nihilism of the period, as exposed by Mr. Turgenieff.

title: The Idiot
text: He could hardly talk Russian, but had fallen in love with one of the Miss Epanchins, and his suit met with so much encouragement that he had been received in the house as the recognized bridegroom-to-be of the young lady.

title: The Idiot
text: But like the Frenchman of whom the story is told that he studied for holy orders, took all the oaths, was ordained priest, and next morning wrote to his bishop informing him that, as he did not believe in God and considered it wrong to deceive the people and live upon their pockets, he begged to surrender the orders conferred upon him the day before, and to inform his lordship that he was sending this letter to the public press,—like this Frenchman, the prince played a false game.

title: The Idiot
text: It was rumoured that he had purposely waited for the solemn occasion of a large evening party at the house of his future bride, at which he was introduced to several eminent persons, in order publicly to make known his ideas and opinions, and thereby insult the “big-wigs,” and to throw over his bride as offensively as possible; and that, resisting the servants who were told off to turn him out of the house, he had seized and thrown down a magnificent china vase.

title: The Idiot
text: As a characteristic addition to the above, it was currently reported that the young prince really loved the lady to whom he was engaged, and had thrown her over out of purely Nihilistic motives, with the intention of giving himself the satisfaction of marrying a fallen woman in the face of all the world, thereby publishing his opinion that there is no distinction between virtuous and disreputable women, but that all women are alike, free; and a “fallen” woman, indeed, somewhat superior to a virtuous one.

title: The Idiot
text: It was declared that he believed in no classes or anything else, excepting “the woman question.”

title: The Idiot
text: All this looked likely enough, and was accepted as fact by most of the inhabitants of the place, especially as it was borne out, more or less, by daily occurrences.

title: The Idiot
text: Of course much was said that could not be determined absolutely.

title: The Idiot
text: For instance, it was reported that the poor girl had so loved her future husband that she had followed him to the house of the other woman, the day after she had been thrown over; others said that he had insisted on her coming, himself, in order to shame and insult her by his taunts and Nihilistic confessions when she reached the house.

title: The Idiot
text: However all these things might be, the public interest in the matter grew daily, especially as it became clear that the scandalous wedding was undoubtedly to take place.

title: The Idiot
text: So that if our readers were to ask an explanation, not of the wild reports about the prince’s Nihilistic opinions, but simply as to how such a marriage could possibly satisfy his real aspirations, or as to the spiritual condition of our hero at this time, we confess that we should have great difficulty in giving the required information.

title: The Idiot
text: All we know is, that the marriage really was arranged, and that the prince had commissioned Lebedeff and Keller to look after all the necessary business connected with it; that he had requested them to spare no expense; that Nastasia herself was hurrying on the wedding; that Keller was to be the prince’s best man, at his own earnest request; and that Burdovsky was to give Nastasia away, to his great delight.

title: The Idiot
text: The wedding was to take place before the middle of July.

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: We suspect, for instance, that having commissioned Lebedeff and the others, as above, the prince immediately forgot all about masters of ceremonies and even the ceremony itself; and we feel quite certain that in making these arrangements he did so in order that he might absolutely escape all thought of the wedding, and even forget its approach if he could, by detailing all business concerning it to others.

She could not bear to share you with another; and you could bring yourself to throw away and shatter such a treasure! Oh, prince, prince!”

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

text: Evgenie Pavlovitch always had a ready tongue, but on this occasion his eloquence, surprised himself.

title: The Idiot
text: “From the very beginning,” he said, “you began with a lie; what began with a lie was bound to end with a lie; such is the law of nature.

title: The Idiot
text: I do not agree, in fact I am angry, when I hear you called an idiot; you are far too intelligent to deserve such an epithet; but you are so far strange as to be unlike others; that you must allow, yourself.

title: The Idiot
text: Now, I have come to the conclusion that the basis of all that has happened, has been first of all your innate inexperience (remark the expression ‘innate,’ prince).

title: The Idiot
text: Then follows your unheard-of simplicity of heart; then comes your absolute want of sense of proportion (to this want you have several times confessed); and lastly, a mass, an accumulation, of intellectual convictions which you, in your unexampled honesty of soul, accept unquestionably as also innate and natural and true.

title: The Idiot
text: Admit, prince, that in your relations with Nastasia Philipovna there has existed, from the very first, something democratic, and the fascination, so to speak, of the ‘woman question’?

title: The Idiot
text: I know all about that scandalous scene at Nastasia Philipovna’s house when Rogojin brought the money, six months ago.

title: The Idiot
text: I’ll show you yourself as in a looking-glass, if you like.

title: The Idiot
text: I know exactly all that went on, in every detail, and why things have turned out as they have.

title: The Idiot
text: You thirsted, while in Switzerland, for your home-country, for Russia; you read, doubtless, many books about Russia, excellent books, I dare say, but hurtful to you; and you arrived here; as it were, on fire with the longing to be of service.

title: The Idiot
text: Then, on the very day of your arrival, they tell you a sad story of an ill-used woman; they tell you, a knight, pure and without reproach, this tale of a poor woman!

title: The Idiot
text: The same day you actually see her; you are attracted by her beauty, her fantastic, almost demoniacal, beauty—(I admit her beauty, of course).

title: The Idiot
text: “Add to all this your nervous nature, your epilepsy, and your sudden arrival in a strange town—the day of meetings and of exciting scenes, the day of unexpected acquaintanceships, the day of sudden actions, the day of meeting with the three lovely Epanchin girls, and among them Aglaya—add your fatigue, your excitement; add Nastasia’ s evening party, and the tone of that party, and—what were you to expect of yourself at such a moment as that?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, yes, yes!” said the prince, once more, nodding his head, and blushing slightly.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, it was so, or nearly so—I know it. And besides, you see, I had not slept the night before, in the train, or the night before that, either, and I was very tired.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Of course, of course, quite so; that’s what I am driving at!” continued Evgenie, excitedly.

title: The Idiot
text: “It is as clear as possible, and most comprehensible, that you, in your enthusiasm, should plunge headlong into the first chance that came of publicly airing your great idea that you, a prince, and a pure-living man, did not consider a woman disgraced if the sin were not her own, but that of a disgusting social libertine! Oh, heavens! it’s comprehensible enough, my dear prince, but that is not the question, unfortunately! The question is, was there any reality and truth in your feelings? Was it nature, or nothing but intellectual enthusiasm? What do you think yourself? We are told, of course, that a far worse woman was forgiven, but we don’t find that she was told that she had done well, or that she was worthy of honour and respect! Did not your common-sense show you what was the real state of the case, a few months later? The question is now, not whether she is an innocent woman (I do not insist one way or the other—I do not wish to); but can her whole career justify such intolerable pride, such insolent, rapacious egotism as she has shown? Forgive me, I am too violent, perhaps, but—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes—I dare say it is all as you say; I dare say you are quite right,” muttered the prince once more.

title: The Idiot
text: “She is very sensitive and easily put out, of course; but still, she...”

title: The Idiot
text: “She is worthy of sympathy? Is that what you wished to say, my good fellow? But then, for the mere sake of vindicating her worthiness of sympathy, you should not have insulted and offended a noble and generous girl in her presence! This is a terrible exaggeration of sympathy! How can you love a girl, and yet so humiliate her as to throw her over for the sake of another woman, before the very eyes of that other woman, when you have already made her a formal proposal of marriage? And you did propose to her, you know; you did so before her parents and sisters. Can you be an honest man, prince, if you act so? I ask you! And did you not deceive that beautiful girl when you assured her of your love?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, you are quite right. Oh! I feel that I am very guilty!” said Muishkin, in deepest distress.

title: The Idiot
text: “But as if that is enough!” cried Evgenie, indignantly.

title: The Idiot
text: “As if it is enough simply to say: ‘I know I am very guilty! You are to blame, and yet you persevere in evil-doing. Where was your heart, I should like to know, your christian heart, all that time? Did she look as though she were suffering less, at that moment? You saw her face—was she suffering less than the other woman? How could you see her suffering and allow it to continue? How could you?”

title: The Idiot
text: “But I did not allow it,” murmured the wretched prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “How—what do you mean you didn’t allow?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Upon my word, I didn’t! To this moment I don’t know how it all happened. I—I ran after Aglaya Ivanovna, but Nastasia Philipovna fell down in a faint; and since that day they won’t let me see Aglaya—that’s all I know.”

title: The Idiot
text: “It’s all the same; you ought to have run after Aglaya though the other was fainting.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, yes, I ought—but I couldn’t!

title: The Idiot
text: She would have died—she would have killed herself.

title: The Idiot
text: You don’t know her; and I should have told Aglaya everything afterwards—but I see, Evgenie Pavlovitch, you don’t know all.

title: The Idiot
text: Tell me now, why am I not allowed to see Aglaya?

title: The Idiot
text: I should have cleared it all up, you know.

title: The Idiot
text: Neither of them kept to the real point, you see.

title: The Idiot
text: I could never explain what I mean to you, but I think I could to Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: Oh! my God, my God!

title: The Idiot
text: You spoke just now of Aglaya’s face at the moment when she ran away.

title: The Idiot
text: Oh, my God!

title: The Idiot
text: I remember it!

title: The Idiot
text: Come along, come along—quick!

title: The Idiot
text: He pulled at Evgenie’s coat-sleeve nervously and excitedly, and rose from his chair.

title: The Idiot
text: “Where to?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Come to Aglaya—quick, quick!”

title: The Idiot
text: “But I told you she is not at Pavlofsk. And what would be the use if she were?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, she’ll understand, she’ll understand!” cried the prince, clasping his hands.

title: The Idiot
text: “She would understand that all this is not the point—not a bit the real point—it is quite foreign to the real question.”

title: The Idiot
text: “How can it be foreign? You are going to be married, are you not? Very well, then you are persisting in your course. Are you going to marry her or not?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, I shall marry her—yes.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Then why is it ‘not the point’?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, no, it is not the point, not a bit. It makes no difference, my marrying her—it means nothing.”

title: The Idiot
text: “How ‘means nothing’? You are talking nonsense, my friend. You are marrying the woman you love in order to secure her happiness, and Aglaya sees and knows it. How can you say that it’s ‘not the point’?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Her happiness? Oh, no! I am only marrying her—well, because she wished it. It means nothing—it’s all the same. She would certainly have died. I see now that that marriage with Rogojin was an insane idea. I understand all now that I did not understand before; and, do you know, when those two stood opposite to one another, I could not bear Nastasia Philipovna’s face! You must know, Evgenie Pavlovitch, I have never told anyone before—not even Aglaya—that I cannot bear Nastasia Philipovna’s face.”

title: The Idiot
text: (He lowered his voice mysteriously as he said this.)

title: The Idiot
text: “You described that evening at Nastasia Philipovna’s (six months since) very accurately just now; but there is one thing which you did not mention, and of which you took no account, because you do not know. I mean her face—I looked at her face, you see. Even in the morning when I saw her portrait, I felt that I could not bear to look at it. Now, there’s Vera Lebedeff, for instance, her eyes are quite different, you know. I’m afraid of her face!” he added, with real alarm.

title: The Idiot
text: “You are afraid of it?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes—she’s mad!” he whispered, growing pale.

title: The Idiot
text: “Do you know this for certain?” asked Evgenie, with the greatest curiosity.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, for certain—quite for certain, now! I have discovered it absolutely for certain, these last few days.”

title: The Idiot
text: “What are you doing, then?” cried Evgenie, in horror.

title: The Idiot
text: “You must be marrying her solely out of fear, then! I can’t make head or tail of it, prince. Perhaps you don’t even love her?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, no; I love her with all my soul. Why, she is a child! She’s a child now—a real child. Oh! you know nothing about it at all, I see.”

title: The Idiot
text: “And are you assured, at the same time, that you love Aglaya too?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes—yes—oh; yes!”

title: The Idiot
text: “How so? Do you want to make out that you love them both?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes—yes—both! I do!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Excuse me, prince, but think what you are saying! Recollect yourself!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Without Aglaya—I—I must see Aglaya!—I shall die in my sleep very soon—I thought I was dying in my sleep last night. Oh! if Aglaya only knew all—I mean really, really all! Because she must know all—that’s the first condition towards understanding. Why cannot we ever know all about another, especially when that other has been guilty? But I don’t know what I’m talking about—I’m so confused. You pained me so dreadfully. Surely—surely Aglaya has not the same expression now as she had at the moment when she ran away? Oh, yes! I am guilty and I know it—I know it! Probably I am in fault all round—I don’t quite know how—but I am in fault, no doubt. There is something else, but I cannot explain it to you, Evgenie Pavlovitch. I have no words; but Aglaya will understand. I have always believed Aglaya will understand—I am assured she will.”

title: The Idiot
text: “No, prince, she will not. Aglaya loved like a woman, like a human being, not like an abstract spirit. Do you know what, my poor prince? The most probable explanation of the matter is that you never loved either the one or the other in reality.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I don’t know—perhaps you are right in much that you have said, Evgenie Pavlovitch. You are very wise, Evgenie Pavlovitch—oh! how my head is beginning to ache again! Come to her, quick—for God’s sake, come!”

title: The Idiot
text: “But I tell you she is not in Pavlofsk! She’s in Colmina.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, come to Colmina, then! Come—let us go at once!”

title: The Idiot
text: “No—no, impossible!” said Evgenie, rising.

title: The Idiot
text: “Look here—I’ll write a letter—take a letter for me!”

title: The Idiot
text: “No—no, prince; you must forgive me, but I can’t undertake any such commissions! I really can’t.”

title: The Idiot
text: And so they parted.

title: The Idiot
text: Evgenie Pavlovitch left the house with strange convictions.

title: The Idiot
text: He, too, felt that the prince must be out of his mind.

title: The Idiot
text: “And what did he mean by that face—a face which he so fears, and yet so loves? And meanwhile he really may die, as he says, without seeing Aglaya, and she will never know how devotedly he loves her! Ha, ha, ha! How does the fellow manage to love two of them? Two different kinds of love, I suppose! This is very interesting—poor idiot! What on earth will become of him now?”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince did not die before his wedding—either by day or night, as he had foretold that he might.

title: The Idiot
text: Very probably he passed disturbed nights, and was afflicted with bad dreams; but, during the daytime, among his fellow-men, he seemed as kind as ever, and even contented; only a little thoughtful when alone.

title: The Idiot
text: The wedding was hurried on.

title: The Idiot
text: The day was fixed for exactly a week after Evgenie’s visit to the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: In the face of such haste as this, even the prince’s best friends (if he had had any) would have felt the hopelessness of any attempt to save “the poor madman.

title: The Idiot
text: Rumour said that in the visit of Evgenie Pavlovitch was to be discerned the influence of Lizabetha Prokofievna and her husband...

title: The Idiot
text: But if those good souls, in the boundless kindness of their hearts, were desirous of saving the eccentric young fellow from ruin, they were unable to take any stronger measures to attain that end.

title: The Idiot
text: Neither their position, nor their private inclination, perhaps (and only naturally), would allow them to use any more pronounced means.

title: The Idiot
text: We have observed before that even some of the prince’s nearest neighbours had begun to oppose him.

title: The Idiot
text: Vera Lebedeff’s passive disagreement was limited to the shedding of a few solitary tears; to more frequent sitting alone at home, and to a diminished frequency in her visits to the prince’s apartments.

title: The Idiot
text: Colia was occupied with his father at this time.

title: The Idiot
text: The old man died during a second stroke, which took place just eight days after the first.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince showed great sympathy in the grief of the family, and during the first days of their mourning he was at the house a great deal with Nina Alexandrovna.

title: The Idiot
text: He went to the funeral, and it was observable that the public assembled in church greeted his arrival and departure with whisperings, and watched him closely.

title: The Idiot
text: The same thing happened in the park and in the street, wherever he went.

title: The Idiot
text: He was pointed out when he drove by, and he often overheard the name of Nastasia Philipovna coupled with his own as he passed.

title: The Idiot
text: People looked out for her at the funeral, too, but she was not there; and another conspicuous absentee was the captain’s widow, whom Lebedeff had prevented from coming.

title: The Idiot
text: The funeral service produced a great effect on the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: He whispered to Lebedeff that this was the first time he had ever heard a Russian funeral service since he was a little boy.

title: The Idiot
text: Observing that he was looking about him uneasily, Lebedeff asked him whom he was seeking.

title: The Idiot
text: “Nothing. I only thought I—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Is it Rogojin?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Why—is he here?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, he’s in church.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I thought I caught sight of his eyes!” muttered the prince, in confusion.

title: The Idiot
text: “But what of it!—Why is he here? Was he asked?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, dear, no! Why, they don’t even know him! Anyone can come in, you know. Why do you look so amazed? I often meet him; I’ve seen him at least four times, here at Pavlofsk, within the last week.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I haven’t seen him once—since that day!” the prince murmured.

title: The Idiot
text: As Nastasia Philipovna had not said a word about having met Rogojin since “that day,” the prince concluded that the latter had his own reasons for wishing to keep out of sight.

title: The Idiot
text: All the day of the funeral our hero was in a deeply thoughtful state, while Nastasia Philipovna was particularly merry, both in the daytime and in the evening.

title: The Idiot
text: Colia had made it up with the prince before his father’s death, and it was he who urged him to make use of Keller and Burdovsky, promising to answer himself for the former’s behaviour.

title: The Idiot
text: Nina Alexandrovna and Lebedeff tried to persuade him to have the wedding in St. Petersburg, instead of in the public fashion contemplated, down here at Pavlofsk in the height of the season.

title: The Idiot
text: But the prince only said that Nastasia Philipovna desired to have it so, though he saw well enough what prompted their arguments.

title: The Idiot
text: The next day Keller came to visit the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: He was in a high state of delight with the post of honour assigned to him at the wedding.

title: The Idiot
text: Before entering he stopped on the threshold, raised his hand as if making a solemn vow, and cried:

title: The Idiot
text: “I won’t drink!”

title: The Idiot
text: Then he went up to the prince, seized both his hands, shook them warmly, and declared that he had at first felt hostile towards the project of this marriage, and had openly said so in the billiard-rooms, but that the reason simply was that, with the impatience of a friend, he had hoped to see the prince marry at least a Princess de Rohan or de Chabot; but that now he saw that the prince’s way of thinking was ten times more noble than that of “all the rest put together.

title: The Idiot
text: For he desired neither pomp nor wealth nor honour, but only the truth!

title: The Idiot
text: The sympathies of exalted personages were well known, and the prince was too highly placed by his education, and so on, not to be in some sense an exalted personage!

title: The Idiot
text: “But all the common herd judge differently; in the town, at the meetings, in the villas, at the band, in the inns and the billiard-rooms, the coming event has only to be mentioned and there are shouts and cries from everybody. I have even heard talk of getting up a ‘charivari’ under the windows on the wedding-night. So if ‘you have need of the pistol’ of an honest man, prince, I am ready to fire half a dozen shots even before you rise from your nuptial couch!”

title: The Idiot
text: Keller also advised, in anticipation of the crowd making a rush after the ceremony, that a fire-hose should be placed at the entrance to the house; but Lebedeff was opposed to this measure, which he said might result in the place being pulled down.

title: The Idiot
text: “I assure you, prince, that Lebedeff is intriguing against you. He wants to put you under control. Imagine that! To take ‘from you the use of your free-will and your money’—that is to say, the two things that distinguish us from the animals! I have heard it said positively. It is the sober truth.”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince recollected that somebody had told him something of the kind before, and he had, of course, scoffed at it.

title: The Idiot
text: He only laughed now, and forgot the hint at once.

title: The Idiot
text: Lebedeff really had been busy for some little while; but, as usual, his plans had become too complex to succeed, through sheer excess of ardour.

title: The Idiot
text: When he came to the prince—the very day before the wedding—to confess (for he always confessed to the persons against whom he intrigued, especially when the plan failed), he informed our hero that he himself was a born Talleyrand, but for some unknown reason had become simple Lebedeff.

title: The Idiot
text: He then proceeded to explain his whole game to the prince, interesting the latter exceedingly.

title: The Idiot
text: According to Lebedeff’s account, he had first tried what he could do with General Epanchin.

title: The Idiot
text: The latter informed him that he wished well to the unfortunate young man, and would gladly do what he could to “save him,” but that he did not think it would be seemly for him to interfere in this matter.

title: The Idiot
text: Lizabetha Prokofievna would neither hear nor see him.

title: The Idiot
text: Prince S. and Evgenie Pavlovitch only shrugged their shoulders, and implied that it was no business of theirs.

title: The Idiot
text: However, Lebedeff had not lost heart, and went off to a clever lawyer,—a worthy and respectable man, whom he knew well.

title: The Idiot
text: This old gentleman informed him that the thing was perfectly feasible if he could get hold of competent witnesses as to Muishkin’s mental incapacity.

title: The Idiot
text: Then, with the assistance of a few influential persons, he would soon see the matter arranged.

title: The Idiot
text: Lebedeff immediately procured the services of an old doctor, and carried the latter away to Pavlofsk to see the prince, by way of viewing the ground, as it were, and to give him (Lebedeff) counsel as to whether the thing was to be done or not.

title: The Idiot
text: The visit was not to be official, but merely friendly.

title: The Idiot
text: Muishkin remembered the doctor’s visit quite well.

title: The Idiot
text: He remembered that Lebedeff had said that he looked ill, and had better see a doctor; and although the prince scouted the idea, Lebedeff had turned up almost immediately with his old friend, explaining that they had just met at the bedside of Hippolyte, who was very ill, and that the doctor had something to tell the prince about the sick man.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince had, of course, at once received him, and had plunged into a conversation about Hippolyte.

title: The Idiot
text: He had given the doctor an account of Hippolyte’s attempted suicide; and had proceeded thereafter to talk of his own malady,—of Switzerland, of Schneider, and so on; and so deeply was the old man interested by the prince’s conversation and his description of Schneider’s system, that he sat on for two hours.

title: The Idiot
text: Muishkin gave him excellent cigars to smoke, and Lebedeff, for his part, regaled him with liqueurs, brought in by Vera, to whom the doctor—a married man and the father of a family—addressed such compliments that she was filled with indignation.

title: The Idiot
text: They parted friends, and, after leaving the prince, the doctor said to Lebedeff: “If all such people were put under restraint, there would be no one left for keepers.

title: The Idiot
text: Lebedeff then, in tragic tones, told of the approaching marriage, whereupon the other nodded his head and replied that, after all, marriages like that were not so rare; that he had heard that the lady was very fascinating and of extraordinary beauty, which was enough to explain the infatuation of a wealthy man; that, further, thanks to the liberality of Totski and of Rogojin, she possessed—so he had heard—not only money, but pearls, diamonds, shawls, and furniture, and consequently she could not be considered a bad match.

title: The Idiot
text: In brief, it seemed to the doctor that the prince’s choice, far from being a sign of foolishness, denoted, on the contrary, a shrewd, calculating, and practical mind.

title: The Idiot
text: Lebedeff had been much struck by this point of view, and he terminated his confession by assuring the prince that he was ready, if need be, to shed his very life’s blood for him.

title: The Idiot
text: Hippolyte, too, was a source of some distraction to the prince at this time; he would send for him at any and every hour of the day.

title: The Idiot
text: They lived,—Hippolyte and his mother and the children,—in a small house not far off, and the little ones were happy, if only because they were able to escape from the invalid into the garden.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince had enough to do in keeping the peace between the irritable Hippolyte and his mother, and eventually the former became so malicious and sarcastic on the subject of the approaching wedding, that Muishkin took offence at last, and refused to continue his visits.

title: The Idiot
text: A couple of days later, however, Hippolyte’s mother came with tears in her eyes, and begged the prince to come back, “or he would eat her up bodily. She added that Hippolyte had a great secret to disclose. Of course the prince went. There was no secret, however, unless we reckon certain pantings and agitated glances around (probably all put on) as the invalid begged his visitor to “beware of Rogojin.”

title: The Idiot
text: “He is the sort of man,” he continued, “who won’t give up his object, you know; he is not like you and me, prince—he belongs to quite a different order of beings. If he sets his heart on a thing he won’t be afraid of anything—” and so on.

title: The Idiot
text: Hippolyte was very ill, and looked as though he could not long survive.

title: The Idiot
text: He was tearful at first, but grew more and more sarcastic and malicious as the interview proceeded.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince questioned him in detail as to his hints about Rogojin.

title: The Idiot
text: He was anxious to seize upon some facts which might confirm Hippolyte’s vague warnings; but there were none; only Hippolyte’s own private impressions and feelings.

title: The Idiot
text: However, the invalid—to his immense satisfaction—ended by seriously alarming the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: At first Muishkin had not cared to make any reply to his sundry questions, and only smiled in response to Hippolyte’s advice to “run for his life—abroad, if necessary. There are Russian priests everywhere, and one can get married all over the world.”

title: The Idiot
text: But it was Hippolyte’s last idea which upset him.

title: The Idiot
text: “What I am really alarmed about, though,” he said, “is Aglaya Ivanovna. Rogojin knows how you love her. Love for love. You took Nastasia Philipovna from him. He will murder Aglaya Ivanovna; for though she is not yours, of course, now, still such an act would pain you,—wouldn’t it?”

title: The Idiot
text: He had attained his end.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince left the house beside himself with terror.

title: The Idiot
text: These warnings about Rogojin were expressed on the day before the wedding.

title: The Idiot
text: That evening the prince saw Nastasia Philipovna for the last time before they were to meet at the altar; but Nastasia was not in a position to give him any comfort or consolation.

title: The Idiot
text: On the contrary, she only added to his mental perturbation as the evening went on.

title: The Idiot
text: Up to this time she had invariably done her best to cheer him—she was afraid of his looking melancholy; she would try singing to him, and telling him every sort of funny story or reminiscence that she could recall.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince nearly always pretended to be amused, whether he were so actually or no; but often enough he laughed sincerely, delighted by the brilliancy of her wit when she was carried away by her narrative, as she very often was.

title: The Idiot
text: Nastasia would be wild with joy to see the impression she had made, and to hear his laugh of real amusement; and she would remain the whole evening in a state of pride and happiness.

title: The Idiot
text: But this evening her melancholy and thoughtfulness grew with every hour.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince had told Evgenie Pavlovitch with perfect sincerity that he loved Nastasia Philipovna with all his soul.

title: The Idiot
text: In his love for her there was the sort of tenderness one feels for a sick, unhappy child which cannot be left alone.

title: The Idiot
text: He never spoke of his feelings for Nastasia to anyone, not even to herself.

title: The Idiot
text: When they were together they never discussed their “feelings,” and there was nothing in their cheerful, animated conversation which an outsider could not have heard.

title: The Idiot
text: Daria Alexeyevna, with whom Nastasia was staying, told afterwards how she had been filled with joy and delight only to look at them, all this time.

title: The Idiot
text: Thanks to the manner in which he regarded Nastasia’s mental and moral condition, the prince was to some extent freed from other perplexities.

title: The Idiot
text: She was now quite different from the woman he had known three months before.

title: The Idiot
text: He was not astonished, for instance, to see her now so impatient to marry him—she who formerly had wept with rage and hurled curses and reproaches at him if he mentioned marriage!

title: The Idiot
text: “It shows that she no longer fears, as she did then, that she would make me unhappy by marrying me,” he thought.

title: The Idiot
text: And he felt sure that so sudden a change could not be a natural one.

title: The Idiot
text: This rapid growth of self-confidence could not be due only to her hatred for Aglaya.
