text: The mother had already been to three or four places to look for Nastasia, but had not found a trace of any kind.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince said nothing, but entered the room, sat down silently, and stared at them, one after the other, with the air of a man who cannot understand what is being said to him.

title: The Idiot
text: It was strange—one moment he seemed to be so observant, the next so absent; his behaviour struck all the family as most remarkable.

title: The Idiot
text: At length he rose from his seat, and begged to be shown Nastasia’s rooms.

title: The Idiot
text: The ladies reported afterwards how he had examined everything in the apartments.

title: The Idiot
text: He observed an open book on the table, Madam Bovary, and requested the leave of the lady of the house to take it with him.

title: The Idiot
text: He had turned down the leaf at the open page, and pocketed it before they could explain that it was a library book.

title: The Idiot
text: He had then seated himself by the open window, and seeing a card-table, he asked who played cards.

title: The Idiot
text: He was informed that Nastasia used to play with Rogojin every evening, either at “preference” or “little fool,” or “whist”; that this had been their practice since her last return from Pavlofsk; that she had taken to this amusement because she did not like to see Rogojin sitting silent and dull for whole evenings at a time; that the day after Nastasia had made a remark to this effect, Rogojin had whipped a pack of cards out of his pocket.

title: The Idiot
text: Nastasia had laughed, but soon they began playing.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince asked where were the cards, but was told that Rogojin used to bring a new pack every day, and always carried it away in his pocket.

title: The Idiot
text: The good ladies recommended the prince to try knocking at Rogojin’s once more—not at once, but in the evening.

title: The Idiot
text: Meanwhile, the mother would go to Pavlofsk to inquire at Dana Alexeyevna’s whether anything had been heard of Nastasia there.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince was to come back at ten o’clock and meet her, to hear her news and arrange plans for the morrow.

title: The Idiot
text: In spite of the kindly-meant consolations of his new friends, the prince walked to his hotel in inexpressible anguish of spirit, through the hot, dusty streets, aimlessly staring at the faces of those who passed him.

title: The Idiot
text: Arrived at his destination, he determined to rest awhile in his room before he started for Rogojin’s once more.

title: The Idiot
text: He sat down, rested his elbows on the table and his head on his hands, and fell to thinking.

title: The Idiot
text: Heaven knows how long and upon what subjects he thought.

title: The Idiot
text: He thought of many things—of Vera Lebedeff, and of her father; of Hippolyte; of Rogojin himself, first at the funeral, then as he had met him in the park, then, suddenly, as they had met in this very passage, outside, when Rogojin had watched in the darkness and awaited him with uplifted knife.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince remembered his enemy’s eyes as they had glared at him in the darkness.

title: The Idiot
text: He shuddered, as a sudden idea struck him.

title: The Idiot
text: This idea was, that if Rogojin were in Petersburg, though he might hide for a time, yet he was quite sure to come to him—the prince—before long, with either good or evil intentions, but probably with the same intention as on that other occasion.

title: The Idiot
text: At all events, if Rogojin were to come at all he would be sure to seek the prince here—he had no other town address—perhaps in this same corridor; he might well seek him here if he needed him.

title: The Idiot
text: And perhaps he did need him.

title: The Idiot
text: This idea seemed quite natural to the prince, though he could not have explained why he should so suddenly have become necessary to Rogojin.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin would not come if all were well with him, that was part of the thought; he would come if all were not well; and certainly, undoubtedly, all would not be well with him.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince could not bear this new idea; he took his hat and rushed out towards the street.

title: The Idiot
text: It was almost dark in the passage.

title: The Idiot
text: “What if he were to come out of that corner as I go by and—and stop me?” thought the prince, as he approached the familiar spot.

title: The Idiot
text: But no one came out.

title: The Idiot
text: He passed under the gateway and into the street.

title: The Idiot
text: The crowds of people walking about—as is always the case at sunset in Petersburg, during the summer—surprised him, but he walked on in the direction of Rogojin’s house.

title: The Idiot
text: About fifty yards from the hotel, at the first cross-road, as he passed through the crowd of foot-passengers sauntering along, someone touched his shoulder, and said in a whisper into his ear:

title: The Idiot
text: “Lef Nicolaievitch, my friend, come along with me.

title: The Idiot
text: It was Rogojin.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince immediately began to tell him, eagerly and joyfully, how he had but the moment before expected to see him in the dark passage of the hotel.

title: The Idiot
text: “I was there,” said Rogojin, unexpectedly.

title: The Idiot
text: “Come along.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince was surprised at this answer; but his astonishment increased a couple of minutes afterwards, when he began to consider it.

title: The Idiot
text: Having thought it over, he glanced at Rogojin in alarm.

title: The Idiot
text: The latter was striding along a yard or so ahead, looking straight in front of him, and mechanically making way for anyone he met.

title: The Idiot
text: “Why did you not ask for me at my room if you were in the hotel?” asked the prince, suddenly.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin stopped and looked at him; then reflected, and replied as though he had not heard the question:

title: The Idiot
text: “Look here, Lef Nicolaievitch, you go straight on to the house; I shall walk on the other side. See that we keep together.”

title: The Idiot
text: So saying, Rogojin crossed the road.

title: The Idiot
text: Arrived on the opposite pavement, he looked back to see whether the prince were moving, waved his hand in the direction of the Gorohovaya, and strode on, looking across every moment to see whether Muishkin understood his instructions.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince supposed that Rogojin desired to look out for someone whom he was afraid to miss; but if so, why had he not told him whom to look out for?

title: The Idiot
text: So the two proceeded for half a mile or so.

title: The Idiot
text: Suddenly the prince began to tremble from some unknown cause.

title: The Idiot
text: He could not bear it, and signalled to Rogojin across the road.

title: The Idiot
text: The latter came at once.

title: The Idiot
text: “Is Nastasia Philipovna at your house?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes.”

title: The Idiot
text: “And was it you looked out of the window under the blind this morning?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Then why did—”

title: The Idiot
text: But the prince could not finish his question; he did not know what to say.

title: The Idiot
text: Besides this, his heart was beating so that he found it difficult to speak at all.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin was silent also and looked at him as before, with an expression of deep thoughtfulness.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, I’m going,” he said, at last, preparing to recross the road.

title: The Idiot
text: “You go along here as before; we will keep to different sides of the road; it’s better so, you’ll see.”

title: The Idiot
text: When they reached the Gorohovaya, and came near the house, the prince’s legs were trembling so that he could hardly walk.

title: The Idiot
text: It was about ten o’clock.

title: The Idiot
text: The old lady’s windows were open, as before; Rogojin’s were all shut, and in the darkness the white blinds showed whiter than ever.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin and the prince each approached the house on his respective side of the road; Rogojin, who was on the near side, beckoned the prince across.

title: The Idiot
text: He went over to the doorway.

title: The Idiot
text: “Even the porter does not know that I have come home now. I told him, and told them at my mother’s too, that I was off to Pavlofsk,” said Rogojin, with a cunning and almost satisfied smile.

title: The Idiot
text: “We’ll go in quietly and nobody will hear us.”

title: The Idiot
text: He had the key in his hand.

title: The Idiot
text: Mounting the staircase he turned and signalled to the prince to go more softly; he opened the door very quietly, let the prince in, followed him, locked the door behind him, and put the key in his pocket.

title: The Idiot
text: “Come along,” he whispered.

title: The Idiot
text: He had spoken in a whisper all the way.

title: The Idiot
text: In spite of his apparent outward composure, he was evidently in a state of great mental agitation.

title: The Idiot
text: Arrived in a large salon, next to the study, he went to the window and cautiously beckoned the prince up to him.

title: The Idiot
text: “When you rang the bell this morning I thought it must be you. I went to the door on tip-toe and heard you talking to the servant opposite. I had told her before that if anyone came and rang—especially you, and I gave her your name—she was not to tell about me. Then I thought, what if he goes and stands opposite and looks up, or waits about to watch the house? So I came to this very window, looked out, and there you were staring straight at me. That’s how it came about.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Where is Nastasia Philipovna?” asked the prince, breathlessly.

title: The Idiot
text: “She’s here,” replied Rogojin, slowly, after a slight pause.

title: The Idiot
text: “Where?”

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin raised his eyes and gazed intently at the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “Come,” he said.

title: The Idiot
text: He continued to speak in a whisper, very deliberately as before, and looked strangely thoughtful and dreamy.

title: The Idiot
text: Even while he told the story of how he had peeped through the blind, he gave the impression of wishing to say something else.

title: The Idiot
text: They entered the study.

title: The Idiot
text: In this room some changes had taken place since the prince last saw it.

title: The Idiot
text: It was now divided into two equal parts by a heavy green silk curtain stretched across it, separating the alcove beyond, where stood Rogojin’s bed, from the rest of the room.

title: The Idiot
text: The heavy curtain was drawn now, and it was very dark.

title: The Idiot
text: The bright Petersburg summer nights were already beginning to close in, and but for the full moon, it would have been difficult to distinguish anything in Rogojin’s dismal room, with the drawn blinds.

title: The Idiot
text: They could just see one anothers faces, however, though not in detail.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin’s face was white, as usual.

title: The Idiot
text: His glittering eyes watched the prince with an intent stare.

title: The Idiot
text: “Had you not better light a candle?” said Muishkin.

title: The Idiot
text: “No, I needn’t,” replied Rogojin, and taking the other by the hand he drew him down to a chair.

title: The Idiot
text: He himself took a chair opposite and drew it up so close that he almost pressed against the prince’s knees.

title: The Idiot
text: At their side was a little round table.

title: The Idiot
text: “Sit down,” said Rogojin; “let’s rest a bit.

title: The Idiot
text: There was silence for a moment.

title: The Idiot
text: “I knew you would be at that hotel,” he continued, just as men sometimes commence a serious conversation by discussing any outside subject before leading up to the main point.

title: The Idiot
text: “As I entered the passage it struck me that perhaps you were sitting and waiting for me, just as I was waiting for you. Have you been to the old lady at Ismailofsky barracks?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes,” said the prince, squeezing the word out with difficulty owing to the dreadful beating of his heart.

title: The Idiot
text: “I thought you would. ‘They’ll talk about it,’ I thought; so I determined to go and fetch you to spend the night here—‘We will be together,’ I thought, ‘for this one night—’”

title: The Idiot
text: “Rogojin, where is Nastasia Philipovna?” said the prince, suddenly rising from his seat.

title: The Idiot
text: He was quaking in all his limbs, and his words came in a scarcely audible whisper.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin rose also.

title: The Idiot
text: “There,” he whispered, nodding his head towards the curtain.

title: The Idiot
text: “Asleep?” whispered the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin looked intently at him again, as before.

title: The Idiot
text: “Let’s go in—but you mustn’t—well—let’s go in.”

title: The Idiot
text: He lifted the curtain, paused—and turned to the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “Go in,” he said, motioning him to pass behind the curtain.

title: The Idiot
text: Muishkin went in.

title: The Idiot
text: “It’s so dark,” he said.

title: The Idiot
text: “You can see quite enough,” muttered Rogojin.

title: The Idiot
text: “I can just see there’s a bed—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Go nearer,” suggested Rogojin, softly.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince took a step forward—then another—and paused.

title: The Idiot
text: He stood and stared for a minute or two.

title: The Idiot
text: Neither of the men spoke a word while at the bedside.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince’s heart beat so loud that its knocking seemed to be distinctly audible in the deathly silence.

title: The Idiot
text: But now his eyes had become so far accustomed to the darkness that he could distinguish the whole of the bed.

title: The Idiot
text: Someone was asleep upon it—in an absolutely motionless sleep.

title: The Idiot
text: Not the slightest movement was perceptible, not the faintest breathing could be heard.

title: The Idiot
text: The sleeper was covered with a white sheet; the outline of the limbs was hardly distinguishable.

title: The Idiot
text: He could only just make out that a human being lay outstretched there.

title: The Idiot
text: All around, on the bed, on a chair beside it, on the floor, were scattered the different portions of a magnificent white silk dress, bits of lace, ribbons and flowers.

title: The Idiot
text: On a small table at the bedside glittered a mass of diamonds, torn off and thrown down anyhow.

title: The Idiot
text: From under a heap of lace at the end of the bed peeped a small white foot, which looked as though it had been chiselled out of marble; it was terribly still.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince gazed and gazed, and felt that the more he gazed the more death-like became the silence.

title: The Idiot
text: Suddenly a fly awoke somewhere, buzzed across the room, and settled on the pillow.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince shuddered.

title: The Idiot
text: “Let’s go,” said Rogojin, touching his shoulder.

title: The Idiot
text: They left the alcove and sat down in the two chairs they had occupied before, opposite to one another.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince trembled more and more violently, and never took his questioning eyes off Rogojin’s face.

title: The Idiot
text: “I see you are shuddering, Lef Nicolaievitch,” said the latter, at length, “almost as you did once in Moscow, before your fit; don’t you remember? I don’t know what I shall do with you—”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince bent forward to listen, putting all the strain he could muster upon his understanding in order to take in what Rogojin said, and continuing to gaze at the latter’s face.

title: The Idiot
text: “Was it you?” he muttered, at last, motioning with his head towards the curtain.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, it was I,” whispered Rogojin, looking down.

title: The Idiot
text: Neither spoke for five minutes.

title: The Idiot
text: “Because, you know,” Rogojin recommenced, as though continuing a former sentence, “if you were ill now, or had a fit, or screamed, or anything, they might hear it in the yard, or even in the street, and guess that someone was passing the night in the house. They would all come and knock and want to come in, because they know I am not at home. I didn’t light a candle for the same reason. When I am not here—for two or three days at a time, now and then—no one comes in to tidy the house or anything; those are my orders. So that I want them to not know we are spending the night here—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Wait,” interrupted the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “I asked both the porter and the woman whether Nastasia Philipovna had spent last night in the house; so they knew—”

title: The Idiot
text: “I know you asked. I told them that she had called in for ten minutes, and then gone straight back to Pavlofsk. No one knows she slept here. Last night we came in just as carefully as you and I did today. I thought as I came along with her that she would not like to creep in so secretly, but I was quite wrong. She whispered, and walked on tip-toe; she carried her skirt over her arm, so that it shouldn’t rustle, and she held up her finger at me on the stairs, so that I shouldn’t make a noise—it was you she was afraid of. She was mad with terror in the train, and she begged me to bring her to this house. I thought of taking her to her rooms at the Ismailofsky barracks first; but she wouldn’t hear of it. She said, ‘No—not there; he’ll find me out at once there. Take me to your own house, where you can hide me, and tomorrow we’ll set off for Moscow. Thence she would go to Orel, she said. When she went to bed, she was still talking about going to Orel.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Wait! What do you intend to do now, Parfen?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, I’m afraid of you. You shudder and tremble so. We’ll pass the night here together. There are no other beds besides that one; but I’ve thought how we’ll manage. I’ll take the cushions off all the sofas, and lay them down on the floor, up against the curtain here—for you and me—so that we shall be together. For if they come in and look about now, you know, they’ll find her, and carry her away, and they’ll be asking me questions, and I shall say I did it, and then they’ll take me away, too, don’t you see? So let her lie close to us—close to you and me.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, yes,” agreed the prince, warmly.

title: The Idiot
text: “So we will not say anything about it, or let them take her away?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Not for anything!” cried the other; “no, no, no!”

title: The Idiot
text: “So I had decided, my friend; not to give her up to anyone,” continued Rogojin.

title: The Idiot
text: “We’ll be very quiet. I have only been out of the house one hour all day, all the rest of the time I have been with her. I dare say the air is very bad here. It is so hot. Do you find it bad?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I don’t know—perhaps—by morning it will be.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I’ve covered her with oilcloth—best American oilcloth, and put the sheet over that, and four jars of disinfectant, on account of the smell—as they did at Moscow—you remember? And she’s lying so still; you shall see, in the morning, when it’s light. What! can’t you get up?” asked Rogojin, seeing the other was trembling so that he could not rise from his seat.

title: The Idiot
text: “My legs won’t move,” said the prince; “it’s fear, I know. When my fear is over, I’ll get up—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Wait a bit—I’ll make the bed, and you can lie down. I’ll lie down, too, and we’ll listen and watch, for I don’t know yet what I shall do... I tell you beforehand, so that you may be ready in case I—”

title: The Idiot
text: Muttering these disconnected words, Rogojin began to make up the beds.

title: The Idiot
text: It was clear that he had devised these beds long before; last night he slept on the sofa.

title: The Idiot
text: But there was no room for two on the sofa, and he seemed anxious that he and the prince should be close to one another; therefore, he now dragged cushions of all sizes and shapes from the sofas, and made a sort of bed of them close by the curtain.

title: The Idiot
text: He then approached the prince, and gently helped him to rise, and led him towards the bed.

title: The Idiot
text: But the prince could now walk by himself, so that his fear must have passed; for all that, however, he continued to shudder.

title: The Idiot
text: “It’s hot weather, you see,” continued Rogojin, as he lay down on the cushions beside Muishkin, “and, naturally, there will be a smell. I daren’t open the window. My mother has some beautiful flowers in pots; they have a delicious scent; I thought of fetching them in, but that old servant will find out, she’s very inquisitive.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, she is inquisitive,” assented the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “I thought of buying flowers, and putting them all round her; but I was afraid it would make us sad to see her with flowers round her.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Look here,” said the prince; he was bewildered, and his brain wandered.

title: The Idiot
text: He seemed to be continually groping for the questions he wished to ask, and then losing them.

title: The Idiot
text: “Listen—tell me—how did you—with a knife?—That same one?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, that same one.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Wait a minute, I want to ask you something else, Parfen; all sorts of things; but tell me first, did you intend to kill her before my wedding, at the church door, with your knife?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I don’t know whether I did or not,” said Rogojin, drily, seeming to be a little astonished at the question, and not quite taking it in.

title: The Idiot
text: “Did you never take your knife to Pavlofsk with you?”

title: The Idiot
text: “No. As to the knife,” he added, “this is all I can tell you about it. He was silent for a moment, and then said, “I took it out of the locked drawer this morning about three, for it was in the early morning all this—happened. It has been inside the book ever since—and—and—this is what is such a marvel to me, the knife only went in a couple of inches at most, just under her left breast, and there wasn’t more than half a tablespoonful of blood altogether, not more.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes—yes—yes—”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince jumped up in extraordinary agitation.

title: The Idiot
text: “I know, I know, I’ve read of that sort of thing—it’s internal haemorrhage, you know. Sometimes there isn’t a drop—if the blow goes straight to the heart—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Wait—listen!” cried Rogojin, suddenly, starting up.

title: The Idiot
text: “Somebody’s walking about, do you hear?

title: The Idiot
text: In the hall.

title: The Idiot
text: Both sat up to listen.

title: The Idiot
text: “I hear,” said the prince in a whisper, his eyes fixed on Rogojin.

title: The Idiot
text: “Footsteps?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Shall we shut the door, and lock it, or not?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, lock it.”

title: The Idiot
text: They locked the door, and both lay down again.

title: The Idiot
text: There was a long silence.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, by-the-by,” whispered the prince, hurriedly and excitedly as before, as though he had just seized hold of an idea and was afraid of losing it again.

title: The Idiot
text: “I—I wanted those cards! They say you played cards with her?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, I played with her,” said Rogojin, after a short silence.

title: The Idiot
text: “Where are the cards?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Here they are,” said Rogojin, after a still longer pause.

title: The Idiot
text: He pulled out a pack of cards, wrapped in a bit of paper, from his pocket, and handed them to the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: The latter took them, with a sort of perplexity.

title: The Idiot
text: A new, sad, helpless feeling weighed on his heart; he had suddenly realized that not only at this moment, but for a long while, he had not been saying what he wanted to say, had not been acting as he wanted to act; and that these cards which he held in his hand, and which he had been so delighted to have at first, were now of no use—no use...

title: The Idiot
text: He rose, and wrung his hands.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin lay motionless, and seemed neither to hear nor see his movements; but his eyes blazed in the darkness, and were fixed in a wild stare.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince sat down on a chair, and watched him in alarm.

title: The Idiot
text: Half an hour went by.

title: The Idiot
text: Suddenly Rogojin burst into a loud abrupt laugh, as though he had quite forgotten that they must speak in whispers.

title: The Idiot
text: “That officer, eh!—that young officer—don’t you remember that fellow at the band? Eh? Ha, ha, ha! Didn’t she whip him smartly, eh?”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince jumped up from his seat in renewed terror.

title: The Idiot
text: When Rogojin quieted down (which he did at once) the prince bent over him, sat down beside him, and with painfully beating heart and still more painful breath, watched his face intently.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin never turned his head, and seemed to have forgotten all about him.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince watched and waited.

title: The Idiot
text: Time went on—it began to grow light.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin began to wander—muttering disconnectedly; then he took to shouting and laughing.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince stretched out a trembling hand and gently stroked his hair and his cheeks—he could do nothing more.

title: The Idiot
text: His legs trembled again and he seemed to have lost the use of them.

title: The Idiot
text: A new sensation came over him, filling his heart and soul with infinite anguish.

title: The Idiot
text: Meanwhile the daylight grew full and strong; and at last the prince lay down, as though overcome by despair, and laid his face against the white, motionless face of Rogojin.

title: The Idiot
text: His tears flowed on to Rogojin’s cheek, though he was perhaps not aware of them himself.

title: The Idiot
text: At all events when, after many hours, the door was opened and people thronged in, they found the murderer unconscious and in a raging fever.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince was sitting by him, motionless, and each time that the sick man gave a laugh, or a shout, he hastened to pass his own trembling hand over his companion’s hair and cheeks, as though trying to soothe and quiet him.

title: The Idiot
text: But alas! he understood nothing of what was said to him, and recognized none of those who surrounded him.

title: The Idiot
text: If Schneider himself had arrived then and seen his former pupil and patient, remembering the prince’s condition during the first year in Switzerland, he would have flung up his hands, despairingly, and cried, as he did then:

title: The Idiot
text: “An idiot!”

title: The Idiot
text: When the widow hurried away to Pavlofsk, she went straight to Daria Alexeyevna’s house, and telling all she knew, threw her into a state of great alarm.

title: The Idiot
text: Both ladies decided to communicate at once with Lebedeff, who, as the friend and landlord of the prince, was also much agitated.

title: The Idiot
text: Vera Lebedeff told all she knew, and by Lebedeff’s advice it was decided that all three should go to Petersburg as quickly as possible, in order to avert “what might so easily happen.”

title: The Idiot
text: This is how it came about that at eleven o’clock next morning Rogojin’s flat was opened by the police in the presence of Lebedeff, the two ladies, and Rogojin’s own brother, who lived in the wing.

title: The Idiot
text: The evidence of the porter went further than anything else towards the success of Lebedeff in gaining the assistance of the police.

title: The Idiot
text: He declared that he had seen Rogojin return to the house last night, accompanied by a friend, and that both had gone upstairs very secretly and cautiously.

title: The Idiot
text: After this there was no hesitation about breaking open the door, since it could not be got open in any other way.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin suffered from brain fever for two months.

title: The Idiot
text: When he recovered from the attack he was at once brought up on trial for murder.

title: The Idiot
text: He gave full, satisfactory, and direct evidence on every point; and the prince’s name was, thanks to this, not brought into the proceedings.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin was very quiet during the progress of the trial.

title: The Idiot
text: He did not contradict his clever and eloquent counsel, who argued that the brain fever, or inflammation of the brain, was the cause of the crime; clearly proving that this malady had existed long before the murder was perpetrated, and had been brought on by the sufferings of the accused.

title: The Idiot
text: But Rogojin added no words of his own in confirmation of this view, and as before, he recounted with marvellous exactness the details of his crime.

title: The Idiot
text: He was convicted, but with extenuating circumstances, and condemned to hard labour in Siberia for fifteen years.

title: The Idiot
text: He heard his sentence grimly, silently, and thoughtfully.

title: The Idiot
text: His colossal fortune, with the exception of the comparatively small portion wasted in the first wanton period of his inheritance, went to his brother, to the great satisfaction of the latter.

title: The Idiot
text: The old lady, Rogojin’s mother, is still alive, and remembers her favourite son Parfen sometimes, but not clearly.

title: The Idiot
text: God spared her the knowledge of this dreadful calamity which had overtaken her house.

title: The Idiot
text: Lebedeff, Keller, Gania, Ptitsin, and many other friends of ours continue to live as before.

title: The Idiot
text: There is scarcely any change in them, so that there is no need to tell of their subsequent doings.

title: The Idiot
text: Hippolyte died in great agitation, and rather sooner than he expected, about a fortnight after Nastasia Philipovna’s death.

title: The Idiot
text: Colia was much affected by these events, and drew nearer to his mother in heart and sympathy.

title: The Idiot
text: Nina Alexandrovna is anxious, because he is “thoughtful beyond his years,” but he will, we think, make a useful and active man.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince’s further fate was more or less decided by Colia, who selected, out of all the persons he had met during the last six or seven months, Evgenie Pavlovitch, as friend and confidant.

title: The Idiot
text: To him he made over all that he knew as to the events above recorded, and as to the present condition of the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: He was not far wrong in his choice.

title: The Idiot
text: Evgenie Pavlovitch took the deepest interest in the fate of the unfortunate “idiot,” and, thanks to his influence, the prince found himself once more with Dr. Schneider, in Switzerland.

title: The Idiot
text: Evgenie Pavlovitch, who went abroad at this time, intending to live a long while on the continent, being, as he often said, quite superfluous in Russia, visits his sick friend at Schneider’s every few months.

title: The Idiot
text: But Dr. Schneider frowns ever more and more and shakes his head; he hints that the brain is fatally injured; he does not as yet declare that his patient is incurable, but he allows himself to express the gravest fears.

title: The Idiot
text: Evgenie takes this much to heart, and he has a heart, as is proved by the fact that he receives and even answers letters from Colia.

title: The Idiot
text: But besides this, another trait in his character has become apparent, and as it is a good trait we will make haste to reveal it.

title: The Idiot
text: After each visit to Schneider’s establishment, Evgenie Pavlovitch writes another letter, besides that to Colia, giving the most minute particulars concerning the invalid’s condition.

title: The Idiot
text: In these letters is to be detected, and in each one more than the last, a growing feeling of friendship and sympathy.

title: The Idiot
text: The individual who corresponds thus with Evgenie Pavlovitch, and who engages so much of his attention and respect, is Vera Lebedeff.

title: The Idiot
text: We have never been able to discover clearly how such relations sprang up.

title: The Idiot
text: Of course the root of them was in the events which we have already recorded, and which so filled Vera with grief on the prince’s account that she fell seriously ill.

title: The Idiot
text: But exactly how the acquaintance and friendship came about, we cannot say.

title: The Idiot
text: We have spoken of these letters chiefly because in them is often to be found some news of the Epanchin family, and of Aglaya in particular.

title: The Idiot
text: Evgenie Pavlovitch wrote of her from Paris, that after a short and sudden attachment to a certain Polish count, an exile, she had suddenly married him, quite against the wishes of her parents, though they had eventually given their consent through fear of a terrible scandal.

title: The Idiot
text: Then, after a six months’ silence, Evgenie Pavlovitch informed his correspondent, in a long letter, full of detail, that while paying his last visit to Dr. Schneider’s establishment, he had there come across the whole Epanchin family (excepting the general, who had remained in St. Petersburg) and Prince S. The meeting was a strange one.

title: The Idiot
text: They all received Evgenie Pavlovitch with effusive delight; Adelaida and Alexandra were deeply grateful to him for his “angelic kindness to the unhappy prince.”

title: The Idiot
text: Lizabetha Prokofievna, when she saw poor Muishkin, in his enfeebled and humiliated condition, had wept bitterly.

title: The Idiot
text: Apparently all was forgiven him.

title: The Idiot
text: Prince S. had made a few just and sensible remarks.

title: The Idiot
text: It seemed to Evgenie Pavlovitch that there was not yet perfect harmony between Adelaida and her fiance, but he thought that in time the impulsive young girl would let herself be guided by his reason and experience.

title: The Idiot
text: Besides, the recent events that had befallen her family had given Adelaida much to think about, especially the sad experiences of her younger sister.

title: The Idiot
text: Within six months, everything that the family had dreaded from the marriage with the Polish count had come to pass.

title: The Idiot
text: He turned out to be neither count nor exile—at least, in the political sense of the word—but had had to leave his native land owing to some rather dubious affair of the past.

title: The Idiot
text: It was his noble patriotism, of which he made a great display, that had rendered him so interesting in Aglaya’s eyes.

title: The Idiot
text: She was so fascinated that, even before marrying him, she joined a committee that had been organized abroad to work for the restoration of Poland; and further, she visited the confessional of a celebrated Jesuit priest, who made an absolute fanatic of her.

title: The Idiot
text: The supposed fortune of the count had dwindled to a mere nothing, although he had given almost irrefutable evidence of its existence to Lizabetha Prokofievna and Prince S.

title: The Idiot
text: Besides this, before they had been married half a year, the count and his friend the priest managed to bring about a quarrel between Aglaya and her family, so that it was now several months since they had seen her.

title: The Idiot
text: In a word, there was a great deal to say; but Mrs. Epanchin, and her daughters, and even Prince S., were still so much distressed by Aglaya’s latest infatuations and adventures, that they did not care to talk of them, though they must have known that Evgenie knew much of the story already.

title: The Idiot
text: Poor Lizabetha Prokofievna was most anxious to get home, and, according to Evgenie’s account, she criticized everything foreign with much hostility.

title: The Idiot
text: “They can’t bake bread anywhere, decently; and they all freeze in their houses, during winter, like a lot of mice in a cellar. At all events, I’ve had a good Russian cry over this poor fellow,” she added, pointing to the prince, who had not recognized her in the slightest degree.

title: The Idiot
text: “So enough of this nonsense; it’s time we faced the truth. All this continental life, all this Europe of yours, and all the trash about ‘going abroad’ is simply foolery, and it is mere foolery on our part to come. Remember what I say, my friend; you’ll live to agree with me yourself.”

title: The Idiot
text: So spoke the good lady, almost angrily, as she took leave of Evgenie Pavlovitch.
